Title: Modeling Learner Behavior in Vocational E-learning Environments Using Machine Learning and Educational Data Mining
Source title: Proceedings of 2025 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Education, ICAIE 2025
Affiliations: Shandong Vocational and Technical University of International Studies, Shandong, Rizhao, China
Authors with affiliations: Fu H., Shandong Vocational and Technical University of International Studies, Shandong, Rizhao, China; Zhang L., Shandong Vocational and Technical University of International Studies, Shandong, Rizhao, China
Abstract: The rapid expansion of vocational e-learning platforms has generated vast amounts of multimodal data on learner interactions. Effectively modeling these behaviors is critical for identifying at-risk students, personalizing learning paths, and improving educational outcomes. This paper proposes an interpretable predictive framework that integrates machine learning (ML) and educational data mining (EDM) techniques to analyze vocational learners’ behaviors. The study utilizes a comprehensive dataset from a simulated vocational e-learning environment, combining traditional engagement metrics with emerging multimodal data sources. Several ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), are employed and enhanced with Explainable AI (XAI) techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that the XGBoost model with SHAP explanation achieves the highest predictive accuracy (91.3%) and F1-score (0.895). The analysis identifies consistent engagement patterns, timely assignment submission, and video interaction behaviors as the most significant predictors. Furthermore, the study introduces a multimodal data framework that correlates behavioral patterns with performance metrics, providing actionable insights for educational interventions. This research offers educators a tool for early identification of at-risk students and contributes to the development of adaptive learning technologies in vocational education. © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Author full names: Vadiee, Farhad (57713062700); Liu, Qinyi (58575526900); Khalil, Mohammad (57002304100)
Title: ORCHID-RANKER: An Agentic Adaptive Recommender for Education with Privacy Guarantees
Source title: Proceedings of the ACM Symposium on Applied Computing
Affiliations: Centre for the Science of Learning and Technology (SLATE), University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway
Authors with affiliations: Vadiee F., Centre for the Science of Learning and Technology (SLATE), University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway; Liu Q., Centre for the Science of Learning and Technology (SLATE), University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway; Khalil M., Centre for the Science of Learning and Technology (SLATE), University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway
Abstract: Digital learning platforms often recommend what activity a student should do next. They usually base this on a few simple signals, such as whether the student accepted the activity, answered correctly, and how long it took. These systems are often complex and hard for teachers to understand or control, and they also need to protect student privacy. We present ORCHID-RANKER, a simple decision module that can be added to existing recommenders in such platforms without changing them. It keeps track of three things for each learner: how ready they seem (knowledge), how willing they seem (engagement), and how uncertain the system is. Using this information, it adjusts a few simple "dials": how difficult the next activities should be, how much to explore new content, how varied the list of activities is, and how many activities to show. The goal is to keep learners in a "just right"zone where tasks are not too easy and not too hard, and to keep them engaged. Behind this decision module, the underlying models are trained with strong privacy protection (differential privacy), so that individual students cannot be easily identified from the data. In simulations on two real course datasets (OULAD and EdNet), ORCHID-RANKER led to higher learning and engagement than standard recommendation methods, while still maintaining formal privacy guarantees.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: A Study on the Innovative Model of Integrating AI into Fundamental Foreign Language Education
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Generative Artificial Intelligence and Education, GAIE 2026
Affiliations: School of Foreign Languages, Shenyang Jianzhu University, Liaoning, Shenyang, China
Authors with affiliations: Song Y., School of Foreign Languages, Shenyang Jianzhu University, Liaoning, Shenyang, China
Abstract: This study proposes and implements an innovative artificial intelligence (AI) system tailored for foundational foreign language education, aiming to provide a practical, scalable, and technology-driven solution for traditional language instruction. The engine adopts a modular architecture that deeply integrates state-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) techniques with adaptive learning algorithms. Its core technical stack comprises three key components: (1) a speech recognition and pronunciation assessment module based on the Wav2Vec 2.0 pre-trained model combined with a Transformer architecture; (2) a personalized learning path recommendation engine that fuses Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) with collaborative filtering algorithms; and (3) a real-time feedback and interaction module that combines a rule-based engine with a fine-tuned large language model (LLM). The entire system is deployed on a local educational cloud platform and seamlessly integrates with mainstream Learning Management Systems (LMS) via RESTful APIs. To evaluate the technical efficacy and pedagogical value of the AI engine, the study conducted an 8-week controlled A/B test involving 32 students. Quantitative analysis revealed that, compared to the baseline system, the optimized AI engine demonstrated superior performance across multiple key technical metrics: the average system response time was reduced to 760 milliseconds, and the average CPU utilization rate was only 32.4%. Moreover, its intelligent features significantly enhanced instructional outcomes, as evidenced by a 27.3% increase in exercise completion rate, a 26.4% rise in the adoption rate of error-correction suggestions, and a high alignment (Jaccard coefficient of 0.81) between the system-generated content and the knowledge points assessed by instructors. Learning outcome assessments further confirmed that students in the experimental group showed significant improvement across all four language skills—listening, speaking, reading, and writing—with the most notable gain observed in speaking proficiency (+15.7%). This study not only empirically demonstrates the positive value of AI in foreign language education but, more importantly, constructs and validates a lightweight, modular, and reusable AI-powered instructional technology stack. This achievement provides a robust technical paradigm and practical reference for resource-constrained educational settings—such as primary and secondary schools—and significantly advances the deep integration of information technology and language education from conceptual vision toward large-scale implementation. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Generalised Distillation of Geospatial Foundation Models

Authors with affiliations: Said A., Research Ireland Centre for Research Training in Machine Learning, Dublin City University, Dublin, Ireland; Dietlmeier J., Insight Research Ireland Centre for Data Analytics, Dublin City University, Dublin, Ireland; McCaul M., Insight Research Ireland Centre for Data Analytics, Dublin City University, Dublin, Ireland; O’Connor N., Research Ireland Centre for Research Training in Machine Learning, Dublin City University, Dublin, Ireland, Insight Research Ireland Centre for Data Analytics, Dublin City University, Dublin, Ireland
Abstract: Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) are large-scale models with millions of parameters, pre-trained on vast amounts of data to support diverse downstream tasks. However, they are typically computationally demanding, which restricts deployment in resource-limited environments. Furthermore, they are predominantly trained using optical data despite the inherent limitations of this modality due to natural phenomena such as cloud cover and atmospheric conditions. Our work aims to leverage multiple modalities by specifically transferring knowledge from a multimodal teacher using optical and radar data, to train a radar-only student model. To ensure computational efficiency, we apply offline feature-based knowledge distillation to a frozen TerraMind-B teacher to compress its multimodal knowledge into a lightweight unimodal TerraMind-S student model. Despite using a smaller student architecture, our distillation approach outperforms TerraMind’s state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on radar data. In particular, we obtain an improvement in mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 11.11% and 2.29% on the Crop Type Mapping South Sudan and Sen1Floods11 datasets, respectively. Lastly, we find that the later layers are more important in enhancing the performance of the student model and that distillation performance is thematically dependent. Title: Using LLMs for Knowledge Component-Level Correctness Labeling in Open-Ended Coding Problems
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, United States
Authors with affiliations: Duan Z., University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, United States; Kankaria A., University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, United States; Kartik D., University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, United States; Lan A.S., University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, United States
Abstract: Fine-grained skill representations, commonly referred to as knowledge components (KCs), are fundamental to many approaches in student modeling and learning analytics. However, KC-level correctness labels are rarely available in real-world datasets, especially for open-ended programming tasks where solutions typically involve multiple KCs simultaneously. Simply propagating problem-level correctness to all associated KCs obscures partial mastery and often leads to poorly fitted learning curves. To address this challenge, we propose an automated framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to label KC-level correctness directly from student-written code. Our method assesses whether each KC is correctly applied and further introduces a temporal context-aware Code-KC mapping mechanism to better align KCs with individual student code. We evaluate the resulting KC-level correctness labels in terms of learning curve fit and predictive performance using the power law of practice and the Additive Factors Model. Experimental results show that our framework leads to learning curves that are more consistent with cognitive theory and improves predictive performance, compared to baselines. Human evaluation further demonstrates substantial agreement between LLM and expert annotations. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Rubric-Grounded LLM Feedback Framework for Academic Writing: An Empirical Study in an Information-Enhanced Classroom Setting
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Big Data and Informatization Education, ICBDIE 2026
Affiliations: School of Marxism, Northeastern University, Liaoning, Shenyang, China
Authors with affiliations: Liang T., School of Marxism, Northeastern University, Liaoning, Shenyang, China; Chen D., School of Marxism, Northeastern University, Liaoning, Shenyang, China; Cui X., School of Marxism, Northeastern University, Liaoning, Shenyang, China
Abstract: Artificial intelligence-based writing feedback has been increasingly adopted in higher education to address constraints related to instructional time and feedback scalability; however, its effectiveness is often undermined by weak alignment with course evaluation standards. To address this limitation, this study empirically examines whether embedding assessment rubrics as explicit constraints in artificial intelligence-generated feedback can improve academic writing outcomes in an informatization education context. A rubric-constrained feedback framework was implemented in an undergraduate academic writing course using a quasi-experimental design (N=66), in which students were assigned to either an experimental group receiving rubric-constrained feedback or a control group receiving unconstrained feedback. Writing performance was measured through score improvements between initial and final drafts, while feedback quality was independently evaluated by instructors. The results show that the experimental group achieved significantly greater overall writing improvement than the control group (t(64)=4.36, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.98), with dimension-level analyses revealing stronger gains in argumentation, text organization, and evidence use. In addition, instructor ratings indicate that rubric-constrained feedback outperforms unconstrained feedback in alignment with evaluation standards, specificity, and practical usability (all p<0.01), demonstrating large effect sizes in key dimensions. These findings suggest that assessment rubrics serve as an effective mediating mechanism between instructional objectives and artificial intelligence-generated feedback, and that embedding artificial intelligence tools within established evaluation frameworks can substantially enhance both learning outcomes and feedback quality, offering practical guidance for data-driven instructional design in informatization education. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Using Artificial Intelligence in Mobile Learning for Students of Technical Specialties
Source title: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies
Affiliations: Oles Honchar Dnipro National University, Dnipro, Ukraine; Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski,”, Sofia, Bulgaria; Technical University “Metinvest Polytechnic” LLC, Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine; National University “Zaporizhzhia Polytechnic,”, Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine

Abstract: Mobile learning has emerged as a pivotal method of education in Ukraine and Eastern Europe, especially in the conditions of war and displacement of students, which allows continuing education of technical students despite the lack of infrastructure and logistics. The research examined the effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced mobile learning among students at three higher education institutions (HEIs): Sofia University St. Kliment Ohridski (Bulgaria), Metinvest Polytechnic Technical University (Ukraine), and National University Zaporizhzhia Polytechnic (Ukraine). The participants in a quasi-experimental study were 183 students, most of whom were in computer science, engineering, mathematics, and applied mechanics. Half were assigned to the experimental group using AI-built mobile learning, and the other half to the control group using standard mobile platforms. The AI-driven platform included adaptive testing, AI-based chatbot tutoring, solution explanation, a recommendation system, and learning analytics. Findings showed that AI had more positive effects (learning gains of 18%, p < 0.05) on learning outcomes, engagement, and time-on-task, and was perceived as more usable and associated with higher self-efficacy among students. The most useful features were adaptive testing and recommendation systems, which facilitated personal and self-managed learning. The results provide insight into the practical importance of AI tools in technical education, showing that they offer scalable solutions for enhancing academic performance, engagement, and resilience in both stable and crisis-affected learning settings. © 2026 by the authors of this article. Abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence technology has enabled large language models to demonstrate significant potential in vocational education, particularly in teaching quality assurance and personalized guidance. This study analyzes the application pathways and pedagogical effectiveness of large language models using the Digital Production and Control Technology course as a case study. Comparative experimental results demonstrate that students receiving large language model-assisted instruction significantly outperformed those receiving traditional teaching methods in academic achievement, learning satisfaction, and learning engagement. Large language models enhanced teaching quality through personalized content recommendation, learning behavior analysis, and intelligent assessment. Their applications encompass instructional assistance, learning analytics, and intelligent evaluation, enabling teachers to acquire resources, monitor student progress, provide feedback, and automatically assess student performance. The research recommends strengthening the application of large language models in vocational education, developing personalized learning resources, and improving learning analytics and feedback mechanisms to enhance vocational engineering education quality.  © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: The Limits of Text-Only LLMs for Think-Aloud Transcript Correction: A Multimodal Comparison in the Context of a Puzzle Video Game
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, United States; University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, United States
Authors with affiliations: Eshgarf N., University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, United States; Carpenter Z., University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, United States; Anderson C.G., University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, United States
Abstract: Think-aloud protocols provide valuable insights into learners’ reasoning, but transcribing verbal data is time-consuming. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) can reduce this burden but can also introduce errors. By analyzing 1,900 utterances from six English think-aloud transcripts of university students playing a puzzle game, we compared text-only and multimodal audio/video approaches to explore whether large language models (LLMs) can correct these errors. Three researchers created reference transcripts by reviewing original audio and video recordings. We compared four prompting strategies with Claude Sonnet 4.5 (text-only) and Gemini 2.5 Flash (multimodal). This identified text-detectable errors (13.6% of utterances), correctable using domain context (game rules and terminology), and Audio/Video-Dependent errors (7.6%) requiring the original recording. For text-detectable errors, all text-only strategies achieved high precision (86–90%) and specificity (>97%). Few-shot with extended thinking achieved the highest recall (89.1%), significantly outperforming zero-shot (84.0%, p=.026). The text-only approach matched the multimodal model on text-detectable errors (89.1% vs. 86.8%, p=.440). A direct re-transcription condition (audio/video only, no source text) achieved substantially lower accuracy (82.8%) and missed 8.5% of utterances, demonstrating that correction-based workflows outperform re-transcription. However, the multimodal approach was essential for Audio/Video-Dependent errors (55.2% vs. ∼2% recall, p<.001). These findings suggest that text-only LLMs can effectively reduce transcript-correction effort, whereas multimodal approaches are necessary when higher accuracy is required. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Unified Explainable Predictive Analytics Pipeline for Learning Management Systems
Source title: SN Computer Science
Affiliations: University Department of Computer Science, Mumbai University, Mumbai, India; Somaiya School of Basic and Applied Sciences, Somaiya Vidyavihar University, Mumbai, India
Authors with affiliations: Pawar M., University Department of Computer Science, Mumbai University, Mumbai, India, Somaiya School of Basic and Applied Sciences, Somaiya Vidyavihar University, Mumbai, India; Dongardive J., University Department of Computer Science, Mumbai University, Mumbai, India
Abstract: High student attrition and inconsistent academic performance remain persistent challenges in higher education, motivating the development of reliable and interpretable predictive decision-support systems. Learning Management Systems (LMS) generate rich behavioural and assessment data; however, existing predictive learning analytics studies often exhibit limited generalizability and insufficient explainability. This study proposes a unified predictive analytics pipeline for LMS data that integrates systematic preprocessing, feature engineering and selection, multi-model benchmarking, handling of class imbalance, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The study benchmarks classical Machine Learning (ML), Ensemble, and Deep Learning (DL) models on two heterogeneous LMS datasets: OULAD for binary dropout prediction and Offee for multi-class grade prediction. Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) is used to alleviate the issue of class imbalance, and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) give both global and instance-level explanations. Experimental results show that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model achieved an accuracy of 0.91 for OULAD binary dropout prediction, and Random Forest (RF) achieved an accuracy of 0.78 for Offee multi-class grade prediction. The proposed pipeline operationalises a complete predict–explain–act educational workflow that combines imbalance-aware prediction with intervention-oriented explainability within a unified decision-support architecture. Unlike prior studies focusing primarily on isolated prediction models and standalone interpretability, the proposed methodology provides cross-dataset validation, operational explainability, and actionable educational analytics suitable for early-warning and academic intervention support systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Title: Edge AI-Enabled PMU Event Classification With Knowledge Distillation and Federated Learning

Abstract: Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) enable analysis and classification of events and abnormalities in modern power systems. However, in large and geographically dispersed networks, centralizing PMU data streams for sub-second decisions is hindered by cross-regional data-sharing restrictions, multi-layer aggregation, as well as communication delays and jitter. Purely local training at the network edge on the PMU devices themselves can avoid these bottlenecks but lacks exposure to diverse operating conditions, leading to suboptimal models. This tension calls for methods that retain data locality and privacy while sharing knowledge efficiently. To this end, this paper proposes an edge AI framework that integrates knowledge distillation and federated learning, driven by the core requirement of different data-sharing constraints. First, we assume a trusted data center, where we develop a large language model-based teacher model that is fine-tuned on global data and efficiently transfers knowledge into student models trained locally via knowledge distillation. Next, we relax such an assumption and design a fair federated learning framework that exchanges gradient information among edge models while enforcing Pareto-optimal fairness to ensure stable and balanced performance. We also customize a lightweight neural network tailored for on-device deployment. With fewer than 5,000 parameters, the model adopts a compact end-to-end architecture to effectively characterize temporal dynamics and frequency-domain information in PMU time series, thereby achieving both high efficiency and strong representational capability. Experiments conducted on real-world PMU measurements demonstrate the superior performance of our framework, and ablation studies further confirm the unique contributions of each design component. © 2010 IEEE.

Title: Construction and Practical Evaluation of a Pharmacovigilance Course Teaching Model Integrating Knowledge Graph and Artificial Intelligence-Based on a Blended Learning Environment

Abstract: This study systematically explores the integrated application model and practical effects of Knowledge Graph and Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in pharmacovigilance course instruction. Leveraging the “Xueyin Online” platform, a novel teaching framework was constructed, featuring a multimodal “Knowledge Graph” as its core, an “AI Workbench” for intelligent support, and a blended online-offline teaching approach. This model systematically reconstructs the pharmacovigilance knowledge network through various visualization forms, aiding students in establishing a structured cognitive system. Utilizing functions such as the AI Teaching Assistant, AI Practice modules, and AI Learning Analytics, it provides personalized learning support and enables data-driven formative assessment. Offline teaching focuses on case studies and scenario simulations, further strengthening knowledge transfer and practical problem-solving skills. A post-course questionnaire survey of 35 pharmacy-related undergraduates showed students gave highly positive evaluations of the Knowledge Graph and AI applications (average score: 4.43/5). The research indicates that the deep integration of Knowledge Graph and AI technologies facilitates a pedagogical shift from “knowledge-based classrooms” to “competency-based classrooms” and from “lecture-based instruction” to “dialogic classrooms,” achieves an organic unity of knowledge impartation, competency cultivation, and value guidance. This study provides an actionable practical pathway for the reform of higher pharmaceutical education in the digital era and offers empirical reference for the deep integration of intelligent technologies with professional education. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: Student dropout remains a critical challenge in global education, representing a significant loss of human capital. Although data-driven approaches like predictive modeling have achieved high accuracy in identifying at-risk students, a “trust gap” persists among educators. Prediction alone is insufficient; stakeholders require interpretable insights to guide effective intervention. This survey explores the paradigm shift from passive “black-box” detection to “actionable prescription” through the lens of Counterfactual Explanations (CFE). We analyze 23 primary studies published between 2021 and 2026, categorizing them using a novel Intervention Pipeline taxonomy that bridges four levels: Identification (predictive models), Interpretation (XAI), Visual Analytics (interactive visualization and human-in-the-loop analysis), and Actionable Recommendations (counterfactuals). Adopting an analytical framework, we systematically interrogate the literature regarding variable risk definitions, data source diversity, prediction horizons, and feature actionability. Our analysis reveals a critical disconnect: while many models prioritize accuracy using immutable features, few focus on the actionable variables necessary for generating feasible pedagogical recommendations. We conclude that while CFE offers a promising path for personalized support, future research must address challenges regarding causal validity, explanation stability, and scalability (individual vs. institutional) to successfully bridge the gap between algorithmic output and practical pedagogical action. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Towards Human-Centered Large Language Models for Personalized Programming Education
Source title: ICER 2026 - Proceedings of the ACM Conference on International Computing Education Research Vol.2
Affiliations: Aalto University, Espoo, Finland
Authors with affiliations: Fan J., Aalto University, Espoo, Finland
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computing education to support programming practice and generate explanations [5, 9]. However, current LLM-based systems are not pedagogically aligned and fail to adapt to learners' prior knowledge, often producing feedback that is too advanced or oversimplified [8].Recent evidence also suggests that LLMs do not consistently outperform traditional machine learning approaches for fine-grained educational tasks, highlighting the need to better understand when and how LLMs should be used. This research aims to develop human-centered LLMs for programming education by leveraging student modeling data, including knowledge states and learning processes. We explore prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning to improve pedagogical effectiveness and enable scalable personalized support.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education, yet evidence concerning its relationship with academic performance remains fragmented across adoption studies, predictive models and evaluations of learning outcomes. This study maps and synthesises Scopus-indexed research published between 2020 and 2025. A bibliometric analysis of 84 records was conducted using VOSviewer and Microsoft Excel, while 29 eligible studies were examined through a PRISMA-guided systematic review and structured content analysis. The review analysed publication patterns, influential contributors, AI application types, educational purposes, research designs, outcome measures and theoretical frameworks. The findings show rapid publication growth, strong reliance on quantitative and predictive designs, and increasing attention to generative AI, adaptive learning, and learning analytics. However, evidence of improved academic performance varies according to whether studies measured perceptions, prediction accuracy, correlations or direct learning outcomes. Important gaps remain in the limited use of pedagogical frameworks, including TPACK, and the scarcity of experimental, longitudinal, and geographically diverse research. The study contributes an outcome-centred synthesis that connects bibliometric patterns with the methodological and pedagogical strengths of the available evidence. © The Authors.

Title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Learning Systems: A Reinforcement Learning Framework with LLM-Powered Assessment for Personalized Online Education and study
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Big Data and Informatization Education, ICBDIE 2026
Affiliations: School of Computer Science, Hubei University, Hubei, Wuhan, China
Authors with affiliations: Ma C., School of Computer Science, Hubei University, Hubei, Wuhan, China; Tan R., School of Computer Science, Hubei University, Hubei, Wuhan, China; Yu S., School of Computer Science, Hubei University, Hubei, Wuhan, China
Abstract: Online education platforms face persistent challenges in delivering effective personalized learning at scale. Current approaches suffer from three critical limitations: (1) inadequate evaluation frameworks that fail to capture multi-dimensional pedagogical capabilities of large language models across varying difficulty levels, (2) static learning path generation that ignores individual student states and temporal knowledge dynamics, and (3) isolated single-agent architectures that lack collaborative intelligence for sustained engagement and knowledge retention. We propose AMALS (Adaptive Multi-Agent Learning Systems), a hierarchical framework integrating LLM assessment, reinforcement learning-based optimization, and multi-agent collaboration. Our approach introduces three key innovations: (1) a difficulty-adaptive evaluation mechanism with exponential decay modeling for robust LLM selection, (2) a Markov Decision Process formulation with composite reward functions balancing immediate gains and long-term retention, and (3) a three-agent collaborative architecture (Tutor-Peer-Evaluator) with dynamic contribution rebalancing. Extensive experiments on simulated student populations demonstrate that AMALS achieves 15-20% improvement in learning performance, 30% higher engagement retention over 30 sessions, and 72% knowledge retention after 30 days compared to single-agent baselines. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Prompt-stable knowledge distillation of vision-language models for efficient waste classification in material recovery facilities
Source title: Resources, Conservation and Recycling
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Monash University, VIC 3800, Melbourne, Australia; Faculty of Science and Technology, Charles Darwin University, Darwin, NT 0909, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Malla H.J., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Monash University, VIC 3800, Melbourne, Australia; Bazli M., Faculty of Science and Technology, Charles Darwin University, Darwin, NT 0909, Australia; Arashpour M., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Monash University, VIC 3800, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: Waste classification in material recovery facilities is difficult to scale due to limited labelled data and the high variability in waste appearance. Vision-language models address these challenges through strong zero-shot performance when supported by well-designed prompt engineering, enabling high accuracy without task-specific fine-tuning. However, their large size, architectural complexity, slow inference speed, and sensitivity to the wording of text descriptions limit their suitability for real-time sorting environments. This study introduces a knowledge distillation framework that transfers the semantic capability of large vision-language models into compact student models. A key innovation is a hybrid prompt learning strategy in which the teacher model uses detailed, optimized textual descriptions while the student model learns from simple, generic prompts during distillation. This design improves the student model’s stability across varied textual descriptions and reduces the need for dynamic prompting to accommodate differences in waste appearance. Experiments on a multi-class waste dataset show that the best distilled student model surpasses the strongest teacher by over 13 % in classification accuracy, improves prompt stability by 79.5 %, and achieves 84.2 % faster inference with 80.0 % lower architectural complexity. The resulting model addresses key practical limitations of vision-language models for waste classification, delivering a complete, practical solution for real-time sorting in material recovery facilities. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Liu J.; Cheng Y.
Title: The Influence of Digital Literacy on Innovative Behavior among Primary and Secondary School Teachers in the AI Era
Source title: CTSD 2026, Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Computer Technology and Sustainable Development
Affiliations: School of Management, Sanda University, Shanghai, China
Authors with affiliations: Liu J., School of Management, Sanda University, Shanghai, China; Cheng Y., School of Management, Sanda University, Shanghai, China
Abstract: In the era of artificial intelligence, digital technologies such as generative AI, large language models, multimodal learning analytics, virtual reality, and the educational metaverse are profoundly reshaping the education ecosystem, with teachers' innovative behavior serving as a core driving force for educational transformation. This study investigates the mechanism through which digital literacy among primary and secondary school teachers influences their innovative behavior, with a specific focus on the mediating role of work autonomy. Adopting a quantitative research approach, the study conducted a questionnaire survey among 162 K-12 teachers in China and analyzed the data using SPSS. The findings indicate that teachers' digital literacy significantly and positively impacts their innovative behavior, while work autonomy plays a partial mediating role in this relationship. Based on the findings, this paper proposes the construction of a synergistic "capacity cultivation-technological empowerment-institutional incentive"framework to advance in-depth innovation among K-12 teachers in the AI era. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: Interpretability in Knowledge Tracing (KT) is crucial for personalized learning. Current mainstream Deep Learning-based KT (DLKT) achieves strong predictive performance with ID-based representations, but students’ latent knowledge states remain opaque to teachers and learners. Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate human-readable text, but explanations from existing LLM-augmented KT approaches are either detached from the predictive state or insensitive to individual trajectories. To bridge this gap, we propose Interpretable Knowledge Tracing via Explicit–Implicit Alignment (IKT-EIA), which anchors implicit student knowledge representations with LLM-derived explicit textual insights. IKT-EIA consists of: (1) Context-Guided Knowledge Integration (CGKI) uses LLMs to generate trajectory-aware textual knowledge from student metadata; (2) Query-Driven Knowledge State Alignment (QKSA) treats the implicit state as a query to retrieve and fuse explicit semantics, producing an aligned knowledge state that supports subsequent explanation analysis; (3) Personalized Explainability Adaptation (PEA) generates structured and adaptive feedback by reading the aligned state together with raw interaction records, tailoring explanations to students’ evolving mastery. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that IKT-EIA maintains competitive predictive performance while producing state-aware explanations that were found useful in a controlled evaluation setting. © 2026

Title: MoL: Mixture of Layers in Cross-Tokenizer embedding model distillation
Source title: Knowledge-Based Systems
Affiliations: Hanoi University of Science and Technology, No. 1, Dai Co Viet road, Hanoi, Viet Nam; Australian National University, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Vu H.A., Hanoi University of Science and Technology, No. 1, Dai Co Viet road, Hanoi, Viet Nam; Truong M.-P., Hanoi University of Science and Technology, No. 1, Dai Co Viet road, Hanoi, Viet Nam; Vu T., Australian National University, Australia; Van L.N., Hanoi University of Science and Technology, No. 1, Dai Co Viet road, Hanoi, Viet Nam
Abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a powerful technique for compressing large text embedding models into smaller, more efficient ones. However, KD in the embedding space remains challenging, not only due to tokenizer mismatches between teacher and student models (Cross-Tokenizer KD—CTKD), but also because of fundamental architectural differences. These discrepancies often lead to representational misalignment, resulting in high distillation loss that degrades student performance. To address this, we propose a similarity-based functional distillation framework that dynamically aligns a particular student layer to a weighted mixture of teacher layers, based on representational similarity. This flexible alignment mechanism produces softer, semantically closer distillation targets, which reduces loss magnitude. Moreover, the student model can absorb more knowledge from multiple teacher layers rather than only one layer. We evaluate our method by distilling leading embedding models—LLM2Vec, BGE-M3, and Qwen3-Embedding into multiple student models (TinyBERT-4L, TinyBERT-6L, and BERTBASE) across a range of embedding-centric tasks, including text classification, sentence-pair classification, and semantic textual similarity. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing CTKD baselines (1–2% improvements), yielding smaller student models with improved accuracy and representation quality. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Publisher-Built Generative AI Assistants in U.S. Higher Education: A Critical Review and a Reproducible TRIAD–JTBD Evaluation Framework
Source title: Algorithms
Affiliations: Department of Business Technology, Miami Herbert Business School, University of Miami, Coral Gables, 33146, FL, United States
Authors with affiliations: Leon M., Department of Business Technology, Miami Herbert Business School, University of Miami, Coral Gables, 33146, FL, United States
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped higher education over six decades, evolving from drill-and-practice programs to adaptive cognitive tutors and, most recently, transformer-based generative models. This article presents a critical review of publisher-built generative AI assistants, adopting an explicitly socio-technical perspective that combines a technological lens with a pedagogical one. It makes three contributions. First, it synthesizes the technical and algorithmic evolution of educational AI, from rule-based and expert systems through knowledge tracing and learning analytics to large language models and retrieval-augmented generation, and organizes these mechanisms into a taxonomy. Second, it introduces a reproducible evaluation framework that couples the TRIAD rubric (Trust, Relevance, Impact, Adoption, and Design) with a Jobs-to-Be-Done (JTBD) lens, complete with anchored scoring criteria, an evidence-and-confidence grading scheme, and reported inter-rater reliability. Third, it applies the framework to eleven assistants released by U.S. publishers, distinguishing peer-reviewed evidence from institutional reports and commercial claims. The analysis reflects a mid-2025 snapshot and is presented as a reusable template rather than a static ranking. Findings reveal substantial variation in privacy safeguards, curricular alignment, documented impact, adoption, and usability. The review identifies application scenarios and recommendations for researchers and institutional leaders seeking to guide the responsible integration of AI in higher education. © 2026 by the author.

Title: From knowledge gaps to learning opportunities: Leveraging student questions and dual use of generative AI to support student learning at scale
Source title: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence

Abstract: University courses with hundreds of students have become common, particularly during early years of university studies. The sheer scale of these courses limits traditional instruction, shifting it towards a one-to-many mode of delivery. This shift reduces student–instructor interaction and tailored instructor feedback which are crucial for student success. Automated feedback systems allow scaling feedback, but they often reduce instructor contributions to student learning. This paper investigates how emerging technologies can support, rather than replace, instructors in tailoring their teaching and feedback to identify and correct student knowledge gaps at scale. To address this challenge, the paper introduces a novel technological solution: the Knowledge Gaps to Mastery (KG2M) approach. KG2M combines discussion forum data with course-specific content and leverages large language models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for the dual purpose of identifying prevalent class-level knowledge gaps and transforming them into targeted learning activities and formative assessments. The approach was deployed across three computer science courses with a combined enrollment of 1,355 students and evaluated through semi-structured interviews with five instructors. Results indicate that instructors found the tool intuitive and pedagogically valuable, particularly for surfacing knowledge gaps and generating actionable teaching insights. The paper reports on the tool, the evaluation, and the current limitations of the approach that emerged during instructor evaluation. © 2025 The Authors.

Abstract: The pervasive integration of artificial intelligence across e-commerce ecosystems has fundamentally transformed the competitive landscape, rendering systematic and reproducible platform evaluation frameworks an operational necessity rather than an academic exercise. Conventional multi-criteria decision analysis approaches for e-commerce evaluation remain structurally constrained by their dependency on human expert panels, which introduce recruitment costs, cognitive biases, limited reproducibility, and the practical infeasibility of assembling genuinely multidisciplinary panels spanning e-commerce strategy, machine learning engineering, and financial technology simultaneously. This study proposes a novel decision support framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM) multi-agent simulation with the Best–Worst Method (BWM) to derive reproducible priority weights for AI-driven e-commerce platform evaluation within a rigorous business intelligence architecture. Twelve domain-differentiated LLM agents—organized into three expertise groups representing e-commerce management, AI and machine learning technology, and digital payment systems—were instantiated with structured system prompts encoding professional domain knowledge and deployed across three independent simulation rounds to perform BWM pairwise comparisons across a comprehensive six-dimensional, 30-sub-criterion evaluation hierarchy. Inter-agent consensus was synthesized through geometric mean aggregation, with consistency verification conducted via BWM’s xi* indicator and inter-round stability assessed through coefficient of variation analysis. Results reveal that Transaction Security and Trust achieves the highest dimension-level weight (w = 0.248), followed by AI Recommendation Effectiveness (w = 0.213), with Personal Data Protection (G = 0.0750), Recommendation Accuracy (G = 0.0607), and Transaction Transparency (G = 0.0549) emerging as the three highest globally ranked sub-criteria. The aggregated consistency indicator xi* = 0.062 confirms logical coherence of the multi-agent judgment consensus, and all dimension weights exhibit CV values below 2.8%, demonstrating exceptional inter-round stability. Spearman rank correlations among the three domain-expertise groups exceed 0.92, confirming strong inter-group convergence. Sensitivity analysis under perturbations of ±10% and ±20% demonstrates that the top-five priority indicators are structurally stable. This study establishes LLM multi-agent BWM simulation as a methodologically rigorous, institutionally accessible, and computationally reproducible alternative to traditional expert elicitation for complex platform evaluation tasks. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: This research explores the conceptualization, development, and deployment of an innovative learning analytics tool, leveraging OpenAI’s GPT-4 model to quantify student engagement, map learning progression, and evaluate diverse instructional strategies within an educational context. By analyzing critical data points such as students’ stress levels, curiosity, confusion, agitation, topic preferences, and study methods, the tool provides a comprehensive view of the learning environment. It also employs Bloom’s taxonomy to assess cognitive development based on student inquiries. In addition to technical evaluation through synthetic data, feedback from a survey of teaching faculty at the University of Iowa was collected to gauge perceived benefits and challenges. Faculty recognized the tool’s potential to enhance instructional decision-making through real-time insights but expressed concerns about data security and the accuracy of AI-generated insights. The study outlines the design, implementation, and evaluation of the tool, highlighting its contributions to educational outcomes, practical integration within learning management systems, and future refinements needed to address privacy and accuracy concerns. This research underscores AI’s role in shaping personalized, data-driven education. © The Author(s) 2025.

Title: From Prediction to Stewardship: Framing Educational Data Science in the Age of Generative AI
Source title: Information (Switzerland)

Abstract: As generative AI expands the technical frontiers of prediction, measurement, and design, a growing tension has emerged between algorithmic fluency and institutional trust. This conceptual article offers a narrative synthesis of recent work in learning analytics, educational data science, human–AI interaction, and AI governance to propose stewardship as a necessary fourth paradigm of educational data science. Stewardship represents the professional, epistemic, and institutional work of governing judgment in an environment where analytic systems are increasingly generative and persuasive. Rather than treating stewardship as a general ethics checklist, the article positions it as the governance of epistemic and pedagogical authority: who determines what counts as evidence, interpretation, and educational action when AI systems help produce those judgments. The synthesis suggests that while GenAI can support bounded analytic tasks, evidence for systemic educational transformation remains limited and uneven. The field’s primary challenge is therefore not technical performance alone, but the governance of interpretation, validation, delegation, and action. By centering provenance, uncertainty, accountable oversight, learner agency, and institutional learning, stewardship provides an actionable framework for anchoring analytic innovation in responsible educational improvement. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: What Students Ask, How a Generative AI Assistant Responds: Exploring Higher Education Students’ Dialogues on Learning Analytics Feedback
Source title: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, LAK 2026
Affiliations: UCL Knowledge Lab, University College London, London, United Kingdom; UCL Knowledge Lab, UCL Centre for Artificial Intelligence, University College London, London, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Uzun Y., UCL Knowledge Lab, University College London, London, United Kingdom; Gauthier A., UCL Knowledge Lab, University College London, London, United Kingdom; Cukurova M., UCL Knowledge Lab, UCL Centre for Artificial Intelligence, University College London, London, United Kingdom
Abstract: Learning analytics dashboards (LADs) aim to support students’ regulation of learning by translating complex data into feedback. Yet students, especially those with lower self-regulated learning (SRL) competence, often struggle to engage with and interpret analytics feedback. Conversational generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) assistants have shown potential to scaffold this process through real-time, personalised, dialogue-based support. Further advancing this potential, we explored authentic dialogues between students and GenAI assistant integrated into LAD during a 10-week semester. The analysis focused on questions students with different SRL levels posed, the relevance and quality of the assistant’s answers, and how students perceived the assistant’s role in their learning. Findings revealed distinct query patterns. While low SRL students sought clarification and reassurance, high SRL students queried technical aspects and requested personalised strategies. The assistant provided clear and reliable explanations but limited in personalisation, handling emotionally charged queries, and integrating multiple data points for tailored responses. Findings further extend that GenAI interventions can be especially valuable for low SRL students, offering scaffolding that supports engagement with feedback and narrows gaps with their higher SRL peers. At the same time, students’ reflections underscored the importance of trust, need for greater adaptivity, context-awareness, and technical refinement in future systems. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: Motivation: Accurately identifying compound–protein interactions (CPIs) is critical for accelerating drug discovery. Recent deep learning methods have achieved impressive results, yet they primarily focus on local structures and neighborhood information, often overlooking high-order interaction patterns shared among similar molecules. Results: In this paper, we propose HKD-CPI, a high-order knowledge-enhanced inductive framework designed to improve generalization to unseen compound–protein pairs. Specifically, HKD-CPI introduces a molecular graph tokenization mechanism that aligns compound molecular graph features with token embeddings from sequence-pretrained large language models (LLMs), effectively infusing sequence-derived semantics into structural representations. To capture shared interaction patterns among functionally similar biomolecules, we construct a hypergraph-based representation to model high-order relationships between feature-similar compound/protein groups and their binding partners. Furthermore, a knowledge distillation strategy is further adopted to transfer high-order interaction knowledge from the hypergraph to a lightweight student model, enabling efficient and robust CPI prediction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HKD-CPI outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in inductive CPI prediction tasks. In particular, it achieves an average improvement of 4.94% in AUROC and 3.64% in AUPRC over the best-performing baseline across five benchmark datasets. Title: From Raw Signals to Understood States: A Perspective on Neuro-Symbolic and LLM-Driven Intelligent Sensing of Human Affective and Cognitive States

Abstract: Intelligent sensor technologies now provide unprecedented multimodal access to human affective and cognitive processes, spanning physiological, ocular, facial, kinematic, ambient, and behavioral streams. Yet, despite dramatic advances in acquisition and deep representation learning, the pipeline from raw signals to psychologically meaningful, actionable understanding remains fragile. Deep-only architectures excel at pattern extraction but struggle with contextual reasoning, uncertainty communication, and human-facing explanation; symbolic-only frameworks resist noisy, high-dimensional streams. This perspective argues that the field’s next inflection point lies not in richer sensors alone but in the interpretive layer that turns signals into states. We propose an integrative view in which neuro-symbolic fusion couples continuous sensor evidence to psychologically grounded symbolic primitives, LLMs act as auditable semantic reasoners rather than opaque classifiers, and explainability is treated as a design constraint rather than a post hoc addition. Synthesizing a decade of work on affective computing, fuzzy learner modeling, neuro-adaptive multimodal interaction, and explainable human–AI collaboration, we motivate a research agenda organized around grounded representations, uncertainty-calibrated LLM reasoning, and reflexive explanation. The aim is a class of sensing systems whose intelligence is measured not by accuracy alone but by the quality of the states they help humans understand. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Structuring versus Problematizing: How LLM-based Agents Scaffold Learning in Diagnostic Reasoning
Source title: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, LAK 2026
Affiliations: ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland; EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland
Authors with affiliations: Güres F.B., ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland; Nazaretsky T., EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland; Neshaei S.P., EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland; Käser T., EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract: Supporting students in developing diagnostic reasoning is a key challenge across educational domains. Novices often face cognitive biases such as premature closure and over-reliance on heuristics, and they struggle to transfer diagnostic strategies to new cases. Scenario-based learning (SBL) enhanced by Learning Analytics (LA) and large language models (LLM) offers a promising approach by combining realistic case experiences with personalized scaffolding. Yet, how different scaffolding approaches shape reasoning processes remains insufficiently explored. This study introduces PharmaSim Switch, an SBL environment for pharmacy technician training, extended with an LA- and LLM-powered pharmacist agent that implements pedagogical conversations rooted in two theory-driven scaffolding approaches: structuring and problematizing, as well as a student learning trajectory. In a between-groups experiment, 63 vocational students completed a learning scenario, a near-transfer scenario, and a far-transfer scenario under one of the two scaffolding conditions. Results indicate that both scaffolding approaches were effective in supporting the use of diagnostic strategies. Performance outcomes were primarily influenced by scenario complexity rather than students’ prior knowledge or the scaffolding approach used. The structuring approach was associated with more accurate Active and Interactive participation, whereas problematizing elicited more Constructive engagement. These findings underscore the value of combining scaffolding approaches when designing LA- and LLM-based systems to effectively foster diagnostic reasoning. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Estimating difficulty for the open-ended reading comprehension questions via Large Language Models

Abstract: Question Difficulty Estimation (QDE) focuses on estimating the difficulty of Reading Comprehension (RC) questions, which can be used in many educational tasks. However, existing question difficulty estimation methods suffer from three critical technical gaps: (1) they are primarily restricted to closed-ended questions with definitive answers; (2) they rely heavily on supervised difficulty labels, which are scarce and expensive to obtain; and (3) they often utilize shallow models that lack the extensive real-world knowledge required to assess subjective, open-ended responses. To address these challenges, we propose a Large Language Models-based Question Difficulty Estimation (LLM-DE) to estimate the difficulty of open-ended questions without using supervised difficulty labels by using Large Language Models (LLMs) to mimic the Human Pretest . LLM-DE first engages several pretest student models to answer the given question and then asks a teacher agent to judge such answers. An expert agent then analyzes judgment scores to predict difficulty using Item Response Theory. To validate the effectiveness of the estimation models without human labels, we subsequently propose a novel Self-Play Comparison Verification technique. Comprehensive experiments on Fairytale Question Answering (FairytaleQA) and Narrative Question Answering (NarrativeQA) datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method over various baselines, including the latest DeepSeek-V3.2 . Quantitatively, LLM-DE achieves a mean score of 66.9 on FairytaleQA, outperforming the strongest baseline, Voting , by 3.5%. This performance gap widens on the more challenging NarrativeQA, where LLM-DE achieves a score of 73.8, surpassing Voting by 5.8%. Finally, with the proposed technique, we have constructed a Difficulty-Aware FairytaleQA (DA-FairytaleQA) reading comprehension dataset. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Research on an Active Classroom Model for Undergraduate Students Based on Generative AI
Source title: Proceedings of the 3rd International Conference on Educational Digitalization and Computer Science in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, EDCS 2026
Affiliations: Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China
Authors with affiliations: Chunhua S., Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China; Wei Y., Shandong Huayu University of Technology, Shandong, Dezhou, China
Abstract: Addressing the issues of insufficient student participation, low-quality interaction, and delayed feedback in traditional undergraduate classrooms, this paper proposes a Generative AI-based Active Classroom Model (GAACM) based on a review of research on generative artificial intelligence, active classrooms, and learning analytics [1]. This model, centered on a large language model, integrates four modules: classroom interaction, learning behavior collection, activity evaluation, and teacher feedback decision-making. It enables dynamic generation of teaching resources, immediate response to classroom questions, personalized learning task delivery, and real-time monitoring of classroom activity. Furthermore, this paper constructs a classroom activity index and an AI-powered classroom interaction process, providing experimental design, evaluation indicators, and comparative analysis. Simulation results show that, compared to traditional classrooms, classes supported by generative AI significantly improve participation rates, questioning frequency, discussion frequency, task completion rates, and test scores. Research indicates that generative AI can provide scalable intelligent teaching assistance capabilities for undergraduate classrooms, but its effective implementation still requires adherence to the fundamental principles of”teacher-led, student-centered, and AI-assisted.” © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: What don’t you understand? Using large language models to identify and characterize student misconceptions about challenging topics
Source title: Education and Information Technologies
Affiliations: Harvard Medical School and Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, United States; Decanato Medicina, Universidad Autónoma de Guadalajara, Zapopan, Mexico
Authors with affiliations: Parker M.J., Harvard Medical School and Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, United States; Zavala-Cerna M.G., Decanato Medicina, Universidad Autónoma de Guadalajara, Zapopan, Mexico
Abstract: This study presents a systematic approach to identifying and characterizing student misconceptions in online learning environments through a novel combination of quantitative performance analysis and large language model (LLM) assessment. We analyzed data from 9 course periods across 5 online biomedical science courses, encompassing 3,802 medical student enrollments. Using data from 40–50 topic-focused quizzes per course, we developed a two-stage methodology. First, we identified challenging central topics using quiz-level performance metrics. Second, we employed LLMs to characterize the underlying misconceptions in these high-priority areas. By examining student performance on first attempts across primarily multiple-choice questions (MCQs), we identified consistently challenging topics that were also central to course objectives. We then leveraged recent advances in generative AI to analyze three distinct data sources in combination: quiz question content, student response patterns, and lecture transcripts. This approach revealed actionable insights about student misconceptions that were not apparent from performance data alone. The quality of the LLM-identified misconceptions was rated as excellent by subject matter experts. We also conducted teacher interviews to assess the perceived utility of our topic identification method. Faculty found that data-driven identification of challenging topics was valuable and corroborated their own classroom observations. This methodology provides a scalable approach to characterizing student difficulties in learning environments where quizzes are used. Our findings demonstrate the potential for targeted and potentially personalized interventions in future course iterations, with clear pathways for measuring intervention effectiveness through follow-up quiz performance. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Abstract: Conventional dyslexia interventions, limited by their static, one-size-fits-all nature, fail to address learner heterogeneity, thus reducing efficacy and engagement. We introduce the Emotion-based Generative Cognitive Imprinting (EGCI) framework, a personalized, emotionally adaptive therapeutic paradigm. EGCI's closed-loop architecture uses WebSockets to connect a Python-based Emotion Sensor (DeepFace, MediaPipe) for real-time affective analysis, a core logic server, and a web interface. Its foundation is a Bayesian Dynamic Affective-Cognitive Learner Model (DACLM) that fuses a learner's cognitive profile with real-time emotion data. The DACLM's state functions as a high-dimensional prompt for a Generative Content Engine (GCE) that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) to dynamically synthesize therapeutic exercises. An optimal intervention policy is derived by a Q-learning agent, which solves a state-aware reinforcement learning problem to co-optimize for skill acquisition and learner well-being. This integration of probabilistic modeling, affective sensing, generative AI, and reinforcement learning yields a scalable, dynamic, and deeply personalized solution poised to advance assistive educational technology.  © 2010-2012 IEEE.

Title: An Immersive Virtual Reality-Based Smart Chemistry Laboratory Framework for Interactive Science Education
Source title: Virtual Worlds
Affiliations: Alliance School of Advanced Computing, Alliance University, Bengaluru, 562106, India
Authors with affiliations: Kosuri H., Alliance School of Advanced Computing, Alliance University, Bengaluru, 562106, India; Achary R., Alliance School of Advanced Computing, Alliance University, Bengaluru, 562106, India
Abstract: Virtual reality (VR) technology presents the potential of transforming science education. Chemistry education, in particular, has traditionally been limited by the safety, infrastructure, and cost of chemistry laboratories, as well as the inability of traditional methods to visualize microscopic phenomena within chemistry. While there are various virtual reality systems that have been published that describe the capabilities of performing individual functions within the virtual chemistry classroom (such as simulating chemistry experiments or visualizing molecules), few have incorporated the various components of an effective chemistry classroom within their software, and the literature offers no unifying architectural framework or accompanying set of design principles for integrating those components systematically. This paper presents a design framework and reference architecture for an immersive virtual reality smart chemistry laboratory. The framework has not yet been implemented as a software system; its value lies in a principle-driven design blueprint—layers, responsibilities, inter-layer data flows, and design rules—that is intended to guide future implementations. The framework divides the virtual chemistry classroom into five major layers and the data that flows between those layers. Each layer has a relationship with other theories of learning, such as constructivism, experiential learning theory, and cognitive load theory, as well as a rule-based system for providing guidance to the user to enhance their learning of chemistry topics. The intelligence of the framework is deliberately staged: its core is a rule-based, explainable expert system that is implementable with current technology, while AI and generative-AI capabilities are positioned as optional future augmentations of specific layers. Additionally, a model for governing the data collected from the virtual chemistry laboratory is presented. Both existing literature and case studies of third-party virtual reality systems are reviewed to indicate the capabilities of each of these systems; these systems are not the implementations of the current framework. As a result, the virtual reality chemistry classroom can enhance engagement in chemistry concepts and topics, allow for accessibility to chemistry concepts, and reduce the potential for chemical exposure to students. The scalable design framework and reference architecture described in this paper can be used to guide the development of next-generation virtual chemistry classrooms. Future efforts in regard to this technology would focus upon actually implementing the proposed framework, deploying it into chemistry classrooms, and evaluating the learning of students who utilize the learning environment. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Teaching the Teacher: The Role of Teacher-Student Smoothness Alignment in Genetic Programming-based Symbolic Distillation

Affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology, Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Kharagpur, India; National University of Singapore, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Singapore; National University of Singapore, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Institute of Data Science, N.1 Institute for Health, Institute for Digital Medicine, Singapore

Abstract: Obtaining human-readable symbolic formulas via genetic programming-based symbolic distillation of a deep neural network trained on the target dataset presents a promising yet underexplored path towards explainable artificial intelligence (XAI); however, the standard pipeline frequently yields symbolic models with poor predictive accuracy. We identify a fundamental misalignment in functional complexity as the primary barrier to achieving better accuracy: standard Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) often learn accurate but highly irregular functions, while Symbolic Regression typically prioritizes parsimony, often resulting in a much simpler class of models that are unable to sufficiently distill or learn from the ANN teacher. To bridge this gap, we propose a framework that actively regularizes the teacher's functional smoothness using Jacobian and Lipschitz penalties, aiming to distill better student models than the standard pipeline. We characterize the trade-off between predictive accuracy and functional complexity through a robust study involving 20 datasets and 50 independent trials. Our results demonstrate that students distilled from smoothness-regularized teachers achieve statistically significant improvements in R2 scores, compared to the standard pipeline. We also perform ablation studies on the student model algorithm. Our findings suggest that smoothness alignment between teacher and student models is a critical factor for symbolic distillation.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Mobile-Based Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Enhancing Personalized Learning in Digital Education
Source title: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies
Affiliations: INTI International University, Nilai, Malaysia; Prince Sattam Bin Abdulaziz University, Al Kharj, Saudi Arabia; Bahauddin Zakariya University, Multan, Pakistan
Authors with affiliations: Akhter S., INTI International University, Nilai, Malaysia; Kumar T., Prince Sattam Bin Abdulaziz University, Al Kharj, Saudi Arabia; Shaheen M., Bahauddin Zakariya University, Multan, Pakistan
Abstract: The proliferation of mobile technologies in educational contexts has catalysed the development of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) that leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to deliver personalized, adaptive learning experiences. This paper presents a comprehensive review and conceptual framework examining the integration of mobile-based intelligent tutoring systems (M-ITS) in digital education environments. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), the technology acceptance model (TAM), and constructivist learning principles, this study investigates how M-ITS architectures comprising student modelling, domain modelling, pedagogical modules, and adaptive interfaces can enhance learner engagement, knowledge acquisition, and academic performance. Through a systematic analysis of recent empirical studies, theoretical frameworks, and technological implementations, the paper identifies critical design principles for effective M-ITS deployment, including personalization algorithms, gamified learning components, natural language processing capabilities, and real-time feedback mechanisms. Evidence suggests that M-ITS significantly improves learning outcomes across diverse learner populations, including neurodivergent students, English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, and higher education cohorts. Furthermore, the role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as an emerging component in M-ITS is examined, highlighting its potential for dynamic content generation and conversational tutoring. The study concludes by proposing a research agenda addressing scalability, data privacy, pedagogical alignment, and cross-cultural adaptability of mobile intelligent tutoring solutions. These findings carry substantial implications for educators, instructional designers, policymakers, and technology developers working at the intersection of mobile learning and AI-driven pedagogy. © 2026 by the authors of this article.

Title: Explainable Political Bias Classification in Indian Media Using Rationale-Guided Distillation
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems

Authors with affiliations: Mandavkar V., School of computing science, Engineering and Artificial Intelligence, VIT Bhopal University, KothriKalan, Madhya Pradesh, Sehore, 466114, India; Kumar M., School of computing science, Engineering and Artificial Intelligence, VIT Bhopal University, KothriKalan, Madhya Pradesh, Sehore, 466114, India
Abstract: This work presents a framework for detecting political bias in Indian media using rationale-guided knowledge distillation. The approach trains a multi-task student model capable of both stance classification and rationale generation. A dataset of short statements and tweets was collected on key policy topics like the CAA, UCC. Each sample includes outlet information, Pro/Anti/Neutral labels, and text-based explanations generated through a teacher ensemble pipeline using Google’s Gemini models and rule-based merging. The student is T5 model which is trained on dual task framework which are labels and rationales through a joint loss that balances classification accuracy and rationale faithfulness. Results show a stable macro F1 around 0.87 for T5-FLAN student model on full set and near perfect accuracy on high disagreement subset while showcasing improved rationale quality and fewer polarity mismatches than the models without rationales. The contributions include a rationale enriched Indian media bias dataset, a validated rationale selection and pseudo labeling pipeline with minimal human intervention, and an efficient, deployable student model that aligns performance with transparency; remaining limitations involve residual subjectivity, dependence on teacher rationale quality, and multilingual generalization, motivating future cross-lingual extensions and human centered rationale evaluation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Empowering data science education through low-code and no-code analytics platforms: A pedagogical roadmap
Source title: Decision Sciences Journal of Innovative Education
Affiliations: Department of Management Science and Information Systems, Spears School of Business, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, United States; Faculty of Business Administration, Department of Management Information Systems, Haliç University, Istanbul, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Delen D., Department of Management Science and Information Systems, Spears School of Business, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma, United States, Faculty of Business Administration, Department of Management Information Systems, Haliç University, Istanbul, Turkey
Abstract: The growing demand for data literacy across disciplines has intensified the need for instructional approaches that balance technical rigor with accessibility, engagement, and real-world relevance. In data science education, code-centric instruction can support technical depth, but it may also divert novice learners’ attention toward syntax and debugging at the expense of problem formulation, interpretation, and decision reasoning. At the same time, the rise of generative AI has changed this landscape by reducing some syntax-related barriers while increasing the importance of validation, critique, and responsible workflow design. This paper positions low-code/no-code (LC/NC) analytics environments as one component of a broader hybrid pedagogy for teaching analytics and data science. Drawing on cognitive load theory, constructivist learning, and prior classroom and practitioner literature, the paper develops a conceptual roadmap for using visual workflow tools, GenAI supports, and selective coding in complementary ways. Rather than arguing that LC/NC platforms replace programming, the paper proposes that they can serve as effective scaffolds for helping diverse learners engage earlier with analytical reasoning, collaboration, and end-to-end workflow thinking. The paper concludes with practical implications for educators seeking to design more inclusive and pedagogically coherent data science curricula. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Teaching of “Basic French”: A Logistic Regression–Based Evaluation

Abstract: This study addresses persistent instructional challenges in the “Basic French” course, including heavy teacher workload, delayed feedback, fragmented learning analytics, and limited opportunities for oral communication. The purpose of this research is to design and implement an AI-supported blended learning model integrating the Chaoxing AI Workbench, a French Assistant dialogue system, and the DeepSeek large language model, and to evaluate through machine learning the key AI-assisted factors that influence learner satisfaction. Questionnaire data (N = 200) were analyzed using a logistic regression model to quantify how perceptions of various AI-assisted learning features contribute to satisfaction. The model achieved strong performance (AUC = 0.841, Accuracy = 0.717). Results indicate that AI-based personalized Q&A support is the strongest positive predictor of learner satisfaction, while AI reliability shows marginal positive effects. Personalized content shows a marginal negative effect, suggesting a mismatch between AI-generated recommendations and learner expectations. These findings demonstrate the significance of AI-driven personalization and feedback in language learning and provide direction for optimizing AI-enhanced French instruction. © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).
