Title: Can We Trust AI’s Self-assessment? Evaluating and Improving LLM Confidence Calibration in Educational Dialogue Coding
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: University of Florida, Gainesville, 32601, FL, United States; Florida State University, Tallahassee, 32306, FL, United States
Authors with affiliations: Li H., University of Florida, Gainesville, 32601, FL, United States; Kuang H., Florida State University, Tallahassee, 32306, FL, United States; Botelho A.F., University of Florida, Gainesville, 32601, FL, United States
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist qualitative coding in educational research, but unlike traditional machine learning models that produce calibrated probabilistic outputs, LLMs report confidence as part of text generation. Whether such “verbalized” confidence can serve as a reliable indicator of prediction quality remains an open question. This study investigates LLM confidence calibration through three studies using 633 student-AI dialogues coded by experts across nine categories. First, evaluating three models with different accessibility profiles, we find universal overconfidence across all models, with discriminative ability (the capacity to rank predictions by correctness likelihood) varying substantially. Second, through an anchoring experiment, we observe that models adopt demonstrated confidence values only when they fall within a high-confidence range, completely rejecting implausibly low anchors. This asymmetric pattern, which we term plausibility-gated anchoring, suggests that verbalized confidence reflects learned priors rather than genuine uncertainty. Third, we explore activation steering as an approach to improve calibration in open-weight models by amplifying representations associated with well-calibrated predictions, finding consistent improvements that generalize to held-out data. These findings offer diagnostic insights for assessing LLM confidence reliability in coding tasks and suggest directions for improving calibration when deploying models in research workflows. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Lightweight lexical augmentation for robust transformer-based student feedback classification
Source title: Discover Education
Affiliations: Department of Computer Applications, Dr. Mahalingam College of Engineering and Technology, Tamil Nadu, Pollachi, India; Department of Mathematics, P. A. College of Engineering and Technology, Tamil Nadu, Pollachi, India
Authors with affiliations: Muthusami R., Department of Computer Applications, Dr. Mahalingam College of Engineering and Technology, Tamil Nadu, Pollachi, India; Saritha K., Department of Mathematics, P. A. College of Engineering and Technology, Tamil Nadu, Pollachi, India
Abstract: Transformer-based models such as RoBERTa achieve state-of-the-art performance in text classification, yet their effectiveness is constrained in educational settings where annotated student feedback is limited, heterogeneous, and institution-specific. This study examines the extent to which a lightweight lexical augmentation strategy can enhance model robustness under such low-resource conditions. A minimal reversible perturbation, character-level inversion of a single randomly selected word per sentence is applied to expand a student feedback dataset without relying on external corpora or generative models. RoBERTa is fine-tuned under two conditions: using real data alone and using a combination of real and synthetically augmented samples. Empirical evaluation demonstrates statistically significant improvements with augmentation. Classification accuracy increases by 3.2%, the F1-score improves by 0.032, and final training loss decreases by approximately 32% (p < 0.05 via paired bootstrap resampling). Confusion matrix analysis further reveals reductions in both false positives (–32.5%) and false negatives (–10.3%), indicating improved sensitivity and specificity in capturing subtle sentiment cues common in educational feedback. These findings show that controlled lexical perturbation despite its simplicity can regularize transformer models effectively, improving generalization without adding computational burden or semantic drift. The approach provides a practical and reproducible pathway for institutions seeking scalable solutions for automated feedback analysis, adaptive learning analytics, and student support systems in data-constrained environments. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Pedagogical transformation through generative AI: a hybrid deep learning comparison with traditional digital learning materials based on GenAI-EduNet framework
Source title: Quality and Quantity
Affiliations: Department of educational sciences, College of education, Majmaah University, AI-Majmaah, 11952, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Alshammari F., Department of educational sciences, College of education, Majmaah University, AI-Majmaah, 11952, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have transformed higher education, yet empirical comparisons with traditional digital resources remain limited. This study proposes GenAI-EduNet, a hybrid deep learning architecture integrating Long Short-Term Memory networks and multi-head self-attention transformers to predict and analyze learning outcomes when students use GenAI tools, specifically Google NotebookLM, versus conventional digital materials. The research adopts a rigorous quasi-experimental quantitative design involving 1847 undergraduate students across two academic semesters, with model training and validation using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) and EdNet. GenAI-EduNet introduces several innovations: a multimodal engagement encoding mechanism with gated attention capturing behavioral, cognitive, and affective dimensions; an adaptive knowledge tracing module based on transformer attention for modeling temporal learning patterns; a dual-branch comparative performance predictor employing inverse propensity weighting for causal inference; and a binary outcome module for pass–fail prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves 94.7% classification accuracy and an AUC of 0.967, outperforming ten state-of-the-art baselines by 8.3%. Quasi-experimental analyses reveal that students using NotebookLM achieved significantly higher learning gains, including post-test scores (d = 0.73, p <.001), higher-order thinking skills (d = 0.74, p <.001), cognitive engagement (d = 0.59, p <.001), and self-efficacy (d = 0.52, p <.001). Overall, the findings highlight the pedagogical value of integrating source-grounded generative AI tools, specifically NotebookLM in higher education and contribute a validated computational framework to learning analytics research in the era of artificial intelligence, supporting evidence-based policy development, curriculum redesign, faculty training, and sustainable digital transformation worldwide. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2026.

Title: From insight to intervention: learning analytics and generative AI support for learning design and educational decision-making
Source title: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Affiliations: Institute of Educational Technology, The Open University, Milton Keynes, United Kingdom; Laboratory for Learning Analytics, Faculty of Organization and Informatics, University of Zagreb, Varazdin, Croatia; Centre for Information Technology in Education, Faculty of Education, The University of Hong Kong, Pok Fu Lam, Hong Kong

Abstract: Recent advances in learning design tools, learning analytics, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have created new possibilities for educators to design, monitor, and adapt learning experiences. Yet evidence that these possibilities routinely translate into student-centred, inclusive, personalised, and effective practice remains limited. This editorial synthesises four contributions to the special issue on learning analytics and AI support for learning design and educational decision-making. Across student, teacher, disciplinary, and institutional levels, the studies show that technology does not become educationally valuable through technical capability alone. Its value is mediated by learning design, community and interaction, digital literacy, educator and learner agency, ethical fitness, organisational strategy, resources, and wide stakeholder engagement. At the same time, the evidence base remains dominated by cross-sectional, self-report, discourse-based, and expert-judgement studies. We argue that the field must now move from demonstrating associations and proposing frameworks towards intervention research that tests causal mechanisms, implementation conditions, longer-term outcomes, and distributional effects. A future agenda should connect learning analytics and GenAI tightly to educational visions, pedagogical intentions, preserve human and epistemic agency, and build trustworthy socio-technical infrastructures that enable educators and learners to act on evidence. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Scalable SRL Conversational Scaffolding for Student-LLM Interaction
Source title: L@S 2026 - Proceedings of the 13th ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale
Affiliations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden; Utrecht University, Utrecht, Netherlands
Authors with affiliations: Viberg O., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden; Wong J., Utrecht University, Utrecht, Netherlands; Ozdere S., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden; Lee Davis R., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract: The growing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) is transforming learning in higher education. While they provide flexible support, concerns remain about over-reliance, uncritical acceptance of outputs, and excessive cognitive offloading. To address these challenges, we foreground self-regulated learning for LLMs (SRL-for-LLM), defined as learners' ability to plan, monitor, and reflect on AI interactions to support learning. Guided by SRL theory, we introduce ChatWise, a proof-of-concept browser extension that combines conversational scaffolding with learning analytics to classify student prompts by SRL strategies and deliver adaptive metacognitive feedback in real time. A two-phase study included the design of ChatWise and a within-subject field study with STEM undergraduates. Log analyses using mixed-effects modeling showed that access to ChatWise more than doubled the likelihood of producing high-quality prompts. Findings further indicate improved prompt refinement, greater strategic awareness, and more reflective engagement with AI-supported learning. These results highlight the potential of SRL-aligned, analytics-driven scaffolding to support more effective student-LLM interactions.  © 2026 Owner/Author.

Title: Cold-Start Syntax Error Prediction in Programming Education: Comparing Sequential Knowledge Tracing and Large Language Models
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: School of Computer Science and IT, University College Cork, Cork, Ireland
Authors with affiliations: Shaka M., School of Computer Science and IT, University College Cork, Cork, Ireland; Brown K.N., School of Computer Science and IT, University College Cork, Cork, Ireland
Abstract: Cold-start conditions pose a fundamental challenge for intelligent tutoring systems, where the systems must support new students and newly introduced exercises with little to no prior interaction data. In the domain of programming education, sequential knowledge tracing (KT) models have been adopted to predict student performance, but they typically focus on pass/fail outcomes and rely on sufficient historical data, limiting their effectiveness for early and fine-grained personalisation. Recent extensions have begun to predict specific syntax errors, yet their behaviour under explicit cold-start settings remains underexplored. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) have shown strong generalisation capabilities in programming tasks, primarily through code generation, but their reliability and effectiveness for targeted syntax error prediction, particularly in cold-start educational scenarios, are not well understood. In this paper, we investigate future syntax error prediction under student and problem cold-start conditions in introductory programming courses. We conduct a comparison between sequential KT models trained for error prediction and LLM-based approaches, including both generative models that simulate student code and a direct LLM-based error classification formulation introduced in this work. Experiments on a large-scale dataset of novice Java programming submissions reveal complementary strengths: LLM-based models provide strong zero-shot generalisation on first attempts for unseen students and problems, while sequential KT models increasingly outperform LLMs as interaction history accumulates by adapting to personalised error patterns. These findings highlight important trade-offs between immediate generalisation and progressive adaptation, and motivate hybrid error-aware tutoring systems that combine LLM generalisation with sequential KT to support early and sustained personalisation in programming education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: An explainable AI framework for multimodal student performance prediction and institutional decision support at PSAU
Source title: Decision Science Letters
Affiliations: Department of Accounting, College of Business Administration in Hawtat Bani Tamim, Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Ali G.M., Department of Accounting, College of Business Administration in Hawtat Bani Tamim, Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Improving student success and supporting evidence-based decision-making in higher education depend on early detection of academically at-risk students. An Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework is proposed in this paper for multimodal student performance prediction to support institutional decision-making at Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University (PSAU). The framework was developed and evaluated using a publicly available educational dataset collected from a higher education institution, integrating data from the Student Information System (SIS), Moodle Learning Management System (LMS), and the eDify mobile learning application. The proposed framework combines comprehensive data preprocessing, Mutual Information-based feature selection, Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization, and an optimized CatBoost classifier. Using repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation, the model's performance was assessed and compared with statistical learning methods, conventional machine learning algorithms, homogeneous ensemble methods, and heterogeneous ensemble approaches. The proposed model demonstrated superior predictive efficacy, attaining an Accuracy of 92.0%, Precision of 92.7%, Recall of 97.9%, F1-score of 95.2%, ROC-AUC of 0.913, PR-AUC of 0.974, Balanced Accuracy of 0.824, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient of 0.726, significantly exceeding all rival models according to the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p < 0.001). Mutual Information feature selection further improved predictive performance while reducing model complexity. Explainability was achieved through CatBoost feature importance and SHAP analyses, which consistently identified assessment outcomes and online learning engagement variables as the most influential predictors. The proposed framework provides a transferable blueprint for implementing explainable early-warning systems at Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University and other higher education institutions to support timely interventions, personalized learning support, and evidence-based institutional decision-making. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Accurate estimation of learners’ skill mastery is essential for adaptive learning systems, particularly in programming education, where evaluating learner performance remains challenging due to the complexity of code assessment and the need to capture partial correctness and diverse learning behaviors. This study aims to improve mastery estimation and adaptive exercise recommendations through a continuous knowledge-tracing approach based on an extension of Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. The proposed approach integrates continuous performance scores from an automated evaluation process that combines structural code analysis, dynamic testing, and large language model–based analysis, while accounting for task difficulty and guidance format. The estimated mastery is then used to recommend programming exercises adapted to the learner’s knowledge state. To evaluate the approach, controlled simulations involving diverse learner profiles and real interaction data were conducted. Results show that the proposed model variants reduce mastery estimation error by up to 70% compared with the baseline model, particularly for learners with low and average proficiency levels. Furthermore, the approach improves estimation stability and generates recommendations consistent with learner progression. The main contribution of this work is a continuous extension of Bayesian Knowledge Tracing that leverages fine-grained assessment data to improve learner modeling and adaptive exercise recommendation in programming education. © 2026 by the authors. Abstract: Within the undergraduate curriculum of mechanics of materials, a central pedagogical challenge in cultivating top-tier innovative engineering talents lies in guiding students to recognize and comprehend the pervasive uncertainties inherent in real-world engineering problems, while maintaining the relative stability of the course's knowledge structure and theoretical framework. This study develops an artificial intelligence (AI)-empowered project-based instructional framework that systematically integrates stochastic analysis and structural reliability theory into the solution process of specific engineering problems. Employing the first-order reliability method (FORM) as the primary analytical tool, snow load is selected as a representative engineering scenario to establish a load-resistance probabilistic model. A double-iteration algorithm is further implemented to achieve numerical evaluation of structural failure probability. Teaching practice indicates that, without compromising the foundational learning objectives of mechanics of materials, the proposed project-based instructional model effectively enhances students modeling competence and engineering decision-making awareness in complex engineering contexts. © 2026, Chinese Academy of Mechanics. Source title: Computer Vision and Image Understanding
Affiliations: College of Science and Engineering, James Cook University, Townsville city, QLD, Australia; The Australian Institute of Marine Science, Townsville, QLD, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Saleh A., College of Science and Engineering, James Cook University, Townsville city, QLD, Australia; Olsen M., The Australian Institute of Marine Science, Townsville, QLD, Australia; Senadji B., College of Science and Engineering, James Cook University, Townsville city, QLD, Australia; Rahimi Azghadi M., College of Science and Engineering, James Cook University, Townsville city, QLD, Australia
Abstract: Monocular Depth and Surface Normals Estimation (MDSNE) is crucial for tasks such as three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction, autonomous navigation, and underwater exploration. Current methods rely either on discriminative models, which struggle with transparent or reflective surfaces, or generative models, which, while accurate, are computationally expensive. This paper presents a novel deep learning model for Monocular Depth and Surface Normals Estimation (MDSNE), specifically tailored for underwater environments, using a hybrid architecture that integrates Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Transformers, leveraging the strengths of both approaches. Training effective MDSNE models is often hampered by noisy real-world datasets and the limited generalisation of synthetic datasets. To address this, we generate pseudo-labelled real data using multiple pre-trained MDSNE models. To curate this data without ground-truth supervision, we propose the Depth Normal Evaluation and Selection Algorithm (DNESA), which scores each candidate teacher’s prediction with three intrinsic image-quality cues (multi-scale gradient alignment with the RGB image, image–depth mutual information, and edge-aware total variation) and selects the top-scoring pseudo-label per image. A lightweight student model is then trained on this curated dataset. AquaMDS uses only 7.58 million parameters, 44× to 113× smaller than the four state-of-the-art foundation-model teachers it distils from (DepthAnything V2, ZoeDepth, Metric3D V2, and Marigold), and runs at 63 FPS on a single GPU. Despite this efficiency, on USOD10K and Atlantis AquaMDS substantially outperforms every prior similarly-sized baseline method and is competitive with the giant teachers under a unified evaluation protocol; on the small Sea-Thru D3 split AquaMDS sits mid-pack among the giant teachers. Key contributions include: a novel and efficient MDSNE model, the DNESA algorithm, a domain-specific data pipeline, and a focus on real-time performance and scalability. Designed for real-world underwater applications, our model facilitates low-cost deployments in underwater robots and autonomous vehicles, bridging the gap between research and practical implementation. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Artificial intelligence and energy education: synergizing technological innovation with human capital development for a sustainable future - for the applied energy 50th anniversary special issue
Source title: Applied Energy

Authors with affiliations: Liu Y., Tianjin University, Tianjin, 300072, China; Fu Y., Tianjin University, Tianjin, 300072, China; Wu J., Cardiff University, Cardiff, CF24 3AA, United Kingdom
Abstract: As Applied Energy commemorates five decades of publishing pioneering research at the nexus of energy systems and sustainability, this perspective article examines an emerging frontier that will shape the next twenty years: the synergistic integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with energy education. The global energy transition demands not only technological innovation but also a workforce equipped with new competencies to understand, design, manage, and govern increasingly complex, data-driven smart energy systems characterized by intermittent renewables and decentralized grids. This paper highlights the dual role of AI in this context, both as a transformative tool for energy research and innovation and as an enabler and catalyst for reimagining energy education. Through a targeted literature review, we identify a critical gap: the absence of domain-specific pedagogical frameworks. While the energy sector urgently needs AI-fluent talent, generic educational AI lacks the physical rigor required for complex power engineering, risking “black-box” overreliance rather than acting as a trustworthy tutor that develops independent critical thinking. To address this, we propose a conceptual framework for AI-enhanced energy education that encompasses three core dimensions: (1) AI as a subject of study within energy curricula, (2) AI as an instructional medium for energy knowledge and skills, and (3) AI as an analytical engine for understanding learning processes and outcomes in energy education. We critically examine the “black-box” risks of AI overreliance, advocating for “Socratic” AI designs that compel students to verify outputs against physical laws, thereby developing independent, trustworthy professional judgment. This framework is empirically grounded through a real-world case study of a power systems course at Tianjin University, demonstrating how a domain-specific Large Language Model (LLM) tackles concrete engineering learning barriers. We conclude with a research agenda for the next decade, identifying priority areas where the Applied Energy community can lead in shaping both the technological and human dimensions of the energy future. © 2026

Affiliations: College of Computer Information Science, Southwest University, Chongqing, China; University of California, San Diego, United States; College of Big Data, Yunnan Agricultural University, Kunming, China
Authors with affiliations: Lu G., College of Computer Information Science, Southwest University, Chongqing, China; Zhan W., University of California, San Diego, United States; Peng L., College of Big Data, Yunnan Agricultural University, Kunming, China; Li L., College of Computer Information Science, Southwest University, Chongqing, China
Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has been shown to improve complex question answering, but existing methods often rely on implicit confidence scores from large language models (LLMs), which limits transparent evaluation and modular extension. To address these limitations, we propose CoTMind, a closed-loop framework that integrates candidate reasoning-step generation, multidimensional evaluation, and candidate-step selection policy optimization. In the generation stage, DeepSeek-LLM-67B decomposes complex questions into successive sub-questions and retrieves evidence via dual channels to form structured reasoning steps, each consisting of a sub-question, supporting evidence, and an answer. In the evaluation stage, hard labels derived from the REVEAL dataset (704 complex questions, 1002 reasoning chains, 3360 steps, and 1250 human annotations) and soft labels generated by DeepSeek-LLM-67B are used to train a lightweight student model, Qwen2.5-0.5B, producing a six-dimensional reward model (6T-DistillRM) that provides fine-grained scores for relevance, step type, correctness, evidence support, chain consistency, and attribution coverage. In the optimization stage, these scores serve as reward signals for Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which optimizes a candidate-step selection policy over fixed generated candidates, rather than directly fine-tuning the backbone generator, to improve the overall quality of the resulting reasoning chains. On five complex QA benchmarks (500 sampled test questions each from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Fermi Questions, and StrategyQA), CoTMind achieves F1 scores of 68.2, 70.8, 36.1, 42.5, and 83.4, respectively, outperforming CoT-Decoding by 6.4, 7.1, 3.7, 4.9, and 2.5 points. These results suggest that CoTMind offers a more structured reasoning framework and yields empirical gains across the evaluated benchmarks, especially on explicit multi-hop QA, with partial transfer to implicit reasoning tasks and more mixed evidence on highly compressed yes/no reasoning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Applying Generative AI to the Learning Analytics Cycle to Support Competency Development in Health Professions Education
Source title: Journal of Learning Analytics
Affiliations: School of Computer Science, The University of Sydney, Australia; CoLAM, FIT at Monash University, Australia; Faculty of Medicine and Health, Charles Perkins Centre, The University of Sydney, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Bucalon B., School of Computer Science, The University of Sydney, Australia; Yan L., CoLAM, FIT at Monash University, Australia; Shaw T., Faculty of Medicine and Health, Charles Perkins Centre, The University of Sydney, Australia; Gašević D., CoLAM, FIT at Monash University, Australia; Kay J., School of Computer Science, The University of Sydney, Australia; Janssen A., Faculty of Medicine and Health, Charles Perkins Centre, The University of Sydney, Australia
Abstract: Professional learning environments offer a unique opportunity for exploring professional competencies due to the use of workplace data, which captures important aspects of professional performance. This data is different from that used in formal learning analytics contexts, as it is not collected by systems designed to understand learning. Instead, workplace data represents the digital fingerprint professionals leave behind when interacting with technologies to do their jobs. Harnessing this data to support workplace learning is challenging for a range of reasons, including being able to identify meaningful metrics to identify individual performance and scaffold the use of this data to support professional learning interventions on knowledge and performance. Generative AI (GenAI) has great potential to enhance professional learning analytics by addressing some of the challenges inherent in using workplace data. These challenges include needing to process large amounts of unstructured data to understand individual performance and transform this data into interfaces and interventions that can support learning. In our paper, we modify Clow’s learning analytics cycle to inform a modified framework describing the intersection of learning analytics with professional learning. Subsequently, we illustrate the potential power of GenAI for supporting professional learning across the framework through three case studies in health professions education. © 2026, Society for Learning Analytics Research (SOLAR). Abstract: Purpose of the study: This study investigates the multidisciplinary integration of artificial intelligence, learning analytics, cognitive psychology, and science education to evaluate three Large Language Model (LLM) configurations. It aims to optimize an adaptive digital scaffolding framework for primary computational thinking (CT) and scientific reasoning under tight latency constraints. Methodology: Deployed via Python 3.11 within an automated benchmarking ecosystem, OpenAI gpt-5-mini, Google gemini-3.5-flash, and Meta llama-3.3-70b-versatile (Groq LPU) were evaluated across 15 Bebras tasks (135 structured API interactions). The multidisciplinary validation applied content and psycholinguistic triage to analyze the interface between technical inference latency and the continuity of students' scientific inquiry processes. Main Findings: Meta Llama-3.3-70b achieved optimal performance with a 0.2687s latency, maximizing the Student Waiting Threshold (SWT) compliance margin to support uninterrupted scientific schema construction. OpenAI GPT-5 Mini exhibited superior Socratic instruction adherence (6.9% failure) but introduced a 2.3764s latency overhead. Gemini 3.5 Flash truncated crucial pedagogical contexts due to its constrained 3-token output distribution. Novelty/Originality of this study: This work introduces a multidisciplinary engineering blueprint that bridges hardware-level computing optimization with technology-enhanced science education. By formalizing a latency-constrained routing protocol, it establishes a theoretical model demonstrating how infrastructure responsiveness directly safeguards the cognitive sustainability of scientific reasoning and problem-solving sequences in primary STEM learning contexts. © 2026, Cahaya Ilmu Cendekia Publisher. Abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), has introduced transformative possibilities for learning analytics (LA) in higher education. Despite growing empirical work, no prior review appears to provide an integrated synthesis of GenAI studies in higher education learning analytics through the combined lens of functional roles and decision support applications. Existing reviews address broader AI-in-education topics or isolated learning analytics functions rather than providing an integrated synthesis of these dimensions. This paper presents a systematic review of 38 studies, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, to address four research questions: (RQ1) what GenAI techniques and models are used in higher education LA research; (RQ2) what functional roles GenAI performs across LA processes; (RQ3) what decision support applications are enabled; and (RQ4) what research gaps and future directions exist. Drawing on studies retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE databases, supplemented by citation snowballing, we propose a taxonomy of six functional roles and identify nine categories of decision support applications. GPT-4 and related models emerged as the dominant technologies, while multimodal LLMs, retrieval-augmented generation, and generative adversarial networks represent emerging AI directions. The review reveals critical gaps in scalability, equity, interpretability, longitudinal evaluation, and ethical governance. These findings provide a foundation for researchers, educators, and institutional decision-makers seeking to leverage GenAI in educational practice. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Beyond the AI spotlight: Mapping the broader landscape of educational technology research

Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly become a dominant topic in educational technology research, raising questions about the visibility of other areas of inquiry that continue to shape the field. In this editorial we examine what the Australasian Journal of Educational Technology (AJET) has published alongside the growth of AI research. We reviewed 143 peer-reviewed research articles published from Volume 39, Issue 1 (2023) to Volume 42, Issue 3 (2026), first identifying articles in which AI was a central focus and then thematically coding the remaining non-AI articles. Fifty articles (35%) were AI-focused, while 93 (65%) addressed other areas of educational technology. These non-AI studies covered a broad range of themes, including professional learning and academic development, assessment and feedback, immersive environments and practice, learning design, learning analytics, collaborative learning, and digital wellbeing. Although non-AI research constitutes nearly two-thirds of the corpus overall, its share of AJET publications has declined as AI-focused research has increased. We argue that making this broader body of work visible matters because it reflects and sustains the conceptual, pedagogical, institutional, and methodological breadth of educational technology research. © Articles published in the Australasian Journal of Educational Technology (AJET) are available under Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives Licence (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). Abstract: [Objective] To address the high computational cost and limited accuracy improvements associated with prompt-enhanced methods for multiple-choice machine reading comprehension (MCRC) based on large language models (LLMs), this study proposes Prompt-MCRC, an prompt-enhanced multiple-choice machine reading comprehension with large language models. [Methods] The proposed model employs a large language model as the teacher model and uses chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting to guide a local student model in extracting and integrating the teacher model’s reasoning patterns and auxiliary signals. A bidirectional matching mechanism is further introduced to strengthen fine-grained semantic associations. In addition, a Japanese multiple-choice machine reading comprehension dataset, JLPT-MC, is independently constructed based on the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test (JLPT). [Results] The proposed model consistently outperformed the standalone local-model baselines on the C3-M, RACE-M, JGLUE, JaQuAD, and JLPT-MC datasets. Compared with the best-performing large language model baselines, it achieved improvements of 0.83 percentage points in F1 score on JaQuAD and 2.89 percentage points in accuracy on JLPT-MC, respectively. [Limitations] Owing to the high cost of manual annotation, the self-constructed dataset is relatively small in scale, which limits the model’s cross-lingual generalization capability to some extent. [Conclusions] By integrating chain-of-thought prompting and a bidirectional matching mechanism, the proposed model improves the reasoning performance of local models on multiple-choice machine reading comprehension tasks and provides a new perspective for multilingual research in this field. © 2026 Chinese Academy of Sciences. Title: A Neuro-Symbolic Hybrid Framework for Automated P&ID Auditing: Integrating Graph Neural Networks with Knowledge-Grounded RAG for Human-in-the-Loop Safety Verification
Source title: ACS Chemical Health and Safety
Affiliations: Houston, 77056, TX, United States
Authors with affiliations: Shinde R., Houston, 77056, TX, United States; Chachad A.M., Houston, 77056, TX, United States; Bhosale S., Houston, 77056, TX, United States
Abstract: Piping and Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs) represent the foundational safety records of chemical process facilities, yet their accuracy frequently degrades in brownfield facilities due to undocumented process modifications and Management of Change implementation. This documentation decay introduces latent topological hazards that traditional manual reviews often fail to detect. The aim of this paper is to automate topology-aware, standards-based safety auditing for P&IDs using a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence framework. The architecture represents P&IDs as labeled property graphs across five core layers: (1) Graph Neural Networks (GNN)-based topological anomaly detection, (2) a standards-populated Knowledge Graph, (3) Graph-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieval for audit finding generation, (4) an engineer review interface, and (5) human feedback-based calibration. The framework is examined conceptually across the three critical process safety scenarios: reversed check valve, incorrect valve fail-state positions, and missing thermal relief in blocked liquid lines. The flagged finding is classified into three severities: Critical, Warning, or Informational, to support safety auditing. An adjacent benchmark synthesis of graph-learning, engineering-drawing analysis, and knowledge-grounded AI studies suggests that the hybrid architecture addresses two key limitations of standalone methods: brittle rule coverage and insufficient audit traceability. Reported adjacent-domain benchmarks include evidence from previously published studies in adjacent domains, indicating that knowledge-graph-enhanced graph models can achieve high topological detection accuracy, that physics-informed graph architectures can attain strong classification performance, and that grounding retrieval-augmented generation in structured knowledge sources can substantially reduce unsupported generation. This human-in-the-loop system supports safety audits by grounding probabilistic AI anomaly detection in deterministic engineering codes. © 2026 The Authors. Published by American Chemical Society.

Abstract: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is a technically complex, high-risk ICU therapy in which preventable interruptions, alarm-related downtime, and circuit failure remain common and strongly influenced by clinician-dependent troubleshooting. High workforce turnover and variable local mentorship further limit consistent skills acquisition, while institutional heterogeneity in practice persists across settings. Despite these realities, structured CRRT training and validated competency assessment frameworks remain inconsistently implemented, creating a critical gap between clinical demands and current educational infrastructure. Simulation-based education offers a uniquely suitable strategy to address these gaps by enabling safe, reproducible deliberate practice of rare-but-critical events, structured development of higher-order decision-making, and multidisciplinary rehearsal of time-sensitive troubleshooting. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on simulation-based CRRT training, spanning traditional low- and high-fidelity in-person approaches as well as technology-enhanced virtual modalities such as screen-based platforms, virtual/augmented reality environments, and embedded learning analytics. We highlight how these approaches can improve accessibility and scalability by delivering standardized, repeatable practice of high-risk workflows (e.g., circuit setup, alarm management, escalation decision-making) across institutions with variable equipment, faculty expertise, and local CRRT volume. We also review emerging artificial intelligence-enabled approaches, including adaptive simulation engines and large language model-driven virtual patients, that may enable dynamic scenario progression, performance-targeted feedback, and more cognitively realistic longitudinal patient trajectories. Finally, we propose practical principles for integrating simulation modalities in a layered framework aligned with competency domains and cognitive demands, while emphasizing how digital innovation could augment hands-on practice, bedside supervision, and expert mentorship to improve CRRT competency, standardization, equity, and safety worldwide. Abstract: Open-ended short responses can reveal more about student understanding than selected-response items yet scoring them during live instruction is rarely feasible. This paper presents a bring-your-own-device (BYOD) mobile classroom system that combines rubric-guided large language model (LLM) scoring of short open-ended answers, real-time teacher analytics through a classroom dashboard, and evidence-based post-quiz feedback generation. The system includes a teacher-reviewed workflow in which instructors can inspect model outputs and, when needed, adjust scores or feedback during formative classroom use. In the reported evaluation, however, teacher override was not applied or analyzed; the agreement metrics compare the system’s initial rubric-guided outputs with expert reference scores. The system was evaluated in three classroom groups (N = 60 students; 480 question-level scoring cases). Three expert raters participated, each assigned to one classroom group, so each response received one expert reference score. In this test, system scores showed strong but not complete agreement with expert reference scores (QWK = 0.887; MAE = 0.089; RMSE = 0.121). Mastery-label accuracy reached 78.3%. Expert raters gave positive scores to the generated feedback reports for groundedness (M = 4.78), specificity (M = 4.37), and actionability (M = 4.57) on a 1–5 scale. Within the limits of this small-scale classroom evaluation, the findings suggest that rubric-guided LLM scoring may support formative assessment in mobile classrooms, provided teacher oversight is maintained for borderline cases. © 2026 by the authors of this article. Title: Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Rice University, Houston, United States; ETH Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland; University of Central Florida, Orlando, United States
Authors with affiliations: Liu N., Rice University, Houston, United States; Chen X., Rice University, Houston, United States; Baraniuk R., Rice University, Houston, United States; Sachan M., ETH Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland; Sonkar S., University of Central Florida, Orlando, United States
Abstract: Effective educational AI depends on modeling student misconceptions. Such models enable realistic learner simulation and diagnostic, adaptive tutoring. However, instruction-tuning large language models (LLMs) on student responses containing misconception errors can degrade reasoning abilities, creating a tension between faithful misconception modeling and preserving correct reasoning in other contexts. To support both learner simulation and tutoring, we study two misconception-aware models: the Novice Student Misconception Model, trained to acquire a single misconception for simulating an individual student, and the Expert Tutor Misconception Model, trained on multiple misconceptions to capture the error patterns a tutor encounters across students. To study the misconception acquisition dynamics of both models, we develop MalAlgoLib, a library that generates algebra problems with correct solution traces and misconception-specific erroneous traces. Our experiments across three LLMs reveal that the student and the tutor model exhibit fundamentally different misconception acquisition dynamics. For the student model, a single misconception is not learned as a context-specific behavior. Models overapply it across problems, degrading correct-solving accuracy unless training includes correct examples to enforce boundaries. In contrast, the tutor model can learn multiple misconceptions jointly without sacrificing correct-solving accuracy. Critically, intermediate reasoning steps are the bottleneck. With final-answer supervision alone, models cannot learn where error enters the solution, so neither the student model nor the tutor model acquires misconceptions regardless of data size. Together, these results, enabled by MalAlgoLib, provide an interpretable account of misconception acquisition under instruction tuning and guidance for training misconception-aware LLMs while preserving correct reasoning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Trajectory prediction and planning are critical for the safe operation of autonomous driving (AD) systems. Existing data-driven and imitation learning pipelines typically rely on geometric pattern fitting and short-horizon statistical correlations, struggling to generalize in complex, interactive scenarios. Although large language models (LLMs) can offer profound semantic understanding and causal reasoning, their massive computational overhead and mismatch with continuous trajectory generation severely hinder their development in real-time AD. In this paper, we propose an LLM-enhanced framework for joint trajectory prediction and planning that combines fast kinematic inference with adaptive semantic reasoning. Inspired by the free energy principle, we introduce a novel Hierarchical Contextual Encoder with an uncertainty-driven trigger. This module dynamically allocates language-model reasoning capacity based on scene complexity and uncertainty, utilizing a lightweight language model (LM) for routine scenarios, and selectively invoking a high-capacity LLM only when deep causal reasoning is required. To enhance the reasoning ability of the LM, we develop a CoT-based latent distillation paradigm that transfers structural reasoning and contextual priors from a teacher LLM to a student model through hidden-space alignment. In addition, we design a Cross-modal decoder that injects semantic intent into geometric trajectory generation, enabling more socially compliant and context-aware decision making. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks demonstrate that LLM-TP2 achieves state-of-the-art performance in both prediction and closed-loop planning, while ensuring the computational efficiency required for practical deployment. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Jiang F.K.; Su H.
Title: Exemplification in ChatGPT and student argumentative writing: A local grammar analysis
Source title: Linguistics and Education
Affiliations: School of Foreign Languages, Beihang University, China; Institute of Language Sciences, Shanghai International Studies University, China
Authors with affiliations: Jiang F.K., School of Foreign Languages, Beihang University, China; Su H., Institute of Language Sciences, Shanghai International Studies University, China
Abstract: Large language models such as ChatGPT are increasingly shaping academic writing practices in higher education, raising questions about how AI-generated texts compare with student writing at the discourse level. This study investigates exemplification, a discourse act that links general claims to concrete cases and plays a central role in argumentative writing. The analysis applied a local grammar approach, beginning with corpus-based retrieval of exemplification markers and proceeding to the annotation of their functional configurations in discourse. A corpus-informed comparison between essays generated by ChatGPT and those authored by British university students shows that ChatGPT produces exemplification more frequently but in a routinised manner, relying heavily on a small set of high-frequency patterns, while student writers employ a broader but less stable repertoire, including clause-initial structures that foreground examples as rhetorical pivots. Both corpora converge on the canonical “Exemplified – Indicator – Exemplification” pattern (e.g., cities have taken innovative approaches. For example, Singapore and London have implemented dynamic pricing …), underscoring its entrenched status in academic discourse. These findings advance discourse-analytic accounts of human-machine writing while demonstrating the value of local grammar for capturing rhetorical functions. Pedagogically, the study highlights the importance of treating exemplification as a rhetorical resource and contributes to current discussions of academic writing instruction and critical AI literacy. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are effective at generating and simplifying text, but they lack the ability to adjust the level of simplification and associated semantics for specific audiences, such as children, and implementing these adjustments is expensive. This limitation leads some approaches to avoid actively utilizing LLMs and instead rely on human intervention for effective simplification, which restricts their scalability and practical application. To resolve this challenge, we propose a framework for developing a lightweight LLM specifically designed to automatically transform complex texts into a format suitable for children, ensuring appropriate vocabulary, semantics, sentence structure, and simplicity. Central to our framework is a novel method called Teacher–Student Task Separation inspired by offline distillation, which smartly addresses the cost issue of directly tuning LLMs for this purpose. We use an LLM as a teacher model to generate children’s language based on prompt engineering with a beginner’s dictionary and children’s stories, without any learning. Then, we train a lightweight LLM as a student model using an advanced dictionary and the data generated by the teacher model. This method, referred to as offline distillation through data, employs task separation to allow the lightweight student model to efficiently capture latent contextual knowledge tailored for children’s language and even outperform the LLM, the base for the teacher model, in quantitative and qualitative evaluations including a new target-specific comprehension metric. Our work provides a cost-effective solution using LLMs to enhance children’s comprehension of diverse content and has the potential for adaptation to other purpose-specific LLMs. 1 1 Code available at https://github.com/sdb-ml/TSTS-LLM . © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: InferNose: A Bio-Inspired Electronic Nose System Using Chain-of-Thought for Olfactory Reasoning
Source title: IEEE Sensors Journal
Affiliations: National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology, Department of Electrical Engineering, Kaohsiung City, 807618, Taiwan
Authors with affiliations: Lee C.-H., National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology, Department of Electrical Engineering, Kaohsiung City, 807618, Taiwan; Fu Z.-X., National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology, Department of Electrical Engineering, Kaohsiung City, 807618, Taiwan
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated remarkable capabilities in auditory and visual perception, but the field of olfaction remains largely unexplored. Its development has been hindered by the inherent subjectivity of odor perception, a lack of cross-modality integration, and a long-standing scarcity of structured sensory data. Together, these challenges make it difficult to achieve automatic reasoning tasks using electronic noses (E-noses). This study presents InferNose to address these fundamental challenges. InferNose is a bio-inspired artificial olfactory framework that unifies e-nose sensing with AI inference to enable semantically grounded olfactory reasoning. InferNose introduces a multimodal chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning paradigm tailored to olfactory cognition. The process is inspired by the hierarchical processing of the human olfactory system from peripheral receptor encoding to cortical interpretation. A transformer-encoder temporal convolutional network (TETCN) encodes raw time-series odor signals into a shared embedding space aligned with linguistic representations. Cross-attention mechanisms enable fine-grained alignment between sensory features and textual descriptors. Knowledge distillation is applied to construct computationally efficient student models. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline is enhanced by FAISS-GPU, and based on expert domain knowledge, it supports knowledge-verified inference. Self-reflection and self-correction mechanisms are further integrated to ensure reasoning interpretability, output accountability, and validation reliability. InferNose, evaluated on the specialty coffee aroma discrimination task, achieves over 90% in classification accuracy. The integration of CoT reasoning yielded a relative performance improvement exceeding 30% over non reasoning baselines. Consistently high BLEU scores confirm the linguistic coherence and semantic fidelity of the system's generated olfactory interpretations. This study marks a shift in the field of artificial olfaction from opaque classification systems toward transparent, reasoning-based approaches. At the same time, it paves the way for the realization of long-term olfactory memory and the expansion of multimodal integration.  © 2001-2012 IEEE.

Title: Seeing through the dark: adaptive switch-guided knowledge distillation via heterogeneous teachers for robust plant disease diagnosis
Source title: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences

Authors with affiliations: Gondal H.A.H., Division of Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Dongguk University, Seoul, South Korea; Im S.J., Division of Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Dongguk University, Seoul, South Korea; Tariq M.H., Division of Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Dongguk University, Seoul, South Korea; Irfan M., Division of Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Dongguk University, Seoul, South Korea; Usman M., Division of Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Dongguk University, Seoul, South Korea; Zeshan M.A., Department of Plant Pathology, College of Agriculture, University of Sargodha, Sargodha, Pakistan; Park K.R., Division of Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Dongguk University, Seoul, South Korea
Abstract: Computational cost during model deployment can be reduced through knowledge distillation (KD) which transfers knowledge from a teacher model to a lightweight student model while maintaining performance. However, KD methods based on a single teacher often provide limited knowledge diversity and may transfer less informative features. Furthermore, the application of KD for plant disease classification in low-light noisy environments has received little attention. To address these limitations, we propose a KD framework using heterogeneous teachers with adaptive feature alignment (KDHT-AFA) that integrates an adaptive feature distillation switch (AFDS) to selectively align intermediate representations. For effective knowledge transfer, we propose a lightweight custom student model with 5.16 million parameters. The model incorporates a regional statistical hybrid attention (RSHA) to enhance important features semantically while increasing sensitivity to local structure and contrast. Additionally, we introduce a new self-collected real low-light plant disease dataset (ReLL-PDD v1) acquired under realistic agricultural conditions. For performance evaluation, we considered two open-source datasets, PlantVillage and the Potato Leaf Disease dataset, along with the ReLL-PDD v1 dataset. Our model achieved a mean accuracy of 86.88% with a harmonic mean of precision and recall (F1-score) of 86.25% on ReLL-PDD v1 dataset. On the PlantVillage and Potato Leaf Disease datasets, it obtained mean accuracies of 92.64% and 88.97% with F1-scores of 91.48% and 88.92%, respectively. Furthermore, the smart pesticide prescription module (SPPM) uses a large language model Meta artificial intelligence (LLaMA) to recommend pesticides for diseases detected by KDHT-AFA. Hence, the proposed KDHT-AFA supports real-time deployment and plant disease monitoring in low-light noisy environments. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Human-AI Collaboration Patterns and Cognitive Load in Solving Engineering Mechanics Problems with LLM: Big Data Mining based on Dialogue Logs

Affiliations: School of Civil Engineering, Wanjiang University of Technology, Anhui, Maanshan, China
Authors with affiliations: Yuan X., School of Civil Engineering, Wanjiang University of Technology, Anhui, Maanshan, China
Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLM) become ubiquitous in engineering education, there is a critical paucity of quantitative frameworks to assess their impact on student cognition. This study addresses this gap by mining fine-grained dialogue logs from an Engineering Mechanics cohort to characterize collaboration patterns. By integrating Natural Language Processing with clustering algorithms, we introduce a novel Log-based Cognitive Load Index (L-CLI) as a behavioral proxy for cognitive states. The results identify discrete collaboration phenotypes, differentiating between superficial "Passive Dependency"and deep "Active Scaffolding". Quantitative analysis demonstrates a significant positive correlation between high L-CLI patterns and problem-solving precision, validating that cognitive engagement remains the governing factor in AI-assisted learning. Abstract: Learning analytics researchers often analyze qualitative student data such as coded annotations or interview transcripts to understand learning processes. With the rise of generative AI, fully automated and human–AI workflows have emerged as promising methods for analysis. However, methodological standards to guide such workflows remain limited. In this study, we propose that reasoning traces generated by large language model (LLM) agents, especially within multi-agent systems, constitute a novel and rich form of process data to enhance interpretive practices in qualitative coding. We apply cosine similarity to LLM reasoning traces to systematically detect, quantify, and interpret disagreements among agents, reframing disagreement as a meaningful analytic signal. Analyzing nearly 10,000 instances of agent pairs coding human tutoring dialog segments, we show that LLM agents’ semantic reasoning similarity robustly differentiates consensus from disagreement and correlates with human coding reliability. Qualitative analysis guided by this metric reveals nuanced instructional sub-functions within codes and opportunities for conceptual codebook refinement. By integrating quantitative similarity metrics with qualitative review, our method bears potential to improve and accelerate the process of establishing inter-rater reliability during coding by surfacing interpretive ambiguity, especially when LLMs collaborate with humans. We discuss how reasoning-trace disagreements represent a valuable new class of analytic signals advancing methodological rigor and interpretive depth in educational research. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Supporting Epistemic Agency Through Multi-theory AI Explanations: A Mindful Learning Analytics Dashboard

Abstract: As generative AI becomes embedded in learning analytics dashboards, these systems increasingly shape how educators interpret and act upon student data. Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, such systems are classified as high-risk, raising critical questions about transparency, accountability, and human oversight. Existing dashboards often prioritise predictive outputs or single authoritative explanations, potentially reducing educators’ role to passive recipients of algorithmic judgments. Yet interpreting learning data is inherently theory-laden and context-dependent. This study proposes a mindful learning analytics dashboard prototype that supports epistemic agency through multi-theory AI-generated explanations. The prototype presents scenario-based cases and generates alternative interpretations grounded in Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) and the ICAP framework, enabling reflective comparison rather than automated acceptance. An exploratory qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured walkthrough interviews with educators and educational stakeholders. The analysis examines how participants evaluate, compare, and negotiate competing AI-generated interpretations. Findings show that participants maintain interpretive authority, calibrate trust through theory and evidence, and engage with AI as a reflective rather than decision-making partner. The study contributes a design approach that shifts AI from providing answers to supporting interpretation, aligning with the goals of mindful Technology-Enhanced Learning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping programming education by enabling adaptive learning support, automated error diagnosis, and data-driven instructional decision-making. Nevertheless, most existing AI applications in this field remain technology-centric, lacking close alignment with pedagogical design principles, disciplinary learning goals, and explicit application of specific computational algorithms. To mitigate this issue, this study proposes an AI-driven intelligent teaching model tailored to higher education programming education. Rooted in the AI-TPACK framework, SAMR model, scaffolding theory and learning analytics, the model integrates intelligent agent infrastructure (driven by LLM fine-tuning and syntax/semantic analysis algorithms), pedagogical coordination, instructional regulation (based on k-means clustering) and process-oriented feedback (supported by hybrid recommendation algorithm) into a cohesive instructional architecture. This paper elaborates on the model’s structural components, core algorithms’ parameter settings and application scenarios, operational mechanisms across pre-class, in-class and post-class stages, and verifies its effectiveness through empirical research. The model provides a structured, interpretable and scalable algorithm-driven approach to optimize programming instruction, offering theoretical insights and practical references for AI-enhanced teaching models in higher education. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Towards explainable knowledge tracing through meta-path-free heterogeneous graph learning with large language models
Source title: Discover Artificial Intelligence

Abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) is fundamental to intelligent tutoring systems because it models student knowledge evolution and predicts future learning performance. However, existing approaches often struggle to simultaneously capture heterogeneous educational relationships, long-term temporal dependencies, and semantic information embedded in instructional content, limiting predictive accuracy, explainability, and cross-dataset transfer. To address these challenges, this paper proposes MHG-KT (Meta-path-free Heterogeneous Graph Knowledge Tracing), an explainable framework that integrates a meta-path-free heterogeneous graph encoder, Transformer-based temporal modeling, and pretrained Llama 3 8B semantic embeddings through a joint cross-modal attention mechanism. Unlike conventional approaches that learn graph and semantic representations independently before feature fusion, MHG-KT enables continuous interaction between heterogeneous relational and semantic representations during temporal learning, allowing structural, temporal, and semantic dependencies to be jointly optimized within a unified framework. The heterogeneous graph encoder models relationships among students, skills, problems, and contextual features without manually engineered meta-paths, while the Transformer captures knowledge evolution and the semantic encoder enriches graph representations using problem statements and instructional hints. The proposed framework was evaluated on three benchmark datasets (ASSISTments, EdNet, and Junyi) against four representative knowledge tracing models (DIMKT, simpleKT, GIKT, and TGNN). Experimental results demonstrate that MHG-KT consistently outperformed all baselines, achieving AUC scores of 0.927, 0.922, and 0.934 on ASSISTments, EdNet, and Junyi, respectively. Abstract: Knowledge tracing and cognitive diagnosis face deployment and cold-start challenges in dynamic educational settings, as existing deep learning and LLM-enhanced methods rely on extensive training or fine-tuning. This paper proposes MA-CD-KT (Multi-Agent Cognitive Diagnosis and Knowledge Tracing), a lightweight system-level multi-agent framework. It decomposes tasks into four specialized agents operating via standardized JSON interfaces. For prediction, an LLM-Fusion mechanism integrates statistical features (core) with LLM semantic arbitration (auxiliary). For explanation, IRT-ZPD (Item Response Theory and Zone of Proximal Development)-based diagnosis generates ability profiles and intervention suggestions. On ASSIST09, DeepSeek achieves AUC 0.823, RMSE 0.4066, Accuracy 0.7635, F1 0.8451; Qwen achieves AUC 0.8251, showing weak backbone dependence. Ablations confirm statistical features drive performance, while the knowledge graph and IRT-ZPD primarily provide explainability. Token analysis shows LLM calls concentrate in low-frequency extraction stages. MA-CD-KT achieves competitive performance while enabling lightweight deployment, rapid cold starts, and interpretable diagnosis for educational scenarios. © ICST Institute for Computer Sciences, Social Informatics and Telecommunications Engineering 2027.

Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science

Authors with affiliations: Chuang C.K., The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong; Dai W., The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong; Li T., Monash University, Melbourne, VIC, Australia; Lin J., The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong; Li X., Monash University, Melbourne, VIC, Australia; Fan Y., Peking University, Beijing, China; Gašević D., Monash University, Melbourne, VIC, Australia
Abstract: Generative AI tools offer immediate, scalable feedback, yet how AI feedback shapes students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) processes—compared with human tutor feedback—remains underexplored. A randomised controlled experiment was conducted on a learning platform (FLoRA), involving 34 university students completing an academic writing task with AI feedback and 31 with human tutor feedback. Feedback was coded using SRL-supportive principles including clarifying goals, facilitating self-assessment, delivering high-quality information, encouraging dialogue, supporting motivation, and closing performance gaps, as well as actionability and politeness. SRL processes were extracted from learning trace data, and Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) modelled co-occurrence patterns between feedback characteristics and subsequent processes. AI feedback was more actionable (70% vs 45%) and more polite, while human feedback was more direct. Although both conditions showed comparable frequencies of individual SRL processes, ENA revealed distinct co-occurrence patterns (d = 1.56, p <.001): AI feedback co-occurred with content integration and quality judgment; human feedback co-occurred with return to source materials. These findings suggest that AI and human feedback support complementary regulatory pathways rather than superior or inferior regulation. To support sustained self-regulated learning, AI feedback systems might embed self-assessment prompts and vary directness based on task demands. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Tuning a laser–wakefield accelerator to a desired electron energy spectrum is normally done by scanning the machine one setting at a time, which consumes scarce beam time and expert attention. We address the inverse problem directly, recovering the experimental settings that produce a target spectrum. To do so we train a conditional diffusion model, built on the Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Models (EDM) framework, on measured electron spectra from the ALFA beamline, conditioned on laser energy, gas-jet backing pressure, and gas-valve opening time. Because EDM samples by integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, the map from settings to spectrum is differentiable end to end, and the settings themselves can be treated as free variables and optimized by backpropagation through the sampler. We propose and evaluate a three-stage strategy, BO (Formula presented) L-BFGS (Formula presented) RAdam, in which Bayesian optimization provides a global warm start across flat regions, L-BFGS exploits local curvature, and a final stochastic phase relaxes the solution away from sharp, bin-aligned minima. Against seven alternative single- and multi-stage strategies, this ordering recovers the target settings with the lowest mean squared error. We position this as a tool for differentiable inverse design in experiment planning, complementary to particle-in-cell simulation rather than a substitute for it. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: A Human-AI Framework for Extracting Learner Experiential Features via Perturbation-based Semantic Sensitivity Analysis: Generating Multimodal Feedback from Educational Text Data

Abstract: In the era of digital intelligence in education, a growing gap exists between observable learner behaviors and the micro-level psychological experiences underlying them. While traditional phenomenological methods offer deep interpretive insights, they rely heavily on retrospective reporting and lack scalability in digitally mediated learning contexts. To address this challenge, this paper presents a Human-AI collaborative framework for modeling learner experience through computational approximation of phenomenological analysis. The framework consists of two components: (1) a Perturbation-based Semantic Sensitivity Analysis (PSSA) algorithm, which operationalizes eidetic variation by measuring semantic stability under controlled linguistic perturbations using large language models and sentence embeddings; and (2) a procedural Experience Synthesis Engine that maps extracted semantic structures into interactive audiovisual and haptic web-based probes. A proof-of-concept case study on digital dissociation among university students demonstrates that the proposed method can identify structurally salient experiential components and generate interpretable experiential proxies. The results suggest that the framework offers a scalable and generative approach for exploring learner experience beyond behavior logs, contributing to empathy-oriented learning analytics. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: DISCORD: Enhancing knowledge distillation via cross-chain of thought and optimal transport alignment between models with different tokenizers
Source title: Knowledge-Based Systems
Affiliations: Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Viet Nam; The Australian National University, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Hai N.L., Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Viet Nam; Le A.D., Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Viet Nam; Vu T., The Australian National University, Australia; Van L.N., Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Viet Nam
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance across various NLP tasks but face deployment challenges due to high computational costs and memory constraints. Knowledge distillation (KD) is a promising solution, transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models. However, existing KD methods often assume shared vocabularies and tokenizers, limiting their flexibility. While approaches like MultiLevelOT, Universal Logit Distillation (ULD) and Dual-Space Knowledge Distillation (DSKD) address vocabulary mismatches, they overlook the critical reasoning-aware distillation aspect. To bridge this gap, we propose DISCORD, a universal KD framework that integrates Chain-of-Thought (CoT) augmentation and introduces Cross-CoT Alignment to enhance reasoning transfer. Additionally, we extend Optimal Transport beyond token-wise alignment to a sequence-level and layer-wise alignment approach that adapts to varying sequence lengths while preserving contextual integrity. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that DISCORD outperforms existing KD methods across different vocabulary settings, improving reasoning capabilities and robustness in both domain-specific and cross-task scenarios. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: Widening access has transformed who enters higher education but not who thrives once inside: inequality resurfaces as first-year failure and dropout, while the rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence (AI) threatens to open new divides. This article presents a whole-institution case study of how one Portuguese public university, Iscte—University Institute of Lisbon, has pursued equitable success in the first year through a single strategy with two reinforcing arms: a reactive arm that detects at-risk students and responds with personalized support, and a proactive arm that builds a baseline of critical AI literacy that is mandatory on one campus and optional on the other. Drawing on institutional records from 2016/17 to 2024/25, it combines a rule-based early warning alarm system, a comparison of machine learning models, and descriptive evidence on the literacy initiatives. The findings show that academic risk is concentrated in identifiable groups, that flagged students who engaged with support re-enrolled at higher rates than those who did not (though not distinguishably so once students who had already formalized a withdrawal are set aside, a group that took up no support and left without exception), and that a common literacy baseline is operationally achievable. The findings also expose the limits of each, as support reaches only a minority of those flagged and exploratory predictive models transfer poorly to the following cohort. Together, these observational results frame reactive support and proactive capacity-building as facets of one inclusion strategy. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Teaching programming logic faces significant challenges, including overcrowded classrooms and insufficient individualized student feedback. To address these issues, this study introduces LogiBots.Ai, an artificial intelligence conversational platform designed for teaching and assessing programming fundamentals. The solution integrates a specialized chatbot, adaptive quizzes, learning analytics, and comprehensive profile management for students, instructors, and coordinators. The platform was evaluated using the System Usability Scale methodology across two distinct groups comprising thirty high school and thirty undergraduate students. Results indicated satisfactory performance across both demographics, with undergraduates achieving an excellent usability score and high schoolers recording a good rating, validating its pedagogical efficacy and overall systemic acceptability.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Author full names: Wu, Sihua (61029150200); Sumettikoon, Piyapong (57929371200)
Title: Knowledge Evolution and Paradigm-Level Change in AI-in-Education Research: A Scientometric Mapping and Critical Review (2015–2025)
Source title: Education Sciences
Affiliations: School of Industrial Education and Technology, King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang (KMITL), Bangkok, 10520, Thailand
Authors with affiliations: Wu S., School of Industrial Education and Technology, King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang (KMITL), Bangkok, 10520, Thailand; Sumettikoon P., School of Industrial Education and Technology, King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang (KMITL), Bangkok, 10520, Thailand
Abstract: Bibliometric commentary increasingly frames the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a paradigm shift in AI-in-education (AIED) research, yet rarely distinguishes publication growth from genuine reconfiguration of the knowledge base or of teacher–learner roles. This study maps knowledge evolution in AIED from 2015 to 2025 by integrating four analytical strands across Web of Science and Scopus: scientometric mapping (including keyword and reference bursts and co-citation analysis), structural topic modeling (STM), design-weighted coding of full texts, and triangulation across these strands. Two transition windows emerged. The weaker 2019–2020 window (Jensen–Shannon divergence, JSD = 0.058; retained under the permutation rule but not under a stricter interval-based rule) reflects a research-front transition toward learning analytics and prediction, accompanied by knowledge-base reconfiguration but no detectable change in teacher–learner roles. The 2022–2023 window (JSD = 0.187, the period maximum) coincides with the generative-AI surge and couples a newly formed co-citation community with a topic-specific rise in coagency whose direction is clear but whose magnitude is imprecisely estimated. Because these effects concentrate in 36.6% of the weighted corpus and recent citations remain right-censored, we classify the change, under our pre-specified labeling scheme, as localized paradigm-level reconfiguration rather than a field-level paradigm shift. The label is an operational classification within that scheme, not an independent determination that a paradigm shift has occurred. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Beyond Keywords: Automated Prerequisite Extraction and Evaluation with MAPLE

Authors with affiliations: Jesus A., Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal; Santos A.M., Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal; Antunes C., Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal, INESC INOV Lab, Lisbon, Portugal
Abstract: Massively Open Online Courses (MOOCs) often fail to model student knowledge effectively because they usually rely on flat keyword lists lacking prerequisite structure. We propose MAPLE (Multi-stage Automated Prerequisite Learning and Evaluation), a framework that uses GPT-4o-mini to extract prerequisite-structured concept graphs from video transcripts and maps them to practice problems. Evaluated on three university-level courses, MAPLE achieves extraction quality competitive with TopicRank while adding critical structural dependencies. We introduce two novel metrics, coverage and groundedness, to demonstrate the graph’s suitability for student modeling. Our results show that MAPLE provides a principled, assessment-grounded foundation for downstream probabilistic knowledge tracing, bridging the gap between course content and latent student understanding. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.
