Title: Evaluating Feedback by Iterative Repair of Multi-step Solution Documents
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Computer Vision Lab, CAIDAS & IFI, University of Würzburg, Würzburg, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Lengfeld T., Computer Vision Lab, CAIDAS & IFI, University of Würzburg, Würzburg, Germany; Seitz J., Computer Vision Lab, CAIDAS & IFI, University of Würzburg, Würzburg, Germany; Timofte R., Computer Vision Lab, CAIDAS & IFI, University of Würzburg, Würzburg, Germany
Abstract: Large language models increasingly produce structured, multi-step outputs such as mathematical solution traces, proofs, and reasoning chains. When such outputs contain errors, feedback can guide iterative revision. However, assessing feedback as a standalone step does not capture how it shapes the solution trajectory over successive revision attempts. We address this gap by formalizing multi-step mathematical solutions as process documents whose state evolves through revision, and by introducing a closed-loop evaluation protocol for iterative document repair. In each episode, a tutor model localizes the earliest incorrect step in the current solution and issues policy-dependent feedback; the student model then produces a revised solution. This loop repeats under a bounded iteration budget, and the outcomes are decomposed into immediate solves, feedback-induced corrections, and persistent failures. We instantiate the protocol on mathematical reasoning traces from ProcessBench, covering four benchmarks at varying difficulty (GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH), and evaluate diverse student–tutor model pairings under three feedback policies that differ only in information granularity. Results show that even minimal positional guidance enables non-trivial repair, while more explicit correction yields larger gains for weaker students on harder problems. By jointly varying the feedback specificity and the iteration budget, we construct empirical control landscapes that reveal how these two parameters interact with student competence to shape repair dynamics, providing a structured methodology for studying feedback as an intervention on evolving document states. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: AI systems increasingly shape children's learning, from adaptive platforms and classroom analytics to GenAI used for creative and academic support. Alongside promises of personalisation and engagement, these systems raise persistent concerns for children's rights, including privacy, play, protection from commercial exploitation, and non-discrimination in the presence of bias. This workshop focuses on designing rights-respecting, child-centred AI for learning. Bringing together researchers, designers, educators, policymakers, and practitioners, it examines how concepts such as privacy, participation, play, and fairness can be operationalised in AI design. Through case studies and structured activities, participants will discuss shared design challenges, practical design principles and methods, and identify priorities for future child-centered AI research and practice for the IDC community.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Challenges, Strategic Framework, and Advancement Pathways for Constructing Future Learning Centers in Higher Education: A Perspective Empowered by Artificial Intelligence and Big Data Analytics Technologies
Source title: AIDME 2026 - Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Digital Media and Education
Affiliations: Undergraduate School, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, China; Party and Government Office, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, China; Wuhan Business School, Wuhan, China
Authors with affiliations: Liu J., Undergraduate School, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, China; Xu L., Party and Government Office, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, China; Yu W., Wuhan Business School, Wuhan, China
Abstract: While the conceptual vision for Future Learning Centers in higher education has gained considerable traction, their practical implementation is fraught with deep-seated structural and operational challenges. This paper provides a critical, computationally-informed examination of the primary impediments hindering the effective realization of these centers, moving beyond superficial diagnoses to identify four core bottlenecks: the persistent vision-practice chasm, superficial and fragmented industry-education integration, the "trilemma"of educational data utilization - encompassing multi-source heterogeneous data fusion, privacy-preserving computation, and the scarcity of actionable algorithmic insights -, and the structural lag of institutional frameworks. In response, this paper proposes a comprehensive "Five-Dimensional Integrated Framework"that coherently aligns objectives, a technology layer grounded in large language models, knowledge graphs, distributed learning analytics, and embodied interaction systems, spaces, pedagogical paradigms, and institutional safeguards. Furthermore, it delineates a set of computationally-enhanced strategic advancement pathways, emphasizing the crucial roles of open, modular standards development, the systematic benchmarking and replication of algorithm-driven pedagogical models, and the engineering of cyber-physical learning infrastructures. The paper argues that overcoming the "form without spirit"syndrome requires a concerted, cross-disciplinary effort to translate aspirational rhetoric into scalable, resilient, and continuously optimizable educational transformation, treating the future learning center as a complex, human-in-the-loop computational ecosystem rather than a mere spatial or technological overlay.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Content-Grounded Learning Behavior Analysis for Contextualized Feedback
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan
Authors with affiliations: Shimada A., Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan; Miyazaki Y., Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan; Hirotaka S., Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan
Abstract: Fine-grained learning behavior analysis based on interaction logs enables detailed investigation of students’ study strategies, but the resulting representations are often difficult for educators to interpret. This study proposes a content-grounded learning behavior analysis framework that generates contextualized feedback by grounding behavior differences in instructional content. Learning behaviors are analyzed independently, while instructional pages are grouped into semantically coherent content clusters that serve as explanatory contexts, and a large language model (LLM) is used solely as an explanation layer to transform fixed analysis results into human-readable feedback. The framework is evaluated using learning logs and lecture materials from real-world university courses through a within-subject user study. Results show that feedback integrating analytical evidence with explanatory descriptions is perceived as more understandable and useful than feedback presenting either component alone. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: This study presents an AI-powered Student and Teacher Management System designed to transform digital education by enabling individualized learning, easing administrative duties, and improving academic achievements. The major goal is to create an integrated platform that employs artificial intelligence to help students learn through adaptive tools while also supporting educators with intelligent matter and performance management. The methodology uses a modular, cloud-hosted architecture with React.js for the frontend, Node.js (Express.js) for the backend, and MongoDB for data management. Advanced AI techniques, including Natural Language Processing (NLP), Machine Learning (ML), and Optical Character Recognition (OCR), are used to power services like AI chatbots, document assistants, adaptive testing, and career assistance. The system is meant to be scalable, secure, and responsive, with extensive testing and deployment across multiple cloud platformsThe system's effectiveness is demonstrated by the findings, which reveal that the NLP chatbot achieved 94.7% accuracy and the document processing system reached 92.8% precision. With a 99.8% availability rate and an API response time of 167 ms, the platform could support up to 8,250 concurrent users. Students experienced a 14.4% improvement in knowledge retention, a 24% decrease in learning time, and a significant increase in self-study (143.8%) and peer collaboration (152.4%). These findings illustrate the system's ability to improve both short-term academic achievement and long-term engagement. © 2026 Author(s)

Abstract: With the continuous innovation and development of large model technology, using large models for newly launched product recommendation has become a mainstream approach in the industry to achieve accurate recommendation. However, existing recommendation methods based on large and small models suffer from excessively long recommendation response time and insufficient recommendation accuracy. This paper aims to use model distillation to enable the student model (small model) to learn parameters from the teacher model (large model), so as to significantly reduce the recommendation response time in new product recommendation scenarios and improve the recommendation accuracy compared with the standalone small model. The proposed method is verified on the Amazon Baby dataset. Experimental results show that our method enables the distilled model to achieve a substantial reduction in latency and an improvement in performance under both fixed and incremental data settings. We also discuss the adaptability of the model in cold-start scenarios. Finally, parameter tuning is realized through interactive dialogue with Deepseek. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Authors: Bian C.; Ye S.; Lu W.
Title: Do Instructional Behaviors Generalize Across Disciplines? an Empirical Study with Fine-Tuned Multimodal LLMs
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Department of Education, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, China
Authors with affiliations: Bian C., Department of Education, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, China; Ye S., Department of Education, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, China; Lu W., Department of Education, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, China
Abstract: Instructional behavior description extracts instructional behavior labels and structured descriptions from multimodal classroom data to support teaching evaluation and student feedback. Although instructional behaviors are often assumed to generalize across domains, examining cross-domain differences is essential for understanding how pedagogical intent and classroom enactment vary in practice. Accordingly, this study adopts cross-disciplinary comparison as a concrete research object to empirically examine domain-context dependence in instructional behavior description. We construct a multimodal classroom dataset composed of nearly 1,000 classroom video segments from authentic secondary school lessons, organized into Humanities and Science contexts to provide empirical data support. To enhance Multimodal Large Language Models’ (MLLMs) instructional behavior recognition and description under educational data and computational constraints, we apply LoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, to adapt three representative open-source MLLMs. We conduct intra-disciplinary evaluations, cross-disciplinary train–test swap experiments, and discipline-specificity analyses to systematically examine how instructional behavior recognition and description vary within and across disciplines. Results show that LoRA consistently improves performance in both contexts, while cross-disciplinary transfer leads to substantial performance degradation and clear directional asymmetry. Discipline-specificity analysis further reveals systematic differences in instructional behavior distributions and description keywords between Humanities and Science. These results provide empirical evidence that instructional behavior description is discipline-context dependent rather than one-size-fits-all, highlighting the risk of deploying discipline-agnostic instructional analytics in real classrooms and underscoring the necessity of discipline-aware educational AI systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Lightweight Medical SAM with Self-prompting for Ultrasound Breast Tumor Segmentation

Abstract: Purpose: Breast cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related death among women worldwide. Accurate tumor segmentation plays a crucial role in the diagnosis of tumor status. Foundation model based medical image segmentation methods show promising performance due to their extensive domain knowledge. However, their heavy computational burden, slow inference speeds, and reliance on manual prompts hinder both deployment efficiency and adaptability. Methods: We propose a lightweight self-prompting (Tiny-SAM) model for ultrasound breast tumor segmentation. First, we developed an efficient distillation method for SAM-Med2D that uses soft labels to decouple teacher model distillation and hard labels to guide student model training, saving computational cost while maintaining high performance. Second, we introduced the cross-attention mechanism to reduce high target-prompt correlation, enabling self-prompting and automating segmentation process. Finally, we improved the traditional multi-head attention mechanism through dynamic combination, enhancing computational efficiency. Results: We conducted extensive experiments on 593 images from a public dataset and 3,513 images from a private dataset to validate our model. Compared to SAM-Med2D, our model reduced the parameters by approximately 20 times and improved computational efficiency by 3 times, demonstrating overall superior performance. Compared to prompt-based methods, our approach achieved Dice coefficient improvements of 0.31% (attaining 0.8509) and 1.52% (attaining 0.8576) on two datasets, while surpassing other automatic segmentation methods of 3.44% and 0.95%, respectively. Conclusions: Our AI-model based method improves both the accuracy and efficiency of automatic breast cancer segmentation, and shows significant potential for clinical adoption. Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping education by enabling personalized learning and increasing student engagement. The rapid adoption of tools such as ChatGPT, however, raises questions about efficacy, academic integrity, and ethics. This study aims to fill a critical gap by providing a systematic comparative evaluation of classical, deep learning, and transformer-based models for sentiment analysis of ChatGPT-related educational discourse, identifying the best-performing approach, and deploying it in an explainable, user-friendly web application for non-technical stakeholders. This study examines public sentiment regarding ChatGPT in education by using a comparative framework that includes transformer-based model, deep learning, and classical machine learning approaches. Previous research in this area has mainly depended on small-scale surveys or static datasets, often without utilizing modern natural language processing (NLP) techniques. This study aims to fill those gaps by gathering 236,275 tweets related to ChatGPT in education and implementing a systematic benchmarking process. Neutral tweets were removed, resulting in a binary classification of positive and negative labels. The data was divided into an 80/20 split for training and testing. A Naive Bayes model with TF-IDF vectorization served as the classical baseline. For the deep learning tier, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) models with Word2Vec embeddings were used. The transformer tier was represented by a fine-tuned DistilBERT model. The models were evaluated based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The fine-tuned DistilBERT achieved the highest accuracy at 98.81%, indicating a strong performance of transformer-based models compared to classical machine learning and deep learning approaches in this dataset. In contrast, the LSTM model achieved 95.40%, the Bi-LSTM reached 94.66%, and the Naive Bayes model recorded an accuracy of 81.77%. A Streamlit-based web application was developed that integrates LIME-based explainability to make sentiment predictions accessible to educators and policymakers. However, it is important to note that this study is limited to English-language Twitter data and relies on a single-domain, single train-test split; therefore, the results may not fully generalize beyond this context. While these findings are promising, broader generalization warrants further investigation. Future research should explore multilingual datasets, additional social media platforms, and more advanced transformer architectures to enhance generalizability and expand applicability in diverse educational contexts. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: The Pocket Tutor Has a Price: Scaffolding Self-Paced Learning with AI
Source title: Big Data and Cognitive Computing
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, University of Idaho, Moscow, 83844, ID, United States
Authors with affiliations: Jamil H.M., Department of Computer Science, University of Idaho, Moscow, 83844, ID, United States
Abstract: The dominant narrative casts large language models (LLMs) as a low-cost realization of Bloom’s two-sigma tutor: patient, always available, personalizing at scale. Self-paced online learning, the fastest-growing segment of higher and continuing education and the backbone of the data-science workforce pipeline, is where this promise is most attractive and most dangerous. Through an integrative synthesis of cognitive science, learning theory, computing-education evidence, and the economics of services, we argue that self-paced settings strip away the implicit scaffolding of the classroom (instructor presence, peers, accountability, ambient feedback), so unguided LLM access defaults to cognitive offloading, metacognitive disengagement, and fragmented learning that erodes durable competence. Recent large-scale evidence, including a survey of over ninety-five thousand undergraduates that found sharply elevated failure rates in introductory computing, is consistent with this. Rather than reject LLMs, we ask what a protective, holistic environment must do, grounding the answer in cognitive load theory, self-regulated learning, desirable difficulties, the zone of proximal development, and the ICAP framework, and we translate it into a layered reference architecture organized around a persistent learner model: longitudinal tracking, a curriculum coherence graph, adaptive personalization, cognitive gating, reflective agents, and process-based assessment with human checkpoints. Our central claim is economic: the configurations that protect cognition are far more resource-intensive—in compute, data and provenance infrastructure, authored artifacts, money, time, and human labor—than the near-free configuration that harms it. We characterize this cost asymmetry and its equity and workforce consequences and argue that resourcing the protective environment is, in effect, educational and workforce policy. © 2026 by the author.

Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models into technical education exposes a critical fault line between building genuine conceptual mastery and merely outsourcing cognition. We examined this tension by tracking 123 computer science students across three AI-supported assessments and one unassisted final exam, comparing a standard control group against a cohort trained in structured Prompt Engineering (PE). Interaction logs and semantic similarity metrics revealed two drastically different approaches to the tool. Untrained students treated the LLM as a shortcut: 76.6% of their submissions heavily mimicked the model's raw output. While this passive extraction maximized short-term grades, it was strongly associated with a severe cognitive dependency. For this group, higher AI usage correlated with worse performance on the independent final exam. The PE-trained students, meanwhile, paid an early "transition cost."Their initial scores dropped as they took on the higher cognitive load of breaking down tasks and reformulating AI responses. Yet, this early friction paid off. When AI support was removed, the trained cohort retained significantly more knowledge, achieving a much higher Transfer Index (59.0% vs. 48.7%). Our data challenges the assumption that educational interfaces should be seamless. To prevent cognitive offloading, educators must treat prompt engineering not as a technical trick, but as a metacognitive skill that injects the "productive friction"necessary for resilient, independent learning.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: The TME Framework: Multimodal Learner Modeling for Active Listening Skills in Collaborative Problem Solving
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: New York University, 370 Jay Street, New York City, NY, United States
Authors with affiliations: Huang X., New York University, 370 Jay Street, New York City, NY, United States; Ochoa X., New York University, 370 Jay Street, New York City, NY, United States; Hiterer D., New York University, 370 Jay Street, New York City, NY, United States
Abstract: Active listening is an important social–emotional skill for productive and inclusive collaboration, yet it remains difficult to assess in small-group collaborative problem-solving (CPS) activities. Teachers cannot continuously observe multiple groups simultaneously, while existing assessment approaches rely either on self-report—which is prone to bias—or on manual coding, which is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We present the Theory-Measurement-Evaluation (TME) framework, a theory-based and explainable approach for modeling active listening in CPS grounded in the HURIER active listening framework. TME comprises three interlocking models. First, a Theory Model operationalizes HURIER into eight constructs, each translated into observable behavioral indicators. Second, a Measurement Model automatically extracts construct-aligned multimodal behavioral traces from audio and video and situates them within layered collaboration context derived from idea-evolution analysis across multiple time scales (micro-moments, collaboration phases, and whole-conversation dynamics). Building on evidence generated by the Measurement Model, we introduce an Evaluation Model that applies Bayesian Skill Tracing to estimate time-varying construct expression while preserving uncertainty. This produces an interpretable Multimodal Learner Model that combines quantitative metrics, exemplary behaviors, and descriptive narratives, and can be used by both human stakeholders and intelligent agents for downstream applications such as providing feedback or personalized learning. We evaluate the faithfulness and usefulness of the learner model outputs through expert ratings. Results suggest that TME can assess active listening skills from multimodal CPS data in a scalable and interpretable way. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: The current teaching method of foreign languages is more and more adopting the method of using intelligent software to observe the learner's behavior and adapt teaching methods accordingly, but the teaching software currently used in the field of English learning still has many limitations such as relying on rigid rule sets or single-pass learning prediction models which cannot track and adapt the learners' learning competence and motivation from one teaching moment to the next. This paper introduces a self-adaptive cognitive AI agent model framework which continuously models the learners' behaviour and then uses a perception-reason-plan-act cognitive loop to select tasks, plan tasks, and make tasks more or less difficult for the learners in reading, writing, listening, and speaking. The framework combines a continuous learner behaviour modelling module with a skill-domain model based on the CEFR framework and a module on self-evaluation which recalibrates the adaptation policy based on observed outcomes. The framework's main behaviour-modelling premise – that the signals of interaction that are continuously captured better predict learner outcomes than profile information – is tested empirically using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD), a real, publicly accessible, anonymized collection of 32,593 course enrollments and 173,912 graded submissions. The design premise for the framework is that early, continuously updated behavioural signals can drive timely adaptive intervention, and logistic regression and random forest classifiers based on behavioural features (completion rate, submission timing and score trajectory) exhibit an AUC of 0.958 and 0.965 respectively, predicting at-risk outcomes with materially the same accuracy as behaviour-plus-demographics, and a variant using only the first three submissions reaches AUC 0.853, supporting this premise. The results of these empirical studies are then applied to the proposed architecture for developing English skills, and a roadmap for implementing the architecture and further domain-specific validation before classroom deployment is then described. © 2026, Technical institute of Bijeljina. Title: AI-enhanced gamification in education: an integrative review of trends, impacts, and corrective role potential
Source title: Journal of Computers in Education
Affiliations: Graduate School, Universitas Negeri Yogyakarta, Yogyakarta, Indonesia; Faculty of Education, Technische Universität Dresden, Dresden, Germany

Abstract: While educational gamification successfully drives student engagement, it faces persistent criticism for fostering extrinsic reward dependency, superficial achievement (“fast leveling”), and inequitable learning experiences. This study posits Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a critical corrective mechanism to these structural limitations, repositioning static game mechanics within dynamic, adaptive learning ecosystems. Adopting an Integrative Review methodology based on Whittemore and Knafl’s framework, this study synthesizes 61 empirical and theoretical studies (2003–2025) identified through systematic two-way snowballing. Complementary bibliometric data from Scopus and ScienceDirect reveals an exponential “J-curve” growth in the field, marking a decisive disciplinary shift from computer science architectures to pedagogical applications in Social Sciences. The findings indicate that AI integration mitigates traditional gamification pitfalls by (1) personalizing difficulty through adaptive algorithms, (2) replacing superficial rewards with intelligent, real-time feedback, and (3) enhancing inclusivity for diverse learner profiles. Crucially, this review proposes the “AI Corrective Role Framework,” a conceptual model grounded in convergent evidence that operationalizes how AI acts as a learner-centered function to deepen cognitive retention and as a decision-making instrument for institutional strategy. These insights offer researchers and policymakers a robust roadmap for implementing sustainable, evidence-based, and equitable gamified learning environments in the era of Generative AI. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Pedagogical Agent in an E-Learning Environment

Abstract: This study examines the development and pedagogical impact of an AI-based pedagogical agent designed for modern e-learning environments. The research addresses a key challenge in digital education: the lack of personalization and immediate feedback in traditional e-learning systems. AI-driven agents “support and motivate learners through instructional interaction” and provide adaptive, data-driven learning experiences that surpass the limitations of rule-based systems. The study begins with a systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020, analyzing 46 publications from 2020 to 2025 to identify current AI architectures, pedagogical roles, and the empirical evidence of learning impact. The findings highlight the growing use of machine learning, deep learning, multimodal analytics, and large language models in educational agents. These systems perform roles such as tutor, coach, evaluator, dialogue partner, and consultant, offering cognitive, metacognitive, emotional, and analytical support. Modern agents “continuously monitor user interaction, analyze engagement, and adapt learning content”, enabling highly personalized learning pathways. The study also presents the design of a multimodal pedagogical agent capable of explanation, task generation, diagnostics, and adaptive feedback. Experimental results with students (n = 20) show improved performance, reduced errors, and higher engagement when learning with the agent. Overall, the research demonstrates that AI-based pedagogical agents enhance learning effectiveness and support autonomous learning in higher education. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: The assessment of students' psychological status is one of the major aspects for detecting problems in terms of students' mental health at school which influence the performance of learners. However, there have been improvements in application of AI methods to achieve accurate assessment. However, the current assessment models fail to provide an assessment of prediction uncertainty which makes them less effective in the educational context. In order to solve this problem, an Uncertainty-Aware Bayesian Adaptation (UABA) framework is suggested in the paper, and it includes data preprocessing, posterior estimation of the Bayes model, adaptive learning, and confidence-aware classification in order to deliver a reliable student psychological assessment. The novel thing about the UABA framework is that in addition to predicting the psychological condition of students, it provides a measure of confidence of each prediction with the help of Bayesian uncertainty estimation. The Bayesian adaptive mechanism helps optimize the parameters of the model continuously based on the incoming data, thereby reducing overconfident incorrect predictions and decision-making. The UABA framework has been applied to a benchmark student psychological assessment dataset and benchmarked with different machine learning and deep learning models such as SVM, Random Forest, CNN, LSTM and Transformer. Experimental results revealed that the proposed UABA model had a maximum accuracy of 97.82%, precision of 97.56%, recall of 97.31%, F1 score of 97.43% and AUC of 98.11% among all the comparative models. In addition to this, the false positive rate, false negative rate, prediction confidence, and calibration score of the framework were 2.18%, 2.69%, 97.92%, and 98.26%, respectively, achieving better than the other models in terms of prediction performance and uncertainty estimation. These results further support the viability of uncertainty aware Bayesian adaptation as a reliable methodology in psychological evaluation of students with the use of AI. © 2026, International Academic Institute for Science and Technology. Title: RL-Robotutor: a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for multimodal robot tutoring

Abstract: Personalised robot tutoring requires real-time pedagogical decision-making under uncertain and multimodal learner states. Existing intelligent tutoring and robot-assisted learning systems often rely on static rules, single-modality learner modelling, or short-term correctness-oriented optimisation, which limits their capacity to balance knowledge acquisition, engagement, retention, and safe embodied interaction. RL-Robotutor is presented as a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that integrates cognitive knowledge-tracing signals, facial-expression and gaze-derived affective cues, and behavioural interaction logs through transformer-based fusion. A PPO-trained meta-policy selects among specialised modules for learner assessment, curriculum adaptation, strategy selection, and reflective feedback, while a hybrid reward combines immediate learning performance, engagement, long-term learning gain, and safety. The evidence is reported by source: five public knowledge-tracing datasets assess the cognitive prediction component; controlled simulator experiments assess policy learning, reward ablation, and multimodal fusion; and a randomised robot-tutoring study assesses embodied interaction with 120 undergraduate participants. RL-Robotutor outperforms rule-based, flat reinforcement-learning, knowledge-tracing, and LLM-based comparators. In the human study, the learning gain is 0.62, compared with 0.40 for the rule-based robot condition. The full hybrid reward improves simulator learning gain by 19% over correctness-only optimisation, and full multimodal fusion improves simulator engagement by 17% over text-only modelling. Jetson Orin deployment achieves 48 ms inference latency with an absolute AUC reduction of 0.007, supporting real-time edge execution. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Cross-Domain Analysis of the Effectiveness of LLMs in Essay Assessment: From the Technical Rigor of IME to the Large-Scale Context of ENEM
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Military Engineering Institute (IME), Praça General Tibúrcio, 80 - Urca, RJ, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
Authors with affiliations: da Silva D.C.A., Military Engineering Institute (IME), Praça General Tibúrcio, 80 - Urca, RJ, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; Ferreira C.L., Military Engineering Institute (IME), Praça General Tibúrcio, 80 - Urca, RJ, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; Silva S.D.S.C., Military Engineering Institute (IME), Praça General Tibúrcio, 80 - Urca, RJ, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
Abstract: This study expands on a previous investigation into the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) for essay assessment, moving from the specific context of the Military Institute of Engineering (IME) entrance examination to the large-scale scenario of the Brazilian National High School Exam (ENEM). The methodology compared a state-of-the-art LLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) with experts in human classification. The results show that advanced LLMs exhibit excellent reliability (ICC > 0.95) and extremely high overall alignment (r > 0.98) with human assessors. More significantly, the study reveals that the AI’s accuracy is enhanced by structured rubrics like ENEM’s. However, the analysis also identified the persistence of a subtle algorithmic leniency, where the model tends to overestimate the quality of subjective criteria, such as argumentative depth - a limitation already observed in the initial phase of the study. It is concluded that while LLMs are robust automation tools, human supervision remains crucial for calibrating judgments on profound qualitative aspects. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Northwestern University, Evanston, 60208, IL, United States
Authors with affiliations: Xie D., Northwestern University, Evanston, 60208, IL, United States; Anderson K., Northwestern University, Evanston, 60208, IL, United States; Eze T., Northwestern University, Evanston, 60208, IL, United States; Lin C., Northwestern University, Evanston, 60208, IL, United States; Shin B., Northwestern University, Evanston, 60208, IL, United States; Worsley M., Northwestern University, Evanston, 60208, IL, United States
Abstract: Collaboration literacy requires adapting to the evolving demands of group work within complex discussions, making it difficult to develop and assess. Traditional analytics metrics capture behavioral signals while missing the semantic dimensions of how learners approach collaboration and build on each other’s ideas. We present Collaboration Literacy through Artifact Reasoning and Augmentation (CLARA), an agentic analytics system that extracts semantic representations from transcripts as analytics artifacts: concept maps representing emergent ideas and relationships, and collaboration assessment characterizing collaboration quality across seven dimensions. While users explore these artifacts through the dashboard, the same artifacts are indexed into distinct vector database collections for agent retrieval and reasoning. This architecture establishes a human-AI common ground where users and AI can operate over shared representations. Evaluation results show that CLARA produces reliable collaboration quality analysis and, owing to the artifacts serving as knowledge infrastructure, improves both retrieval performance and response quality over transcript-only baselines. Our work suggests that AI-produced artifacts may scaffold human interpretation and ground AI reasoning in learning analytics workflows. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Population-Guided Intent-Aware Query Rewriting for Web Search

Affiliations: School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University, Changchun, China; Engineering Research Center of Knowledge-Driven Human-Machine Intelligence, MOE, Changchun, China; Baidu Inc, Beijing, China
Authors with affiliations: Guo Y., School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University, Changchun, China, Engineering Research Center of Knowledge-Driven Human-Machine Intelligence, MOE, Changchun, China; Zhang S., Baidu Inc, Beijing, China; Li A., Baidu Inc, Beijing, China; Zhang J., Baidu Inc, Beijing, China; Li W., Baidu Inc, Beijing, China; Liu S., Baidu Inc, Beijing, China; Shi D., Baidu Inc, Beijing, China; Tian Y., School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University, Changchun, China, Engineering Research Center of Knowledge-Driven Human-Machine Intelligence, MOE, Changchun, China
Abstract: Query rewriting is a core component of web search, yet traditional methods mainly rely on large language model (LLM) prompting, fine-tuning, or personalized rewriting based on user history. These approaches often overlook population-level intent signals in large-scale query logs, leading to misalignment with mainstream search intent. Moreover, although large models achieve high rewriting quality, their computational demands and deployment complexity limit industrial applicability. To address this, we propose Population-Guided Intent-Aware Rewriting (PGIR), which captures dominant population intent via a Semantic Clustering Unit (SCU) and generates intent-aware rewrites through a Rewriting Unit (RU), aligning queries with mainstream search goals without requiring user history.Building upon PGIR, we further introduce PGIR-DPA, a dual-phase adaptation strategy that transfers capabilities from a teacher LLM to lightweight student models, achieving high-quality rewriting while ensuring industrial scalability. Extensive offline and online experiments, including A/B testing on Baidu Search, show substantial improvements in rewrite quality and a 6.28% relative increase in user satisfaction. The framework has been fully deployed in Baidu's production search system, operating stably at scale, validating its industrial feasibility and commercial value. © 2026 Owner/Author.

Title: Read the Room or Lead the Room: Understanding Socio-Cognitive Dynamics in Human-AI Teaming
Source title: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, LAK 2026
Affiliations: University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Choi J., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States; Samadi M.A., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States; Jaquay S., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States; Park S., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States; Nixon N., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States
Abstract: Research on Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) has traditionally examined how humans rely on one another cognitively and socially to accomplish tasks together. With the rapid advancement of AI and large language models, however, a new question emerge: what happens to team dynamics when one of the “teammates" is not human? In this study, we investigate how the integration of an AI teammate – a fully autonomous GPT-4 agent with social, cognitive, and affective capabilities – shapes the socio-cognitive dynamics of CPS. We analyze discourse data collected from human-AI teaming (HAT) experiments conducted on a novel platform specifically designed for HAT research. Using two natural language processing (NLP) methods, specifically Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) and Group Communication Analysis (GCA), we found that AI teammates often assumed the role of dominant cognitive facilitators, guiding, planning, and driving group decision-making. However, they did so in a socially detached manner, frequently pushing agenda in a verbose and repetitive way. By contrast, humans working with AI used more language reflecting social processes, suggesting that they assumed more socially oriented roles. Our study highlights how learning analytics can provide critical insights into the socio-cognitive dynamics of human-AI collaboration. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: A System-Oriented Analytical Framework for Assessing Digital Learning Platforms and Student Psychological Adaptation Using Data-Driven Methods
Source title: International Academic Journal of Science and Engineering
Affiliations: School of Management Studies, Vels Institute of Science, Technology and Advanced Studies (VISTAS), Pallavaram, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India
Authors with affiliations: Janifa D., School of Management Studies, Vels Institute of Science, Technology and Advanced Studies (VISTAS), Pallavaram, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India; Gokulakrishnan A., School of Management Studies, Vels Institute of Science, Technology and Advanced Studies (VISTAS), Pallavaram, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India
Abstract: Digital learning has enabled more flexible, accessible, and intelligent learning experiences. The present evaluation methods for digital learning platforms focus mainly on educational results and system usability, neglecting the mental adaptability of learners in dynamic online learning contexts. Based on the mentioned gap, this study proposes a new cognitive resilience assessment model in digital learning environments based on the system-oriented adaptive cognitive resilience framework (SACRF), which evaluates digital learning platforms and analyzes students' mental adaptability by making data-driven intelligent assessments on the basis of behavioral learning analytics, engagement features, psychological resilience variables, emotion adaptation, and system performance characteristics integrated into a single system. Furthermore, a novel dynamic psychological adaptation index (DPAI) is proposed to measure students' coping ability under the impact of academic stress, changing environments, and the transition of technology adaptation. A machine learning model and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) approach are integrated to make the influential features and intelligent prediction on adaptation and learning results as explainable as possible, as well as an adaptive intervention method, which is implemented to deliver immediate, individualized recommendations to improve learning engagement, mitigate psychological stress, and maintain the learning process. The proposed SACRF can attain an adaptation prediction accuracy up to 95.4% with the average 30-35% improvement on cognitive resilience and about 25% improvement on early risk detection compared to benchmark approaches on different evaluation indices. The conclusion suggests that psychological adaptation analytics are necessary in the digital learning platform evaluation to support an adaptive, intelligent, and learner-centric learning environment, and the framework presents a stable and well-scaled method for boosting sustainable digital education. © 2026, International Academic Institute for Science and Technology. Title: GeoPaperLLM: A Fine-Tuning Based Two-Stage Framework for Hierarchical Classification of Geoscience Literature
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Zhejiang Lab, Zhejiang Province, Hangzhou, 311100, China
Authors with affiliations: Miao Y., Zhejiang Lab, Zhejiang Province, Hangzhou, 311100, China; Luo S., Zhejiang Lab, Zhejiang Province, Hangzhou, 311100, China; Zhan K., Zhejiang Lab, Zhejiang Province, Hangzhou, 311100, China
Abstract: The boom in AI4Science has driven the rapid development of geoscience domain-specific large language models (LLMs). Literature subject classification (LSC) is a foundational core task in this process, which screens target domain corpus to support LLM training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and evaluation. However, this task is plagued by three key challenges: low full-text classification efficiency, inadequate geoscience-specific optimization, and a lack of high-quality hierarchical labeled datasets. To address these challenges, this study designs a two-stage hierarchical classification framework for geoscience subject identification, first judging geoscience affiliation and then identifying 8 secondary sub-disciplines. We construct a dedicated benchmark dataset with 280,000 subject-annotated entries covering papers, dissertations, and books. A lightweight inference LLM is trained via teacher-student paradigm: the teacher model generates CoT reasoning processes for disciplinary affiliation, and the student model is fine-tuned with CoT and subject label data to output JSON-formatted hierarchical results. Comparative experiments demonstrate that our model achieves superior classification accuracy while maintaining a balance between deployment cost and inference efficiency, providing high-quality corpus support for training geoscience LLMs and serving as a valuable reference for discipline classification in other scientific domains. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Abstract: Large foundation models such as BERT achieve remarkable phishing detection accuracy but are impractical for real-time deployment on resource-constrained devices, while lightweight models offer low latency but limited generalization. This paper proposes CloudPhishNet, a three-tier collaborative phishing detection framework that synergizes large and small models across a cloud-edge-client continuum. The cloud tier deploys a fine-tuned BERT model for deep semantic analysis and serves as the knowledge distillation teacher; the edge tier uses a CatBoost classifier for secondary validation; and the client tier employs an aggressively pruned CatBoost variant for rapid local screening. A soft-label knowledge distillation pipeline transfers the teacher’s semantic understanding to lightweight student models, improving pruned-model accuracy by up to 0.38 points. A reinforcement learning mechanism integrating Q-learning, DQN, and PPO dynamically orchestrates cross-layer workload offloading based on real-time device states. Experiments on benchmark phishing datasets demonstrate that CloudPhishNet achieves 96.9% detection accuracy—only 1.2 points below cloud-only BERT—while reducing inference latency by 86.4% and processing 75% of samples locally. The client model compresses to 0.02 MB (98% compression ratio) while retaining 97.4% F1 performance. The DQN-based offloading strategy outperforms all heuristic baselines in average reward. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Preserving Human Judgment in AI-Enabled Education: The SAM Model for AI Readiness, Assessment, and Human-in-the-Loop Decision Making

Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) shifts educational focus from access to information toward judging machine-generated claims and regulating the division of epistemic work. This conceptual article proposes the SAM model—self-regulation (S), ambiguity tolerance (A), and methodological competence (M)—as a bounded person-level resource model within broader AI readiness, with educators’ AI readiness as a central application. S denotes regulatory capacity, A a disposition-like willingness to tolerate unresolved epistemic ambiguity, and M the capacity to evaluate claims, differentiated into cross-domain M1 and domain-specific M2. SAM’s distinctive claim is configurational: M should predict independently assessed judgment more strongly at higher S and, under high ambiguity, when A is higher. These relations, the M1/M2 distinction, limited compensability, and incremental prediction beyond shared and neighboring accounts remain hypothetical. The model separates resources from enacted processes, contextual affordances, and outcomes and requires independent performance criteria. For AI-based assessment and learning analytics, educators’ interpretations of AI-derived evidence and construct inferences from behavioral traces require validated mappings addressing alternative explanations, comparability, fairness, and use. SAM thus offers a research agenda predicting when AI support preserves human judgment rather than merely improving supported performance. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: The design framework for pedagogical agents supporting constructivist learning with generative AI

Abstract: While generative AI lowers the barrier to creating pedagogical agents, unguided designs risk undermining learner agency and exposing learners to hallucinated content. This paper argues that a constructivist framing provides a strong theoretical basis for realigning pedagogical agent design to promote active knowledge construction and problem-solving. Guided by constructivist principles, we propose a design framework that (1) incorporates context-aware, in-the-moment guidance within authentic, open-ended learning activities; (2) supports the development of interpretation through productive cognitive conflict; (3) encourages collaboration and group discussions; (4) allows artifact co-creation with formative evaluation; and (5) fine-tunes cognitive apprenticeship strategies and intervention timing. We demonstrate how agents implement these principles by applying generative AI and multimodal learning analytics across various constructivist learning settings, including science labs, simulations, and computational modeling environments. We also highlight key safeguards essential for designing and deploying responsible pedagogical agents, including roles in collaboration, teacher oversight, prompt-before-answer rules, positive and open attitudes toward agent use, and maintaining activity authenticity. Grounding pedagogical agents in constructivist principles enables effective use of generative AI's capabilities while addressing its risks, thereby supporting deeper constructivist learning. © 2026

Title: The Educational Economics Simulation Hub: Exploring Power Law Signatures in Student Learning, Engagement, and Strategy
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Secondary School “Einaudi-Molari”, RN, Santarcangelo di Romagna, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Silvestri M., Secondary School “Einaudi-Molari”, RN, Santarcangelo di Romagna, Italy
Abstract: This paper presents the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of the Educational Economics Simulation Hub, a platform of 24 economic simulation games developed and deployed in secondary school classes as both a teaching tool and a research instrument, combining evidence-based learning design with data-driven behavioural analytics. Each simulator immerses students in a concrete economic role, provides immediate feedback, and feeds a nine-competency assessment framework monitored via a teacher dashboard. Analysing 12,349 strategic decisions from 57 students across four eligible simulators, we find preliminary evidence consistent with three Power Law distributions: the Power Law of Practice (β=0.528, R2=0.952), Pareto engagement (α=1.839, R2=0.846), and Zipf strategy frequency (α=2.051, R2=0.829). The platform was built through vibe coding—natural language collaboration with generative AI—showing that teachers without high programming skills can design research-grade experiential learning environments. These findings are exploratory (N=57) and require larger-scale replication. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: AI-Empowered BIM Course Teaching Reform: A Cross-Integration and Project-Driven Approach
Source title: Proceedings of the 3rd International Conference on Educational Digitalization and Computer Science in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, EDCS 2026
Affiliations: Department of Engineering Management, Hunan University of Information Technology, Changsha, China
Authors with affiliations: Liao Y., Department of Engineering Management, Hunan University of Information Technology, Changsha, China
Abstract: Addressing persistent challenges in BIM course instruction-disconnect between curriculum and industry practice, delayed feedback, and insufficient integration of emerging technologies-this study employs the “Building Information Modeling (BIM) Technology Applications” course as a case study to investigate AI embedding strategies across the entire instructional process. The course team developed a “Cross-Integration and Project-Driven” model deploying AI at three stages: pre-class, the SuperStarLearn platform captures preparation data to generate learning analytics; in-class, an AI-powered drawing review tool using Structured Similarity Index (SSIM) image comparison algorithms automatically detects discrepancies between student models and reference standards, reducing evaluation from days to minutes; post-class, students use domestic AI platforms-DeepSeek and Doubao AI-to develop Python scripts (pandas/matplotlib) or Excel formulas (VLOOKUP/SUMPRODUCT) for carbon emission calculation and analysis. Empirical results show final exam scores rising from 71.3 to 76.3 points. The core novelty lies not in any single tool, but in the systematic integration pathway linking pre-class, in-class, and post-class AI applications into a coherent instructional loop-a holistic framework largely absent in prior research. This study offers a replicable framework for integrating AI tools within engineering education. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: Data augmentation (DA) is a widely adopted approach for mitigating data insufficiency. Conducting DA in private domains requires privacy-preserving text generation, including anonymization or perturbation applied to sensitive textual data. The above methods lack formal protection guarantees. Existing Differential Privacy (DP) learning methods provide theoretical guarantees by adding calibrated noise to models or outputs. However, the large output space and model scales in text generation require substantial noise, which severely degrades synthesis quality. In this paper, we transfer DP-based synthetic sample generation to DP-based sample discrimination. Specifically, we propose a DP-based DA framework with a large language model (LLM) and a DP-based discriminator for private-domain text generation. Our key idea is to (1) leverage LLMs to generate large-scale high-quality samples, (2) select synthesized samples fitting the private domain, and (3) align the label distribution with the private domain. To achieve this, we use knowledge distillation to construct a DP-based discriminator: teacher models, accessing private data, guide a student model to select samples under calibrated noise. A DP-based tutor further constrains the label distribution of synthesized samples with a low privacy budget. We theoretically analyze the privacy guarantees and empirically validate our method on three medical text classification datasets, showing that our DP-synthesized samples significantly outperform state-of-the-art DP fine-tuning baselines in utility. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Abstract: This work provides a practical AI solution for home-school collaborative personalized after-school learning. This paper presents Smart Math Companion, a generative AI-powered personalized learning system for junior high school after-school mathematics education. To address the challenges of limited learning engagement and insufficient family support, the system employs an LLM-agent-based framework that transforms after-school learning from isolated problem solving into a continuous process of personalized planning, interactive exploration, multimodal learning, and reflective feedback. Specifically, the system constructs a dynamic learner model covering knowledge, motivation, and cognition to support personalized learning planning and adaptive exercise generation. It further integrates agent-based inquiry and problem transformation mechanisms to facilitate conceptual understanding and transferable problem-solving skills. To enhance learning accessibility, the system generates multimodal learning resources, including visual explanations, AI podcasts, and interactive mathematical visualizations. In addition, a learning analytics module converts student learning traces into interpretable reports and actionable tutoring suggestions for parents, forming a closed loop of learning, analysis, guidance, and improvement. Preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed framework in enhancing learning experiences and supporting home-school collaborative personalized learning. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Gamified Learning for EFL Public Speaking: Feasibility, Design Framework, and a Preregisterable Evaluation Protocol

Abstract: Gamified speaking practice is increasingly common in EFL courses, yet many implementations are difficult to evaluate and may produce short-lived engagement gains. This paper proposes a theory-grounded, AI-assisted gamified framework for university EFL public speaking that combines brief speaking missions with rubric-referenced coaching powered by large language models. Grounded in self-determination theory, the design emphasizes meaningful choice, calibrated challenge, and opt-in social support to support sustained practice while seeking to avoid undermining learner autonomy. We contribute (1) design principles and testable hypotheses linking game mechanics to speaking pedagogy, (2) a modular, prototype-oriented architecture for blended or mobile deployment, and (3) a preregisterable, semester-long evaluation protocol with standardized short academic mini-talk tasks and blinded rubric-based rating with rater calibration. We also outline responsible AI safeguards for audio data, transparency, and teacher oversight. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: With generative artificial intelligence driving the growth of dialogic data in education, automated coding is a promising direction for learning analytics to improve efficiency. This surge highlights the need to understand the nuances of student-AI interactions, especially those rare yet crucial. However, automated coding may struggle to capture these rare codes due to imbalanced data, while human coding remains time-consuming and labour-intensive. The current study examined the potential of large language models (LLMs) to approximate or replace humans in deductive, theory-driven coding, while also exploring how human–AI collaboration might support such coding tasks at scale. We compared the coding performance of small transformer classifiers (e.g., BERT) and LLMs in two datasets, with particular attention to imbalanced head–tail distributions in dialogue codes. Our results showed that LLMs did not outperform BERT-based models and exhibited systematic errors and biases in deductive coding tasks. We designed and evaluated a human–AI collaborative workflow that improved coding efficiency while maintaining coding reliability. Our findings reveal both the limitations of LLMs – especially their difficulties with semantic similarity and theoretical interpretations – and the indispensable role of human judgment, while demonstrating the practical promise of human–AI collaborative workflows for coding. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Artificial Intelligence-Empowering Formative Assessment: Research Progress and Future Directions

Authors with affiliations: Yang Y., Zhejiang Institute of Economics and Trade, Zhejiang, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: Formative assessment is crucial for achieving a high standard of education, yet it often lacks personalisation and timeliness. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into formative assessment has therefore become a central theme in contemporary digital education research. Based on the Web of Science (WoS) database, this paper employs bibliometric analysis and CiteSpace visualization to examine the literature on generative AI-empowered formative assessment from 2019 to 2025. Annual publication trends, keyword co-occurrences, and thematic clusters are analyzed. The findings reveal a research evolution from”theoretical investigation” to”technological adoption”to”multidisciplinary implementation” with research hotspots focusing on intelligent feedback, large language models, deep learning, and adaptive assessment. Contemporary research, however, still remains constrained by technical dependency, low-quality data, and inherent limitations of foundation models and potential ethical risks. Accordingly, this study proposes a systematic framework comprising four dimensions of object, data, technology, and application to reconstruct learner-centered evaluation paradigms, enable cross-layer coordination, and realize a closed-loop intelligent assessment system. The findings have significant theoretical and practical implications for digital transformation and paradigm reconstruction of educational assessment in the era of AI. © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: GluKDnet: A Lightweight Blood Glucose Prediction Model Based on Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation
Source title: Big Data and Cognitive Computing
Affiliations: College of Information Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, 110819, China
Authors with affiliations: Teng A., College of Information Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, 110819, China; Sun X., College of Information Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, 110819, China; Li H., College of Information Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, 110819, China; Yu X., College of Information Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, 110819, China
Abstract: Accurate blood glucose prediction is essential for glycemic management in people with diabetes, but the size of many high-performing models complicates execution on resource-constrained artificial pancreas controllers. We propose GluKDnet, a lightweight glucose-forecasting model for prospective Android-smartphone-based mobile edge controllers. GluKDnet transfers the representational capacity of a time-series foundation model to a compact causal CNN through heterogeneous knowledge distillation. The teacher model, MOMENT, is adapted to continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data through risk-event-aware masking, which prioritizes abnormal glucose levels, rapid glucose fluctuations, and CGM-defined dawn phenomenon and Somogyi effect patterns during masked reconstruction. A transient-state and steady-state distillation module jointly aligns ordered patch-level dynamics and day-level summaries between teacher and student. Using DLCP3 for teacher pretraining and leave-one-patient-out evaluation on OhioT1DM, GluKDnet achieves RMSE values of 20.04, 32.04, and 45.33 mg/dL for 30, 60, and 120 min prediction, respectively, with about 53K parameters. Auxiliary evaluation on T1D-UoM shows a similar offline accuracy–parameter count pattern. On a vivo V2072A Android smartphone, the 30 min model achieved a mean API inference latency of 0.470 ms (P95: 0.855 ms), a maximum sampled process proportional-set-size memory of 47.06 MiB, and a median incremental device energy estimate of 0.277 mJ per inference. These device measurements characterize the exported student model under one hardware and software configuration; insulin dosing and prospective closed-loop clinical evaluation remain outside the scope of this study. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: The advancement of digital technologies and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed learning environments in higher education; while tools such as ChatGPT offer personalized experiences and immediate feedback, their relationship with academic performance remains insufficiently understood in university contexts. This study analyzed the use of technological resources in the AI era, considering frequency of use, perceived usefulness, familiarity, and type of use, as well as their contribution to university students’ academic performance and identifying technological and contextual factors associated with it. A data-mining approach was employed, applying 10 supervised regression algorithms using 10-fold cross-validation, complemented by interpretability analysis using SHAP values to identify relevant predictors. Regularized regression models (Elastic Net; Lasso) showed the best relative predictive performance. The SHAP analysis revealed that the field of study (≈ 0.41) and study cycle (≈ 0.34) are the dominant predictors, while the use of AI for academic writing (≈ 0.10) emerged as the technological variable with the greatest positive contribution to academic GPA within the model. Academic performance was mainly associated with structural factors related to students’ educational trajectories, while AI tools showed a complementary role. The predictive contribution of technology appears to depend more on pedagogical integration than on frequency of use alone. These findings suggest the need to integrate digital strategies into higher education, implementing them in a differentiated manner by discipline and academic level, and promoting the guided and purposeful use of AI and technological resources in learning processes. Title: LLM-Assisted Resource-Aware Weakly Supervised Multimodal Extraction of Climate-Risk Signals from ESG Documents
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Université Paris Cité, Paris, 75013, France; University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, 230052, China
Authors with affiliations: Theang P., Université Paris Cité, Paris, 75013, France; Thuon N., University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, 230052, China
Abstract: Climate-risk evidence in ESG reports is often distributed across narrative text, KPI tables, targets, and governance disclosures, making block-level extraction difficult under limited annotation. We propose a resource-aware framework that combines rule-based weak supervision, selective multimodal teacher refinement, and compact student models. ESG PDFs are parsed into a report–page–block corpus, and initial labels are generated using keyword and heuristic rules. Qwen2.5-VL reviews only 1,000 ambiguous blocks using the page image and block text; accepted outputs are merged with a manually corrected gold subset. We compare TF-IDF and DistilBERT under weak-only, weak+gold, weak+LLM, and weak+LLM+ gold supervision using a company-level gold-only test set. TF-IDF is a strong low-cost baseline, whereas DistilBERT benefits most from improved supervision. The best weak+LLM +gold DistilBERT model reaches 0.8694 macro-F1 on 102 gold test blocks, compared with 0.8459 for TF-IDF. The results indicate that multimodal LLMs are most useful as selective supervision refiners, while compact models remain suitable for efficient deployment. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Kim G.; Jeong W.-K.
Title: LaGuadia: Language-Guided Adaptive Distillation from Pathology Foundation Models
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, College of Informatics, Korea University, Seoul, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Kim G., Department of Computer Science and Engineering, College of Informatics, Korea University, Seoul, South Korea; Jeong W.-K., Department of Computer Science and Engineering, College of Informatics, Korea University, Seoul, South Korea
Abstract: Pathology Foundation Models (PFMs) offer powerful Whole Slide Image (WSI) representations but suffer from massive computational costs. While Knowledge Distillation (KD) can create efficient student models, existing multi-teacher methods often use suboptimal uniform weighting that ignores tissue heterogeneity. We propose LaGuadia (Language-Guided Adaptive DistillAtion), a framework that develops a compact pathology image encoder by dynamically integrating expertise from multiple PFMs under clinical linguistic guidance. Our approach utilizes a multi-stage pipeline: first, extracting visually observable clinical keywords from pathology reports; second, aligning visual features with these keywords via a Vision-Language meta-teacher (MedSigLIP) to provide dense semantic guidance; and finally, performing adaptive KD where teacher contributions are weighted based on their semantic alignment with the clinical narrative. Experiments on WSI captioning, visual question answering, and slide-level classification tasks demonstrate that an 87M parameter LaGuadia student model matches or exceeds foundation-scale models such as GigaPath and UNI, achieving strong factual consistency and robust generalization. These results highlight clinical language as an effective semantic anchor for building efficient and reliable digital pathology systems. Abstract: Nonverbal communication is essential for effective oral presentations, shaping audience engagement and conveying confidence beyond spoken words. Multimodal Learning Analytics (MmLA) research has advanced the automatic detection of presenters’ behaviors—such as posture, gestures, and eye contact—but continues to explore how to provide actionable feedback that fosters reflection and skill development. Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offer new opportunities to automate the analysis of nonverbal cues and generate narrative evaluations that go beyond raw metrics. This study investigates the integration of a Learning Analytics Dashboard (LAD) with a Large Language Model (LLM) to deliver both numerical and narrative feedback across five dimensions of nonverbal communication: body posture, eye contact, hand gestures, facial expression, and use of space. Twenty-two undergraduate students participated in the study, receiving numerical feedback through a LAD and narrative feedback from either a human expert or an LLM. Findings revealed no significant differences in students’ perceptions of human- and LLM-generated feedback, while also highlighting the potential of LLM-based feedback to support reflection despite certain technical limitations. These results suggest that LLMs can meaningfully enhance learning analytics dashboards by delivering actionable, human-like feedback that supports the development of nonverbal communication skills. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Explainable Rating Prediction and Sentiment-Segmented Summarization for E-Governance Applications

Abstract: E-governance applications have become essential platforms for citizen-government interaction, with user feedback crucial in improving service quality and transparency. However, existing approaches face significant challenges, including inconsistency between textual reviews and star ratings, lack of interpretability in automated rating predictions, and the inability to generate actionable, sentiment-specific insights from unstructured textual reviews. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a unified framework for explainable rating prediction and sentiment-segmented summarization. Our approach employs a neural network for accurate rating prediction and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) module for interpretable justifications of predicted ratings. We also leverage large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate targeted summaries from user textual reviews segmented by sentiment (positive, negative, neutral). A comprehensive evaluation on real-world e-governance data shows that the framework generates clear and logical rating explanations, with human evaluators assigning an average score of 4.2 out of 5 for clarity and justification quality. Similarly, LLMs-generated summaries are highly readable and often outperform human-written ones, particularly for non-native English speakers. Title: Understanding the role of learning analytics and generative artificial intelligence on decision-making and learning design practice in higher education
Source title: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Affiliations: Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Claassen A., Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia; Ebbert D., Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia; Kovanović V., Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia; Mirriahi N., Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia; Dawson S., Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia
Abstract: High-quality learning design is an important contributor to student success. Higher education institutions can leverage the combined potential of learning analytics (LA) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to enhance instructors’ learning design practices. However, the way LA and GenAI are being used in combination for learning design is not well understood. In this context, one theory that can provide valuable insights into instructors’ technology integration into learning design (LD) practice is Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using SDT as an interpretative lens, this study illuminates the factors in instructors’ learning design practices when utilising LA and GenAI. For this purpose, we employed quantitative ethnography to explore how instructors utilise LA and GenAI for LD. Eleven focus groups were conducted with instructors from a large Australian university. Using thematic analysis, we created a codebook consisting of ten codes that were applied to our dataset and then analysed using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA). Our results show that instructors’ LA-informed LD discussions primarily revolved around course, contextual, and creative problem-solving considerations, as well as student support. The predominant GenAI factors were assessment design, contextual consideration, creative problem solving and design for student self-determination. Based on our results, we discuss the integration of LA and GenAI in LD practice and decision-making, highlighting the practical implications of our findings. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: AI-generated podcasts and learning outcomes: The role of behavioral engagement and scaffolding
Source title: Computers and Education
Affiliations: Department of Information and Technology Management, University of Tampa, Tampa, FL, United States
Authors with affiliations: Rezvani E., Department of Information and Technology Management, University of Tampa, Tampa, FL, United States
Abstract: The growing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education raises questions about their effectiveness in fostering learning. This study examines whether AI-generated podcasts can support student learning in a predominantly in-person course. Using data from two semesters with near identical course designs (n = 171), we compare learning outcomes between a semester without podcasts and a semester in which students had access to AI-generated podcasts aligned with course chapters and supplemented by study guides. Exam performance was higher in the semester with podcast availability, while final course grades were similar across semesters. To explore how podcasts relate to learning outcomes, we analyze variation in student engagement with the podcasts during the semester with podcast availability using learning management system analytics. To mitigate potential endogeneity in engagement, we employ an instrumental-variable approach in which access to study guides serves as an instructional scaffold that encourages podcast use. The results indicate that greater engagement is positively associated with both exam performance and final course grades, though the estimated effects are modest in magnitude. Overall, the findings suggest that AI-generated podcasts, when paired with scaffolding such as study guides, can enhance engagement and support learning in higher education. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Artificial intelligence in medical education: a narrative review across four functional domains
Source title: Currents in Pharmacy Teaching and Learning
Affiliations: Department of Pharmacology, Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran; Department of Pharmacology, Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Shiraz, Iran; Petroleum Industry Health Organization, Shiraz, Iran; Department of Pharmaceutics, Faculty of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences, Tehran Medical Sciences, Islamic Azad University, Tehran, Iran
