Title: CIHML: A Heterogeneous Mutual Learning Knowledge Distillation Framework Based on Intermediate Layer Alignment
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 13th International Conference on Machine Intelligence Theory and Applications, MiTA 2026
Affiliations: Yantai University, School Of Computer And Control Engineering, Yantai, China; Dongfang Electronics Co., Ltd, Yantai, China
Authors with affiliations: Cheng S., Yantai University, School Of Computer And Control Engineering, Yantai, China; Tong X., Yantai University, School Of Computer And Control Engineering, Yantai, China; Li T., Dongfang Electronics Co., Ltd, Yantai, China
Abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning technology, knowledge distillation has become a key method for improving the performance of lightweight models, particularly demonstrating significant potential in the fine-tuning of large language models. However, existing distillation methods primarily focus on aligning the output layers, neglecting the consistency of semantic representation and structural modeling in the model's intermediate layers. This results in limited performance of the student model in complex tasks. Additionally, when faced with multi-task or multi-modal scenarios, there is a lack of systematic design for collaborative learning mechanisms between heterogeneous models, which impacts distillation effectiveness and model generalization capabilities. To address these issues, we propose a Deep Mutual Learning (DML) framework based on an intermediate layer alignment mechanism. By introducing Cross-layer Intermediate Representation Alignment (CIRA), we achieve efficient alignment of semantic representations between teacher and student models at the intermediate layer, thereby enhancing the student model's semantic modeling capabilities. Additionally, for multi-task and multi-modal environments, we design a Heterogeneous Mutual Distillation (HML) strategy to effectively coordinate the collaborative optimization of models with different architectures and tasks, enhancing knowledge sharing and task adaptability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms traditional KD and single-model fine-tuning on multiple public datasets, with the student model achieving substantial improvements in accuracy, convergence speed, and inference efficiency. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: LongCoT-Transfer: Transferring Complex Reasoning from Large to Small LLMs for Sequential Decision-Making
Source title: 38th Chinese Control and Decision Conference, CCDC 2026
Affiliations: College of Artificial Intelligence, Nankai University, Tianjin, China
Authors with affiliations: Wu H., College of Artificial Intelligence, Nankai University, Tianjin, China; Li Z., College of Artificial Intelligence, Nankai University, Tianjin, China; Li H., College of Artificial Intelligence, Nankai University, Tianjin, China; Fang Y., College of Artificial Intelligence, Nankai University, Tianjin, China; Guo X., College of Artificial Intelligence, Nankai University, Tianjin, China
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT, Claude and DeepSeek-R1 excel at complex reasoning, but their size and computational cost limit low-latency, resource-efficient deployment. In contrast, lightweight LLMs are easier to deploy but often lack the planning and decision-making abilities required for deep, multi-step reasoning, limiting their ability to perform sequential decision tasks independently. To address these challenges, we propose LongCoT-Transfer, a method that transfers complex reasoning capabilities from large teacher models to lightweight student models through distillation and filtering of high-quality long chain-of-thought (LongCoT) trajectories. Applied in the text-based LLM-Cave, it first generates raw reasoning trajectories by the teacher model interacting with the environment, then employs a novel dual-filtering mechanism based on task success and cumulative reward to select highquality samples, forming a refined supervised fine-tuning(SFT) dataset.Additionally, we propose a multi-dimensional capability evaluation mechanism that combines task success, cumulative reward, and action efficiency to comprehensively assess the method. Experimental results show that lightweight models trained with LongCoT-Transfer achieve task success and generalization performance competitive with GPT-4o, and significantly outperform those trained with standard chain-of-thought(CoT) distillation, validating the effectiveness of our reasoning transfer framework. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Effective peer feedback is essential for developing critical reflection in higher education, yet its impact is often limited by the inconsistent quality of student-generated comments. This paper presents the implementation and deployment of AICoFe (AI-based Collaborative Feedback), a system designed to bridge this gap through a human-centered AI approach. We describe a modular architecture that orchestrates a multi-LLM pipeline—utilizing GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Llama 3.1—to synthesize quantitative rubric data and qualitative observations into coherent, actionable feedback. Key to the system is a”teacher-in-the-loop” mediation workflow, where educators use specialized Learning Analytics dashboards to curate and refine AI-generated drafts before delivery. Furthermore, we detail the underlying data infrastructure, which employs a hybrid SQL and MongoDB strategy to ensure traceability and manage semi-structured feedback versions. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: Learning Management Systems (LMS) generate rich activity and interaction logs that can be exploited using machine learning techniques. This study models temporal engagement patterns, such as early, middle, late, weekend, and night activity, derived from Moodle logs in multiple undergraduate courses. It constructs temporal feature vectors per-student, applies k-means clustering to uncover behavioral patterns, and then uses ANOVA and Kruskal–Wallis tests to assess whether patterns differ in final grades. Results show that the predictive value of temporal patterns is highly course-dependent; in some courses, structured early engagement aligns with higher achievement, whereas in others, heavy weekend and night usage is associated with the best outcomes. To complement the obtained quantitative analyses, a Large Language Model (LLM) (i.e., ChatGPT) is evaluated as a zero-shot classifier that receives only natural-language summaries of temporal behavior and predicts performance tiers. While accuracy is limited, the model produces a coherent approach, indicating value as an interpretable layer on top of statistical analysis. The work demonstrates a generalizable pipeline for temporal feature engineering, unsupervised profiling, and LLM-based reasoning over LMS data for early risk detection in digital learning environments. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Topic-Level Feedback Summarization for an Explanation-Based Classroom Response System
Source title: SIGCSE TS 2026 - Proceedings of the 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V.2

Authors with affiliations: Esiason J., North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, United States; Min W., North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, United States; Lee S., North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, United States; Ozogul G., Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, IN, United States; Zheng X., Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, IN, United States; Jeong Y., Indiana University Bloomington, Bloomington, IN, United States; Lester J., North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, United States
Abstract: Fostering engagement among undergraduate computer science students in large-lecture settings can be challenging for instructors. Didactic teaching styles common in such lectures may not be as effective as dialogic teaching, but the overhead involved with dialogic teaching may preclude its use in large introductory computer science courses. Classroom response systems such as multiple-choice “clicker” systems provide a way for students to engage with an instructor, but evidence suggests that multiple-choice questions may not foster deep thought in the way that open-ended questions do. Open-ended questions foster deeper engagement and AI-enabled learning analytics offer a powerful method of automatically assessing student responses, but grading text responses produced by students and summarizing class-wide performance during lectures presents unique difficulties, especially for algorithmic questions prevalent in computer science lectures. We present a system for delivering, assessing, and summarizing students’ responses to open-ended question prompts during such lectures. A central part of this system is the effective summarization of topic-level student responses to provide actionable feedback to the instructor. This poster presents an early phase of this summarization work, analyzing both the quantitative semantic accuracy and qualitative usefulness to instructors of an LLM-based system that summarizes student feedback. Semantic accuracy is found to be high and consistent across different summarization methods. Instructor interviews identified several key qualities of summaries that would be useful, including format preferences and features that would allow selective insight into student responses related to misconceptions. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: EM-KD: Distilling Efficient Multimodal Large Language Model with Unbalanced Vision Tokens
Source title: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
Affiliations: Southeast University, China; Baidu Inc, China
Authors with affiliations: Feng Z., Southeast University, China, Baidu Inc, China; Yang S., Baidu Inc, China; Duan B., Baidu Inc, China; Yang W., Southeast University, China; Wang J., Baidu Inc, China
Abstract: Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) compress vision tokens to reduce resource consumption, but the loss of visual information can degrade comprehension capabilities. Although some priors introduce Knowledge Distillation to enhance student models, they overlook the fundamental differences in fine-grained vision comprehension caused by unbalanced vision tokens between the efficient student and vanilla teacher. In this paper, we propose EM-KD, a novel paradigm that enhances the Efficient MLLMs with Knowledge Distillation. To overcome the challenge of unbalanced vision tokens, we first calculate the Manhattan distance between the vision logits of teacher and student, and then align them in the spatial dimension with the Hungarian matching algorithm. After alignment, EM-KD introduces two distillation strategies: 1) Vision-Language Affinity Distillation (VLAD) and 2) Vision Semantic Distillation (VSD). Specifically, VLAD calculates the affinity matrix between text tokens and aligned vision tokens, and minimizes the smooth L1 distance of the student and the teacher affinity matrices. Considering the semantic richness of vision logits in the final layer, VSD employs the reverse KL divergence to measure the discrete probability distributions of the aligned vision logits over the vocabulary space. Comprehensive evaluation on diverse benchmarks demonstrates that EM-KD trained model outperforms prior Efficient MLLMs on both accuracy and efficiency with a large margin, validating its effectiveness. Compared with previous distillation methods, which are equipped with our proposed vision token matching strategy for fair comparison, EM-KD also achieves better performance. © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). Title: Engagement Intensity as a Learner-Modeling Signal for Adaptive AI Ethics Instruction
Source title: CEUR Workshop Proceedings
Affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, CA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Oh Y., University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, CA, United States; Talton L., University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, CA, United States; Bui A., University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Los Angeles, CA, United States
Abstract: Adaptive AI ethics instruction in graduate research training benefits from intake measures that reflect differences in prior LLM experience. Prior coursework or workshop attendance is an obvious candidate, but it is not clear whether it is associated with pre-instruction ratings on key AI perception items. We compare three candidate intake features, self-reported usage frequency, self-rated LLM familiarity, and prior AI education, across five baseline perception outcomes in 93 bioscience graduate and postdoctoral trainees enrolled in a required research ethics course. Usage frequency shows Holm-corrected associations with all five outcomes, self-rated familiarity with three, and prior AI education with none. A threshold-like pattern at the lower end of the scale is most visible for training interest and accuracy trust rather than appearing as a uniform gradient across all five outcomes. In a short intake survey, reported LLM use is more consistently associated with these perceptions than prior coursework or workshops, with self-rated familiarity serving as a secondary indicator. These results suggest that simple pre-instruction behavioral signals can inform lightweight intake profiling for adaptive AI ethics education. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: This paper presents a bibliometric study of the scientific literature on multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) in education, with the objective of comprehending the intellectual landscape, key contributors, and most prominent and emerging themes in this rapidly developing area of scientific inquiry. The search was conducted on the Scopus database using a Boolean search approach that combined search terms on multimodal AI and education, resulting in a final list of 123 documents published between 2015 and 2026. The VOSviewer software application was used to create co-authorship networks at the author, institutional, and country levels, as well as keyword cooccurrence maps, to explore collaboration and thematic dynamics. The results show that scientific publication in this area was surprisingly low until 2022, when it suddenly jumped to almost 70 publications in 2025, which indicates the explosive development of generative and multimodal AI systems. The United States of America and China emerged as the most productive countries, followed by India and the United Kingdom, while the most influential authors were Giannakos, Michail N., Di Mitri, Daniele, and Cukurova, Mutlu. In the theme analysis, it was revealed that the primary research focus is on multimodal learning analytics, educational technology, and large language models, which have the potential to be applied in emotionally intelligent learning systems, AI-based instructional design, and AI literacy education. These findings indicate the quick maturity and growing educational relevance of the area, as well as the need for more diverse and rigorous research to tap into the full transformative potential of multimodal AI in education. Despite providing a full overview of this everchanging discipline, this research is constrained by both database limits and bibliometric limitations, indicating the requirement for further research in multiple databases and qualitative analysis.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The high pace of increase of computer science education and competitive programming has further enhanced the need of learning support systems that are intelligent. However, many learners struggle with the algorithmic thinking, data organization, and solving attitude due to restricted access to individual advice and conceptual feedback. Conventional programming platforms offer static hints or complete solutions that fail to adapt to individual learning needs, often limiting the development of problem-solving skills. This paper suggests a smart code guidance and adaptive learning platform based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to carry out real-time semantic analysis of learners' code and create dynamic hints and suggestions. The system identifies logical gaps, misconceptions, and inefficient approaches, and provides context-aware guidance that encourages self-discovery rather than direct answer exposure. The Learner modeling module monitors performance and dynamically suggests specific exercises in order to reinforce weak concepts. The proposed system employs scaling with scaling concept to provide personalized tutoring, conceptual understanding and enhancement of algorithmic problem solving capacity by combining LLM-based reasoning and adaptive learning methods to provide an effective end-to-end solution to intelligent programming education. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Incentivizing Strong Reasoning from Weak Supervision
Source title: EACL 2026 - 19th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Proceedings of the Conference, Vol. 1 - (Long Papers)
Affiliations: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China; University of Washington, United States; Allen Institute for AI; Alibaba Group

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, but enhancing their reasoning abilities typically relies on either reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable signals or supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with high-quality long chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations, both of which are expensive. In this paper, we study a novel problem of incentivizing the reasoning capacity of LLMs without expensive high-quality demonstrations and reinforcement learning. We investigate whether the reasoning capabilities of LLMs can be effectively incentivized via supervision from significantly weaker models. We further analyze when and why such weak supervision succeeds in eliciting reasoning abilities in stronger models. Our findings show that supervision from significantly weaker reasoners can substantially improve student reasoning performance, recovering close to 94% of the gains of expensive RL at a fraction of the cost. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and model architectures demonstrate that weak reasoners can effectively incentivize reasoning in stronger student models, consistently improving performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks. Our results suggest that this simple weak-to-strong paradigm is a promising and generalizable alternative to costly methods for incentivizing strong reasoning capabilities at inference-time in LLMs. Code is publicly available at this link. © 2026 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Abstract: Outcome-Based Assessment (OBA) has become a core requirement in higher education quality assurance because it links curriculum design, assessment evidence, attainment analysis, and continuous quality improvement to measurable student outcomes. In practice, however, OBA is still frequently managed through spreadsheets, disconnected tools, and manual reporting, which weaken traceability and increase administrative burden. Therefore, this paper proposes EduTrack, a centralized Outcome-Based Assessment Management System, designed to operationalize the OBA lifecycle in a single platform. EduTrack supports structured outcome management across the outcome-based mapping hierarchy, assessment planning, rubric-based score processing, role-based access control, evidence management, dashboard-based reporting, and support for continuous improvement. The platform is implemented as an on-premise containerized system using Next.js, NestJS, PostgreSQL, Metabase, Python analytical services, and optional local language model integration through Ollama. Compared with prior OBA frameworks and representative systems, EduTrack emphasizes three differentiators: integrated multi-level traceability from program outcomes to course evidence, combined direct and indirect evidence workflows in one system, and an AI-assisted module whose evaluation pipeline calibrates judge models against human annotations before downstream use. As a result, EduTrack provides a practical, auditable, and extensible foundation for institution-scale OBA management while keeping AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance controlled and accountable.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: CA-MAS-LT: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Tutoring System for Dynamic Learning Environments

Abstract: With the deep integration of artificial intelligence and educational technologies, Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) are evolving from single-agent expert systems toward complex multi-agent collaborative architectures. However, most existing systems still lack the ability to perceive and respond to contextual factors in dynamic learning environments. This study proposes a context-aware multi-agent learning tutoring framework designed to enable personalized instructional regulation in fluctuating learning contexts. The system operates through cooperation among five types of agents: a context-awareness agent, a learner modeling agent, a learning-path planning agent, a content-generation agent, and a monitoring-feedback agent. By sensing students' device states, environmental noise, temporal patterns, emotional states, and behavioral features in real time, the system dynamically adjusts learning paths, instructional content, and interaction strategies. A comparative experiment was conducted in an undergraduate learning scenario. Compared with traditional ITS, the proposed multi-agent system demonstrated significant improvements in knowledge mastery, learner engagement, and system adaptivity. Results indicate that integrating context awareness with multi-agent collaboration effectively enhances instructional intelligence and learning experience, offering a new direction for next-generation adaptive educational systems.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in computer-based academic advising and decision-support systems to improve student retention, progression, and timely intervention at scale. However, most current platforms remain largely reactive, focusing on question answering or risk prediction, and lack the ability to explicitly model student goals, curriculum constraints, and adaptive intervention policies. This survey reviews goal-oriented, multi-Agent, and agentic AI architectures for advising systems, with emphasis on software frameworks enabling policy-driven early-warning and intervention for at-risk students in higher education. It traces the evolution from rule-based degree audits and early-warning analytics to advanced architectures integrating learning analytics pipelines, explainable AI (XAI), affect-Aware modelling, reinforcement learning, and LLM-based agents. A unified taxonomy classifies systems by goal representation, planning horizon, risk awareness, intervention autonomy, and governance. The survey highlights gaps between accurate risk detection and actionable intervention logic, examines closed-loop agentic architectures with human-in-The-loop controls, and outlines research challenges in causal validation, equity, scalability, and deployment. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: KTCF: Actionable Recourse in Knowledge Tracing via Counterfactual Explanations for Education
Source title: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Korea University, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Kim W., Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Korea University, South Korea; Lee C., Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Korea University, South Korea; Kim H., Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Korea University, South Korea
Abstract: Using Artificial Intelligence to improve teaching and learning benefits greater adaptivity and scalability in education. Knowledge Tracing (KT) is recognized for student modeling task due to its superior performance and application potential in education. To this end, we conceptualize and investigate counterfactual explanation as the connection from XAI for KT to education. Counterfactual explanations offer actionable recourse, are inherently causal and local, and easy for educational stakeholders to understand who are often non-experts. We propose KTCF, a counterfactual explanation generation method for KT that accounts for knowledge concept relationships, and a post-processing scheme that converts a counterfactual explanation into a sequence of educational instructions. We experiment on a large-scale educational dataset and show our KTCF method achieves superior and robust performance over existing methods, with improvements ranging from 5.7% to 34% across metrics. Additionally, we provide a qualitative evaluation of our post-processing scheme, demonstrating that the resulting educational instructions help in reducing large study burden. We show that counterfactuals have the potential to advance the responsible and practical use of AI in education. Future works on XAI for KT may benefit from educationally grounded conceptualization and developing stakeholder-centered methods. © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). Title: HISE-KT: Synergizing Heterogeneous Information Networks and LLMs for Explainable Knowledge Tracing with Meta-Path Optimization
Source title: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University, Inner Mongolia, Hohhot, China; School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University, Jilin, Changchun, China
Authors with affiliations: Duan Z., Department of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University, Inner Mongolia, Hohhot, China; Shi Z., Department of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University, Inner Mongolia, Hohhot, China; Yuan H., Department of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University, Inner Mongolia, Hohhot, China; Wang Q., School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University, Jilin, Changchun, China
Abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) aims to mine students’ evolving knowledge states and predict their future question-answering performance. Existing methods based on heterogeneous information networks (HINs) are prone to introducing noises due to manual or random selection of meta-paths and lack necessary quality assessment of meta-path instances. Conversely, recent large language models (LLMs)-based methods ignore the rich information across students, and both paradigms struggle to deliver consistently accurate and evidence-based explanations. To address these issues, we propose an innovative framework, HIN-LLM Synergistic Enhanced Knowledge Tracing (HISE-KT), which seam-lessly integrates HINs with LLMs. HISE-KT first builds a multi-relationship HIN containing diverse node types to capture the structural relations through multiple meta-paths. The LLM is then employed to intelligently score and filter meta-path instances and retain high-quality paths, pioneering automated meta-path quality assessment. Inspired by educational psychology principles, a similar student retrieval mechanism based on meta-paths is designed to provide a more valuable context for prediction. Finally, HISE-KT uses a structured prompt to integrate the target student’s history with the retrieved similar trajectories, enabling the LLM to generate not only accurate predictions but also evidence-backed, explainable analysis reports. Experiments on four public datasets show that HISE-KT outperforms existing KT baselines in both prediction performance and interpretability. © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). Abstract: Student satisfaction is the key indicator of educational quality. However, conventional survey-based evaluations often fail to capture the full complexity of students' perceptions and experiences. This study proposes an LLM-based framework for modeling student perceptions in lecturer satisfaction analysis by integrating structured Likert-scale survey responses with unstructured textual feedback. The dataset was collected from 130 student by using a validated ten-item Likert questionnaire covering clarity, responsiveness, commitment, and interactivity. On the other hand, the questionnaire was also collected the student comment that were processed through GPT-5 embeddings to generate contextual semantic representations, which were subsequently fused with quantitative survey data. A Naïve Bayes classifier was selected for this research because its simplicity, interpretability, and robustness with small educational datasets. This research achieved a mean cross-validation accuracy of 97.1%, a test accuracy of 84.6%, an F1-score of 0.905 for the satisfied class, and a perfect ROC AUC of 1.0. It was trained on 80% of the data and tested on the remaining 20%, employing ten-fold cross-validation. This result was indicated the strongest predictors of satisfaction include clarity of explanation, lecturer responsiveness and commitment to teaching. In addition, semantic and numerical insights can provide a holistic view of students' perceptions. This framework demonstrates the potential of large language models for lecturer evaluation to be interpretable, data-driven and context-aware in higher education. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: 3-D object detection is a core capability for intelligent agents to accurately perceive complex environments. Due to the cost advantage of low-beam light detection and ranging (LiDAR), it has been widely adopted in various large-scale applications. However, the sparse point clouds it generates often degrade model detection performance. To address this issue, existing methods usually perform cross-beam distillation based on the bird’s-eye view (BEV). However, this approach ignores the vertical structural information contained in the front view (FV). In FV, the reliability of structural representations varies significantly with depth and occlusion. Directly distilling such features may introduce noise and limit the model’s effective learning of stereoscopic spatial structures. To overcome this limitation, we propose an orthogonal-view (BEV and FV) driven stereoscopic spatial distillation framework. It improves 3-D detection performance for low-beam LiDAR models. Specifically, we introduce an orthogonal structure semantic distillation. It adaptively enhances reliable structural representations from more informative views and suppresses noise from less informative views. This mitigates the local fine-grained information imbalance caused by the differences between BEV and FV, thereby improving the student model’s object perception capability. Furthermore, to address the erroneous transfer of global structural knowledge between teacher and student models, we propose validity spatial selective distillation. It decouples teacher–student features and adopts a differentiated supervision strategy. This allows the student model to compensate for perceptual unobservable regions and reduces erroneous knowledge transfer, thereby improving scene understanding capability. Extensive experiments are conducted on public benchmark datasets including KITTI, nuScenes, Waymo, ONCE, and CMD. The results show that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness and strong generalization ability. © 2005-2012 IEEE.

Title: Long-Chain Reasoning Distillation via Adaptive Prefix Alignment

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities, particularly in solving complex mathematical problems. Recent studies show that distilling long reasoning trajectories can effectively enhance the reasoning performance of small-scale student models. However, teacher-generated reasoning trajectories are often excessively long and structurally complex, making them difficult for student models to learn. This mismatch leads to a gap between the provided supervision signal and the learning capacity of the student model. To address this challenge, we propose Prefix-ALIGNment distillation (P-ALIGN), a framework that fully exploits teacher CoTs for distillation through adaptive prefix alignment. Specifically, P-ALIGN adaptively truncates teacher-generated reasoning trajectories by determining whether the remaining suffix is concise and sufficient to guide the student model. Then, P-ALIGN leverages the teacher-generated prefix to supervise the student model, encouraging effective prefix alignment. Experiments on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that P-ALIGN outperforms all baselines by over 3%. Further analysis indicates that the prefixes constructed by P-ALIGN provide more effective supervision signals, while avoiding the negative impact of redundant and uncertain reasoning components. Title: From Predictive Analytics to Explainable AI in Higher Education: A Bibliometric Mapping
Source title: Qubahan Academic Journal
Affiliations: Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, 13318, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Talmoudi R., Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, 13318, Saudi Arabia; Choukir J., Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, 13318, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: As higher education increasingly relies on data-driven decision-making, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to predict student success and dropout rates is gaining further importance. The primary aim of this study is to understand the evolutionary research trends of data-driven student success management. A PRISMA-based bibliometric analysis of 457 articles is implemented using the R software version 4.5.3 and the bibliometrix package (Version 5.0). Published articles are retrieved from Web of Science Core Collection indexes (SSCI, AHCI, ESCI), covering a three-decade period (1996-2025). The rigorous inclusion/exclusion criteria restricted the dataset to English-language, and peer-reviewed journal articles. Furthermore, co-word analysis and conceptual structure mapping, utilizing the Louvain clustering algorithm, were applied to extract the thematic architecture of the domain. Performance analysis reveals China and U.S. universities as the most influential affiliations shaping the structural volume of this research field, with Applied Sciences emerging as the dominant journal. Additionally, the network analysis indicates an international collaboration rate of 25%. The thematic map reveals that while predictive modeling-based Early Warning Systems (EWS) have matured into Basic Themes, driving Motor Themes included generative artificial intelligence and psychological constructs. Furthermore, Emerging Themes show that explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is drawing a transformative pathway to the field. Higher education managers should integrate XAI while addressing ethical AI governance. Future higher education data-driven management should focus on building transparent systems leading to the empowerment of human decision-makers. © 2026, Qubahan. All rights reserved.

Title: QA Bot: LLM-Based Quality Assurance for Online Courses
Source title: 2nd International Conference on Human-AI Interaction and Experience Design, HAXD 2026
Affiliations: University of Pittsburgh, Center for Excellence in Digital Education, Pittsburgh, United States
Authors with affiliations: Echeverry N., University of Pittsburgh, Center for Excellence in Digital Education, Pittsburgh, United States
Abstract: The increasing demand for online education requires cost-effective and scalable systems to help instructional designers and instructors ensure course quality. The Quality Assurance Bot (QA Bot) addresses this need by conducting rapid evaluations of courses against established standards and practices, including those created by Quality Matters (QM), the Online Learning Consortium (OLC), and the Center for Applied Special Technology (CAST). The QA Bot working prototype takes a Canvas LMS course export (.imscc) as input to utilize a hybrid approach that combines programmatic course file extraction with Large Language Model (LLM)-based evaluation of course data. The QA Bot prioritizes accessibility by supporting smaller, high-performing models (e.g., Llama 3.1 8B) to enable an open-source release. Performance validation involved comparing course quality evaluations conducted by instructional designers (n = 2 per course) with QA Bot outputs using four LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, DeepSeek-R1 8B, GPT-4o, and Claude Sonnet 4) across seven Canvas courses and 20 OLC Essential Design standards (140 course-standard pairs). Pilot results show that instructional designers rated 77.9% of items as Accomplished or Exemplary, while all LLMs assigned Exemplary ratings to fewer than 1% of items, a consistent and significant pattern of underrating across all models. All models produced negative directional bias (range:-0.34 to-0.99), confirming systematic miscalibration rather than mere content misunderstanding. There is also a systematic tendency for LLM justifications to sound more positive than the numeric ratings they assign, occurring in 31-61% of cases across models. Although models generate justifications with moderate semantic similarity to instructional designers (cosine similarity 0.53-0.56), their numeric ratings diverge substantially from those assigned by instructional designers. This paper presents a work-in-progress system and its integration into the learning engineering process. © 2026 IEEE.

Authors: Shu B.
Title: Lightweight compression and acceleration techniques for large language models in English text processing
Source title: Proceedings of SPIE - The International Society for Optical Engineering
Affiliations: Wuhan Technology and Business University, Hubei, Wuhan, 430070, China
Authors with affiliations: Shu B., Wuhan Technology and Business University, Hubei, Wuhan, 430070, China
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in English text processing, yet their substantial computational and memory requirements limit deployment in environments where latency, hardware availability, and energy consumption must be tightly controlled. Existing compression approaches often lead to unstable accuracy degradation on linguistically complex English tasks, insufficient handling of token-level variability during quantization, and weakened semantic coherence after model distillation. To address these limitations, this study proposes an integrated lightweight framework combining an Adaptive Structural Pruning Module (ASPM), a Token-Aware Hybrid Quantization (TAHQ) strategy, and a Distillation-with-Contrastive-Alignment (DCA) mechanism. ASPM reduces structural redundancy through gradient-based salience scoring; TAHQ assigns mixed precision using entropy-guided token evaluation; and DCA maintains contextual consistency between teacher and student models. The proposed framework's applications extend to optical data processing, where computational efficiency is critical for real-time image analysis and pattern recognition. Experiments conducted on three English datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach reduces model parameters from 310M to 182M, achieves a 2.7×±0.3× improvement in inference speed, lowers perplexity by 9.8%±1.2%, and improves classification accuracy by 3.7%±0.9% compared with standard 8-bit quantization. Robustness evaluations further show 4-8% performance gains under paraphrasing and token perturbation. These results indicate that the framework offers a practical balance between efficiency and linguistic fidelity, supporting resource-moderate deployment of LLMs for both English text applications and optical data tasks, such as real-time image processing. © COPYRIGHT SPIE. Title: Lightweight remote sensing multimodal large language model based on knowledge distillation; [基于知识蒸馏的轻量化遥感多模态大语言模型]

Abstract: Remote sensing multimodal large language models（MLLMs），which integrate rich visual-linguistic modal information，have shown great potential in areas such as remote sensing image analysis and interpretation. However，existing knowledge distillation methods primarily focus on the compression of unimodal large language models，neglecting the alignment of features across modalities，thus hindering the performance of large language models in cross-modal tasks. To address this issue，a lightweighting method for remote sensing MLLMs based on knowledge distillation is proposed. This method achieves effective alignment of multimodal information by aligning the outputs across modalities at the feature level. By introducing the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence as the loss function and combining optimization strategies such as teacher mixed sampling and single-step decomposition，the generalization and stability of the student model are further enhanced. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves higher accuracy and efficiency in four downstream tasks of remote sensing image scene classification，visual question answering，visual localization，and image description，significantly reducing the number of model parameters and the demand for computational resources，thereby providing a new solution for the efficient application of MLLMs in the field of remote sensing. © 2026, Chinese Optical Society. Title: Explainable AI for Agriculture: Teacher-Student Learning in Rice Pest Classification
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Affiliations: Can Tho University, Cantho City, Viet Nam; FPT University, Cantho City, Viet Nam
Authors with affiliations: Quach L.-D., Can Tho University, Cantho City, Viet Nam, FPT University, Cantho City, Viet Nam; Le D.-T., Can Tho University, Cantho City, Viet Nam; Nguyen C.-N., Can Tho University, Cantho City, Viet Nam; Thai-Nghe N., Can Tho University, Cantho City, Viet Nam
Abstract: Pests and diseases cause yield losses of 20–30% and are projected to rise sharply to as much as 60%, posing a significant threat to global food security. In response, various studies have applied artificial intelligence; however, they often fall short in leveraging information compression and feature refinement to optimize model parameters effectively and in incorporating Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques to enhance transparency in smart agriculture. To address these gaps, we introduce a Knowledge distillation (KD) architecture that combines Inception-ResNetV2 (teacher) and ResNet-50 (student) models, enhanced with Grad-CAM-based explainability, to improve both performance and interpretability on a rice pest classification dataset comprising over 3,000 images across 10 classes. The proposed approach achieved accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score of 82.50%, 82.35%, 82.50%, and 82.13% (more than 9% of the baseline model). Furthermore, the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric indicates that the teacher model effectively distilled relevant knowledge, enabling the student model to learn critical features. Nevertheless, XAI-based analysis also reveals the model’s limitations in handling class imbalance and visually similar features, suggesting directions for future improvement. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Title: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Large Language Model for Intelligent Curriculum Adaptation and Learning Outcome Improvement
Source title: International Journal on Informatics Visualization
Affiliations: Department of Humanities, College of Science and Theoretical Studies, Saudi Electronic University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Alhamadi A.A., Department of Humanities, College of Science and Theoretical Studies, Saudi Electronic University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: This study outlines the use of an innovative design based on a Knowledge Graph--Enhanced Large Language Model (KG-LLM) to optimize the adaptability of learning plans and improve results within the framework of modern educational systems. Most existing systems for managing educational curricula do not leverage heterogeneous educational data, resulting in a lack of personalization, gaps in mapping educational competencies, and inadequate evaluation outcomes. To overcome the stated issues, the designed system integrates a cognitive collaborative KG, an LLM with contextual intelligence, adaptive recommendation systems, and a unified learning-intelligence ecosystem to focus on ongoing outcome assessment. The system architecture transforms educational competencies, entities, assessments, learning outcomes, and teaching resources into a network of semantically linked representations, enabling effective retrieval and reasoning about curriculum-related knowledge. The system utilizes context-aware educational knowledge to formulate personalized learning pathways and adapt learning resources accordingly. The implementation of the system has shown improvements in various quantifiable educational outcomes. The system's proposed curriculum adaptation accuracy is 98.84%. Learning outcome achievement accuracy is 97.96%. The system scored 98.37% for OBE alignment. KG precision is 99.21% with recall at 98.74%. Semantic relationship extraction accuracy is 99.08%. The system scored 99.34% for LLM relevance, 98.87% for personalized learning recommendations, 98.25% for curriculum gap identification, and 97.94% for learner engagement improvement. The system achieved 99.12% for optimizing learning pathways and 99.46% for precision adaptive content. The integration of cognitive and contextual intelligence with the continuous feedback mechanism demonstrated a scalable educational ecosystem that improved learner engagement and competency attainment, while providing sustainable, continuous improvement of the curriculum. The system results show the potential of KG-LLM integrated with semantic reasoning for intelligent personalization. For stronger dataset-level validation, the study was revised in a Kaggle notebook to incorporate the public dataset “StudentsPerformance.csv,” which contains demographic and exam score data for academic outcome prediction. © 2026, Politeknik Negeri Padang. Title: Analyzing Educational Video Transcripts with LLMs: Accuracy, Named Entities, and Interpretability
Source title: Journal of Educational Data Mining
Affiliations: University of Tennessee Knoxville, United States
Authors with affiliations: Wang W., University of Tennessee Knoxville, United States; Pritchard C., University of Tennessee Knoxville, United States; Rosenberg J., University of Tennessee Knoxville, United States
Abstract: Digital educational media platforms such as YouTube are increasingly used by teachers and learners, creating a growing record of instructional discourse. For educational data mining (EDM) and learning analytics researchers, transcript-derived text offers a scalable entry point for corpus-level analysis, but automatically generated transcripts can contain errors that disproportionately affect named entities and downstream applications. We report an initial validation study of a transcript-to-entity workflow for educational video analysis. The workflow benchmarks multiple automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, evaluates GPT-4o and GPT-5.5 against a 600-token human consensus named-entity benchmark, compares both LLMs with an off-the-shelf spaCy transformer NER pipeline, and applies the model best aligned with the study-specific coding frame to a 48-episode corpus from the Crash Course U.S. History series. The results reveal an important task-dependent trade-off: spaCy performed best at general entity detection, whereas GPT-5.5 showed stronger aggregate performance for codebook-constrained entity typing on gold-entity rows. This finding supports the use of GPT-5.5 for the study’s type-specific corpus profiling without implying universal model superiority. Across the full corpus, PERSON, GPE, and NORP were the most frequent model-coded categories. Topic modeling comparisons further show that transcript-conditioning choices can change thematic separation and interpretability. Together, the findings demonstrate why transcript quality and entity validity should be evaluated according to the downstream educational research task. The workflow provides a reproducible starting point whose corpus-scale outputs can support navigation, sampling, and targeted human review rather than definitive annotation. © 2026 International Educational Data Mining Society. Title: Rethinking Student Engagement in the Age of AI-Mediated Interaction
Source title: Revista Iberoamericana de Tecnologias del Aprendizaje
Affiliations: Universidad Pablo de Olavide, Spain
Authors with affiliations: Manuel C.-M., Universidad Pablo de Olavide, Spain
Abstract: Conventional course delivery rarely adapts to the individual learner, and quantitative service courses such as Statistics combine high failure rates with frequent absence from the examination: in the cohort studied here only 76.6% of 273 enrolled students sat the first sitting and almost one in three of those failed. What is not known is how students actually use AI learning support placed inside such a course. This paper reports a zero-cost field deployment of topic-aligned interactive exercises plus a retrieval-augmented conversational tutor (an open large language model grounded in the course materials, rendered as a 3D avatar) in two undergraduate Business Statistics courses. The research method is a multi-source quantitative observational learninganalytics design. Authentic, unsupervised platform logs, cleaned with a protocol fixed before analysis, were triangulated with the cohort's institutional grades (273 enrolled; 70.8% pass; mean 5.33/10) and a pilot satisfaction survey; the logs yielded 310 exercise completions from 82 students, of which 153 from 53 students form the primary analytical set. Non-parametric tests (Spearman, Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon) with student-level bootstrap confidence intervals and a Poisson model with quiz fixed effects provide proximal interaction evidence rather than a causal grade claim. Engagement was voluntary and recurrent: 69.8% of Statistics users returned for two or more attempts and 58.5% came back in a different calendar week. The exercises revealed a robust internal structure of curricular difficulty (hardest topic 4.29/10, 95% CI [3.27, 5.37]; Kruskal-Wallis p =.002). Students with a lower first score practised more (Spearman rho = - 0.325, 95% CI [-0.566, -0.058]), but that association did not survive normalisation within the same quiz, indicating that practice followed task difficulty rather than relative underperformance. Repeating the same quiz produced no reliably detectable gain. P-values are nominal and unadjusted. © 2013 IEEE.

Title: Ethical Considerations and the Impact of Large Language Models on Automated Feedback Generation and Data Analysis
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Affiliations: Adani Institute of Digital Technology Management, Gujarat, Gandhinagar, India
Authors with affiliations: Shah A., Adani Institute of Digital Technology Management, Gujarat, Gandhinagar, India; Rawal R., Adani Institute of Digital Technology Management, Gujarat, Gandhinagar, India
Abstract: Artificial intelligence-powered learning analytics (LA) shows great results for assisting teachers with the time-consuming task of providing feedback in context to ethical consideration, leads to fairness, maintaining privacy and transparency in feedback. The study investigated two GPT model versions (3.5 and 4) that produce evaluation advice on students’ writing assessment based on assignments in context of data science subject. Abstract: The rapid emergence of Generative AI (GenAI), which gained momentum following the introduction of transformer architecture by Vaswani et al. (2017), has expanded the scope of what learning analytics (LA) can achieve. Traditional approaches to LA have emphasized the importance of understanding learners and their surrounding contexts (Ferguson, 2012). Yet in an increasingly AI-mediated world, there is a growing need to examine not only learners themselves, but the dynamic context of student-AI interactions (Noy & Zhang, 2023). Insights about how students appropriate, resist, or adapt to GenAI-based agents are integral to their continued learning process, particularly as we see the GenAI become increasingly integrated into educational tools such as intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) (Schmucker et al., 2023). Consequently, this opens an opportunity for LA to evolve beyond tracking traditional learning behaviors, toward analyzing how students seek support and construct meaning through interactions with GenAI-driven ITS. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Mohd Anas Wajid and Claudia Camacho-Zuñiga; individual chapters, the contributors.

Abstract: Medical relation extraction (MRE) is a critical foundation for intelligent healthcare tasks such as clinical text analysis and drug repositioning. Although large language models (LLMs) with massive parameter counts have achieved significant progress in general relation extraction, they still face challenges in the medical domain due to the specialized and fine-grained nature of medical relation types, as well as the scarcity of high-quality annotated data. In contrast, smaller models, while offering the advantage of fine-tunability, are limited by their foundational capabilities, failing to capture certain relatively complex semantic patterns in medical relation extraction. Inspired by human cognitive learning, in which individuals reinforce strengths through self-practice and overcome weaknesses with external guidance and repeated practice, this paper proposes a knowledge distillation (KD) framework named KD4FIRE, which integrates the complementary strengths of larger teacher models and smaller student models. Specifically, KD4FIRE first divides samples into easy and hard categories based on the smaller student model’s performance on an initial seed set. For easy samples, chain-of-thought (CoT) self-reinforcement is applied to consolidate the student model’s existing knowledge. For hard samples, we propose an error-aware chain-of-thought refinement method and an abstraction-based data augmentation approach to explicitly address the student model’s knowledge gaps. Experimental results demonstrate that KD4FIRE significantly improves model performance in low-resource scenarios, providing a practical and efficient solution for fine-grained medical relation extraction. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Abstract: Open and distance learning (ODL) serves cohorts of learners under fragile connectivity, yet most early warning and learning analytics tools remain batch, central dashboards that rely on human interpretation and escalation instead of autonomous support. In parallel, work on agentic artificial intelligence (AAI), multi-agent systems (MAS), and edge to cloud computing has produced architectures for perception, decision making and control in domains. This chapter proposes a conceptual framework that transfers these design patterns to low-resource ODL by treating the ecosystem as a multilayer agentic environment with three core classes of agents: learner support agents at the edge, course and programme orchestrator agents at institutional layers, and governance and ethics agents that encode privacy, fairness and accountability while supervising autonomous control loops. We specify agent roles, data and model flows and oversight mechanisms, and use scenarios such as exam periods and connectivity disruptions to outline implications for designing transparent agentic AI in ODL. Abstract: Effective prediction of academic risk is vital in higher education to enable timely intervention and support student retention. While the introduction of Educational Data Mining (EDM) has enhanced prediction effectiveness, existing research often focuses only on single factors or large scale samples, and is notably deficient in providing transparent explanations for prediction results. To address these gaps, this study proposes an Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework for predicting and interpreting academic risk within a high-dimensional, small sample context. Based on a dataset from a specific student cohort, we employed an ML model combined with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method as the XAI framework. The findings provide two major contributions to the “Data-Related Challenges in ML” discussion. Firstly, by leveraging the XAI framework, it successfully enhances data interpretability, revealing the out-of-class peer support as the feature with the strongest association with academic risk, which is a complex and often underestimated data dimension, surpassing traditional academic metrics. Specifically, learning support from peers is identified as the most critical feature in mitigating risk at both the group and individual levels. Secondly, methodologically, this framework validates a reliable approach for extracting meaningful, trustworthy, and interpretable knowledge from limited and specific cohort data, offering a solution for applications with highly contextualized and precise interventions, where large, generalizable datasets are impractical. In conclusion, this study enhances the transparency and trustworthiness of ML in EDM, ensuring responsible intervention strategies in academic risk prediction. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: A Systematic Review of Language Models in Virtual Learning Environments: Impacts on Personalization, Engagement, and Performance
Source title: 17th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems and Applications, IISA 2026
Affiliations: Universidade Federal de Itajubá, Instituto de Matemática e Computação, Itajubá, Brazil
Authors with affiliations: De Almeida G.R., Universidade Federal de Itajubá, Instituto de Matemática e Computação, Itajubá, Brazil; De Souza A.D., Universidade Federal de Itajubá, Instituto de Matemática e Computação, Itajubá, Brazil; Drummond I.N., Universidade Federal de Itajubá, Instituto de Matemática e Computação, Itajubá, Brazil
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the field of education, particularly through the advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Small Language Models (SLMs), which enable more personalized, adaptive, and accessible learning experiences. This study aims to systematically investigate the effects of LLMs and SLMs in Virtual Learning Environments (VLEs), analyzing their impact on student engagement, retention, academic performance, and satisfaction. The research was conducted following the PRISMA protocol, encompassing the stages of identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion, resulting in 15 empirical studies selected for analysis. The findings indicate that the use of language models contributes to the personalization of learning paths, the provision of continuous feedback, and learner support, thereby enhancing motivation and performance. However, a predominance of studies focused on LLMs was observed, revealing a significant gap in research on SLMs, which show great potential for contexts with computational constraints and privacy requirements. The evidence also highlights methodological limitations, such as small sample sizes and a lack of standardized evaluation metrics. It is concluded that language models represent a promising advancement for digital education, provided they are employed with methodological rigor, ethical responsibility, and pedagogical alignment.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Flexible Multi-Level Optimal Transport for Universal Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Distillation on LLMs and Beyond

Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a prevalent technique for compressing large language models (LLMs). Existing KD methods are constrained by the need for identical tokenizers (i.e., vocabularies) between teacher and student models, as they assume a consistent semantic correspondence across logit dimensions, limiting their versatility in handling LLMs of different architecture families. In this paper, we introduce the Multi-Level Optimal Transport (MultiLevelOT), a novel approach that advances the optimal transport for universal cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation. Our method aligns the logit distributions of the teacher and the student at both token and sequence levels using diverse cost matrices, eliminating the need for dimensional or token-by-token correspondence. At the token level, MultiLevelOT integrates both global and local information by jointly optimizing all tokens within a sequence to enhance robustness. At the sequence level, we efficiently capture complex logit distribution structures using a flexible Sinkhorn loss with relaxed marginal constraints, allowing partial transport and absorbing unmatched tokens, thereby serving as an efficient OT-based surrogate while tolerating unaligned mass. Extensive experiments on tasks of extractive QA, generative QA, summarization, instruction- following, math reasoning, and Big-Bench-Hard demonstrate that the MultiLevelOT outperforms state-of-the-art cross-tokenizer KD methods. Our approach is robust to different student and teacher models across model families, architectures, and parameter sizes. We further validate MultiLevelOT in multimodal-input settings and introduce task-specific technical extensions for both multi-teacher text distillation and structured visual-token distillation. © 1979-2012 IEEE.

Title: Design and Implementation of an AI-Powered Educational Chatbot with Learning Analytics and Adoption Prediction
Source title: 2026 1st International Conference on Innovation and Growth in Next-Gen Intelligent Technology and Engineering, IGNITE 2026
Affiliations: Pravara Rural Engineering College, Department of Computer Engg, M.S, Loni, India

Abstract: The increasing adoption of artificial intelligence in education has led to the development of intelligent systems that support personalized and interactive learning. This paper presents the design and implementation of an AI-powered educational chatbot integrated with learning analytics and adoption prediction mechanisms. The proposed system is developed using a Flask-based web framework, a locally hosted large language model via Ollama, and an SQLite database to ensure secure, efficient, and scalable operation. The chatbot provides real-time academic assistance while simultaneously collecting structured user feedback through session ratings, response-level feedback, and survey instruments. Learning analytics are performed by mapping user responses to key adoption constructs, enabling quantitative evaluation of system usability and effectiveness. Furthermore, a machine learning-based Random Forest regression model is employed to predict student adoption intention using empirically collected data. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: In modern online learning environments, Knowledge Tracing (KT) enables personalized and adaptive learning by modeling students' evolving knowledge states from their past interactions. However, limited initial learning data in online systems leads to data sparsity, restricts KT models in predicting. To address this, we propose an improved Knowledge Tracing model (IeMaKT) based on large language models and enhanced attention networks. The model employs LLMs to extract auxiliary information from problem content, such as difficulty, concept complexity, and learning requirements. By employing hyperbolic and rotary positional encoding attention capture hierarchical and relational dependencies among problems and knowledge concepts. Experiments on two real-world educational datasets show that IeMaKT consistently outperforms 8 baseline models and achieves excellent results under sparse-interaction conditions. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Enhancing Adult Digital Literacy for Lifelong Learning: Application Scenarios and Practical Paradigms of Artificial Intelligence Tools
Source title: Procedia Computer Science
Affiliations: School of Teacher Education, Maanshan Teachers' College, Maanshan, China
Authors with affiliations: Liu D., School of Teacher Education, Maanshan Teachers' College, Maanshan, China
Abstract: Nowadays, the adult learners experience the problems in their lifelong learning process such as the lack of competence in the use of digital tools, poor adaptability to intelligent technologies, and poor effectiveness of learning transfer, impeding the process of further enhancement of their digital literacy. In this paper, a four-stage model of digital literacy improvement is developed based on the Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology, including perception, interaction, generation, and evaluation. The work of learning is jointly structured with the help of an intelligent assistant and a Large Language Model (LLM), creating custom learning courses and a dynamic knowledge feedback system. This paper utilized a sample sample of 312 adult learners (18-55 years) as a study sample, where surveys through questionnaires and learning data mining was used to confirm the usefulness of AI-assisted learning. The findings indicated that the digital information acquisition ability of the learners increased by 38.8% after the model had been applied, the level of their average problem solving efficiency scored 84.5, and their level of learning engagement attained a top score of 92.1. The findings suggest that AI technologies possess high adaptive and transfer-promoting potential to improve the digital literacy of adult learners and may be considered an effective element of a lifelong learning support system.  © 2026 The Authors.

Abstract: Automated assessment of programming tasks remains a persistent challenge in computer science education, especially when scalability, consistency, and formative feedback are required. This study presents the design and evaluation of an AI-assisted continuous assessment system that leverages Large Language Models to evaluate programming assignments, generate feedback, and support learning analytics. The system integrates rubric-based evaluation, prompt engineering, and human-in-the-loop validation to ensure both reliability and transparency. A mixed-method experiment was conducted in an undergraduate programming course involving over 1100 student submissions across multiple assignments and subjects. Results show a strong correlation (R2 = 0.87) between LLM-based and instructor traditional grading, with substantial reductions in assessment time (over 75%) and increased consistency. Qualitative feedback from instructors and students highlighted the ability of the tool to provide immediate, explainable, and unbiased feedback, improving engagement and learning outcomes. Despite these advantages, limitations include occasional misclassifications and the need for pedagogical oversight. The findings indicate that LLM-assisted systems can significantly enhance scalable and equitable continuous assessment in programming education, provided that ethical use and human validation remain integral components. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Abstract: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) for object detection remains challenging under adverse weather due to significant distribution shifts. While recent Vision Foundation Model (VFM) based methods show promise, they often encounter limitations in extreme domain gaps and pseudo-label noise. This paper proposes two enhancements to the DINO Teacher framework: (1) a multi-round self-training strategy to refine the labeling model progressively, and (2) a depth-guided spatial modulation mechanism using geometric priors from a DINOv3based depth estimator. By modulating the input space, the student model is encouraged to emphasize spatial cues that are less sensitive to visibility degradation in foggy environments. Experiments on Foggy Cityscapes demonstrate that our approach reaches 56.5% mAP with a VGG-16 backbone and 59.8% mAP with ResNet-50. These results demonstrate competitive performance compared with the DINO Teacher baseline and recent Vision Language Model (VLM) based methods, particularly for tail categories such as bus and train.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: A lightweight text chunking method fusing weakly supervised distillation and discourse relation discrimination
Source title: Proceedings of SPIE - The International Society for Optical Engineering

Authors with affiliations: Cheng Z., School of Electronic and Electrical Engineering, Shanghai University of Engineering Science, Shanghai, 201620, China; Fan T., School of Electronic and Electrical Engineering, Shanghai University of Engineering Science, Shanghai, 201620, China
Abstract: The performance of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is highly dependent on the quality of text chunking in its knowledge base. For logically structured long documents such as textbooks and social science literature, existing chunking methods struggle to balance semantic integrity with boundary accuracy, often fragmenting coherent arguments and undermining the quality of retrieved context. This paper proposes a lightweight text chunking method, DH (Distilled- Hybrid), which fuses weakly supervised distillation with discourse relation discrimination to address this challenge. The method transfers the powerful implicit semantic boundary detection capabilities of a Large Language Model (LLM) to a lightweight student model via knowledge distillation. Concurrently, it innovatively designs a Discourse Relation Classifier (DRC) to explicitly capture logical connections between sentences. The core hypothesis is that these implicit semantic and explicit logical signals are highly complementary. A small fusion network jointly leverages them to make a unified decision, ensuring semantic integrity while precisely maintaining the logical continuity of the text. Experiments on a dataset from the textbook Outline of Modern Chinese History show that our method improves the boundary prediction consistency metric (F1@ ± 1) by 16.5% over a semantic similarity baseline and significantly enhances downstream retrieval performance, achieving notable gains on key metrics such as Recall@5 and nDCG@5. The method achieves an inference speed of under 50ms per thousand characters on a CPU, presenting a solution that effectively balances chunking effectiveness and computational efficiency.  © COPYRIGHT SPIE. Abstract: Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have significantly enhanced text analysis and generation capabilities, introducing new tools that may help reduce student dropout rates. Concurrently, the growing adoption of Learning Management Systems (LMS) has contributed to an increase in educational data volume, creating opportunities for intervention through learning analytics applications. In this context, this study conducts a systematic review of research published over the past decade to investigate how NLP has been used to identify or mitigate the risk of student dropout in LMS such as Moodle and Canvas LMS. A search was performed across the Scopus and Web of Science databases, yielding a total of 142 results. After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, 19 studies employing diverse approaches were selected and analyzed. Although relevant applications have been proposed, the results suggest that few studies provide data demonstrating the efficacy of such interventions, underscoring the need for further evidence to guide the implementation of NLP in these environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Abstract: Accurate modeling of learners’ evolving cognitive states is essential for intelligent educational systems, yet many existing knowledge tracing and graph-based approaches rely on static structures or purely sequential representations that inadequately capture dynamic structural changes in learning processes. This study proposes a Learner Cognitive Graph (LCG) framework that integrates dynamic heterogeneous graph modeling, structured behavioral data acquisition, and reinforcement learning-based intervention optimization. A Dynamic Cognition Graph (DCG) is formally defined as a sequence of temporally evolving graph snapshots representing interactions among learners, knowledge concepts, and exercises. A reverse Turing test-based agent with structured prompting is introduced to collect reasoning-oriented behavioral evidence, improving data reliability for cognitive modeling. Temporal message passing, multi-scale memory updating, and self-supervised learning objectives are employed to construct dynamic cognitive representations. Personalized intervention is formulated as a Markov decision process to optimize long-term learning outcomes. Experiments conducted on real-world and simulated educational datasets demonstrate improved knowledge mastery prediction accuracy, cognitive state transition modeling, and intervention efficiency compared with representative baselines. Authors with affiliations: Quartulli A.A., Department of Electrical and Information Engineering (DEI), Polytechnic University of Bari, Bari, 70125, Italy; Mignogna G., Department of Electrical and Information Engineering (DEI), Polytechnic University of Bari, Bari, 70125, Italy; Zizzo V., Department of Electrical and Information Engineering (DEI), Polytechnic University of Bari, Bari, 70125, Italy; Mongiello M., Department of Electrical and Information Engineering (DEI), Polytechnic University of Bari, Bari, 70125, Italy
Abstract: Effective software engineering education today requires tools that adapt to individual learner proficiency and progress, while ensuring positive student engagement. Gamified platforms represent an effective approach to learning and maintaining motivation, but their efficacy depends on a robust underlying architecture. This systematic literature review analyzes state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI)-based adaptive architectures designed to support gamified learning tools, highlighting their architectural models (such as intelligent tutoring systems, multi-agent systems, and immersive virtual reality/augmented reality environments), adaptation mechanisms (including Generative AI and chatbots), and personalization strategies. A significant focus is placed on Process Mining and Learning Analytics as methodological approaches to organize learning paths and guide dynamic adaptation based on student behavior. The results of the selected studies demonstrate advantages such as increased engagement, longer-term participation, and personalized learning pace. However, challenges remain, such as common assessment criteria, integrating different technologies, and system scalability. The findings offer concrete insights for designing the next generation of effective gamified learning tools, based on data and software engineering processes. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: This article proposes and empirically tests an integrated approach to monitoring university digital transformation in a single-institution setting. The approach combines the measurement of students' digital competence (Digital Competence Index, DCI) and teachers' digital pedagogical competence (Digital Competence in Education, DCEdu) with selected indicators of course process quality and digital governance practices. The study is based on two standardised online surveys administered in the LMS Moodle environment (students: n = 386; teachers: n = 89), with index normalisation to a 0-100 scale and domain decomposition. The results revealed substantial internal heterogeneity in students' digital competence and marked inter-faculty differentiation in DCI, primarily associated with the size of the lower segment of the distribution. The largest differences in DCI were associated with accessibility barriers, internet stability, and regularity of interaction with the LMS. For teachers, the aggregated DCEdu index appeared relatively insensitive to basic infrastructure conditions but showed strong variation across pedagogical governance variables, especially the formalisation of rules for students' use of generative artificial intelligence and cyber hygiene training. The study formulates a set of institutional recommendations focused on minimum course standards, authentic rubric-based assessment, formal regulations for the use of generative AI, and mandatory training in cyber hygiene and data management. © 2026, International Association of Engineers. Title: Distillation for Adaptation Language Models to Russian Language

Affiliations: Lomonosov Moscow State University, Moscow, Russian Federation
Authors with affiliations: Kovalev G.P., Lomonosov Moscow State University, Moscow, Russian Federation; Tikhomirov M.M., Lomonosov Moscow State University, Moscow, Russian Federation
Abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to morphologically rich languages like Russian presents a major challenge, as multilingual models often exhibit limited transfer due to predominantly English-centric pre-training. This study investigates knowledge distillation (KD) as a more effective alternative to supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for the final calibration stage of language adaptation. We introduce an efficient offline top-K distillation approach that transfers knowledge from a 32B Russian-adapted teacher model to a 4B student model through tokenizer alignment and direct logit transfer. Experimental results demonstrate that KD consistently surpasses SFT, achieving up to a 4.22% performance improvement, with top-100 distillation yielding the highest gains (3.27% on average) albeit with increased memory consumption (62 GB vs. 7 GB for top-10). Moreover, the advantages of KD are most pronounced for student models with lower adaptive capacity (i.e., smaller LoRA α values). These findings underscore the efficacy of KD as a practical and scalable approach for language adaptation, while emphasizing the necessity of balancing performance improvements against computational efficiency. © The Authors 2025.
