Source title: 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence and Networking, QPAIN 2026
Affiliations: Leading University, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Sylhet, Bangladesh
Authors with affiliations: Islam N., Leading University, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Sylhet, Bangladesh; Akib M.A.T., Leading University, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Sylhet, Bangladesh; Arifuzzaman M., Leading University, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Sylhet, Bangladesh
Abstract: In the realm of higher education, the persistence of student attrition presents a formidable obstacle, frequently compounded by the skewed nature of socio-academic datasets which conventional classifiers struggle to model accurately. Identifying students at risk of discontinuation at an early stage is paramount, enabling educational institutions to deploy targeted pedagogical and socio-economic measures. To mitigate this issue, this research engineers a robust Heterogeneous Stacked Generalization framework, focusing on the effective integration of established techniques rather than a fundamentally new modeling approach, to forecast students' intentions regarding higher education with enhanced precision. We synergize five base learners: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, and CatBoost, coordinated by a Logistic Regression meta-learner. To rectify data sparsity and severe class imbalance, we employ the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) prior to model training. The proposed architecture achieves 92.00% classification accuracy and an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.98, significantly outperforming standalone baseline models. Furthermore, we bridge the gap between predictive accuracy and interpretability by integrating Explainable AI (XAI) techniques. Using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and PDP (Partial Dependence Plots), we reveal that financial stability (parental salary) and consistent academic performance are the primary determinants of retention. This study demonstrates that ensemble learning, combined with synthetic balancing and interpretability, offers a reliable tool for educational policymakers. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: AI-driven adaptive stealth assessment for socially regulated learning in collaborative environments
Source title: Journal of Research on Technology in Education
Affiliations: PRINCE Research Laboratory, Sousse University, ISITC, Hammam Sousse, Tunisia
Authors with affiliations: Hadyaoui A., PRINCE Research Laboratory, Sousse University, ISITC, Hammam Sousse, Tunisia; Cheniti-Belcadhi L., PRINCE Research Laboratory, Sousse University, ISITC, Hammam Sousse, Tunisia
Abstract: Conventional digital assessments often overlook learners’ real-time progress, peer interactions, and cognitive demands. This study addresses these limitations by introducing GenSolve, an adaptive artificial intelligence (AI)-driven stealth assessment framework designed to adjust scenario complexity, deliver personalized feedback, and monitor group regulation using socially regulated learning (SoRL) principles. A six-week quasi-experimental study involving 250 undergraduates compared GenSolve to traditional instruction. Results showed a 17.6% gain in problem-solving accuracy, a 21% increase in group cohesion, and a 12.7% improvement in delayed retention. AI-generated feedback reduced repeated errors by 23.4% and improved self-regulation, while SoRL mechanisms supported a 36% rise in independent conflict resolution. GenSolve contributes a scalable, ethically guided model for real-time collaborative assessment, offering practical advances in adaptive evaluation for digital learning environments. © 2026 ISTE.

Title: Implementing Adaptive AI Tutors to Enhance Problem-Solving Skills in Computer Engineering Students
Source title: 2026 International Conference on Technical Education, ICTechED 2026
Affiliations: United Arab Emirates University, College Of Information And Technology, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates
Authors with affiliations: Kumar P.M., United Arab Emirates University, College Of Information And Technology, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates; Alshamsi A.M.S., United Arab Emirates University, College Of Information And Technology, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates; Murugan T., United Arab Emirates University, College Of Information And Technology, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates
Abstract: Rising abstraction and technical sophistication of computer engineering education mandate the use of intelligent instruction systems, which can develop organized problem-solving and computational reasoning skills. The present paper suggests NeuroSolve-AIT, a new Adaptive Artificial Intelligence Tutoring system, which can be used to increase higher-order analytical performance among students of computer engineering. NeuroSolve-AIT, unlike traditional e-learning systems, is based on a multi-layer adaptive architecture combining deep knowledge tracing, the instructional policy optimization based on reinforcement learning, and cognitive diagnostic modeling to build personal learning paths. A semantic evaluation module that is powered by a transformer is used to scan student generated code and textual explanations and detect procedural discrepancies and conceptual gaps in real-time. Three entities are used to justify domain-specific reasoning: a graph-based concept dependency network dynamically translates prerequisite relationships between fundamental subjects like data structures, digital systems, algorithms, and machine learning. The structure also reflects meta-learning practices that help quickly adapt to different problem fields but in a pedagogical stable environment. An explainable AI layer has interpretable feedback, explaining to the students how solutions can be improved step-by-step as opposed to showing them the answers. There are also the adaptive difficulty calibration mechanisms that control the cognitive load by matching the complexity of the task and the level of increasing proficiency of the learner. NeuroSolve-AIT is a learner-centered, scalable ecosystem that is developed by synthesizing cognitive modelling, semantic reasoning and adaptive optimization in order to systematically reinforce analytical thinking, debugging skills and algorithmic problem-solving skills in computer engineering learning. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Offline-First PWA for Teaching Informatics in Wartime Conditions: Architecture and Survey Results
Source title: 2026 49th MIPRO ICT and Electronics Convention, MIPRO 2026 - Proceedings
Affiliations: Sumy State Pedagogical University Named after A. S. Makarenko, Sumy, Ukraine
Authors with affiliations: Turchyn D., Sumy State Pedagogical University Named after A. S. Makarenko, Sumy, Ukraine; Yurchenko A., Sumy State Pedagogical University Named after A. S. Makarenko, Sumy, Ukraine; Semenikhina O., Sumy State Pedagogical University Named after A. S. Makarenko, Sumy, Ukraine
Abstract: The paper focuses on the design and evaluation of an offline-first Progressive Web App (PWA) for teaching informatics in wartime conditions, where online learning takes place amid recurring disruptions to Internet connectivity and power supply. The proposed solution is based on a layered architecture: a client-side PWA with local progress persistence and an event queue; an offline/edge layer built on service workers and caching; and an online layer that supports synchronization, AI-based hints, and teacher analytics. Pedagogical support is implemented as a stepwise scaffolding model that strengthens learners' autonomy while limiting the delivery of ready-made solutions; the motivational layer emphasizes resilience through non-competitive mechanisms of individual progress. The empirical evaluation was conducted through surveys of pupils (n = 33), teachers (n = 10), and experts (n = 5), using a five-point Likert scale and open-ended questions. The analysis combined descriptive statistics (M, SD) with a thematic synthesis of comments. The results show high ratings for usability under unstable connectivity and for alignment with the needs of war-affected border regions. Pupils rated the multi-level hints and AI support particularly highly, whereas teachers provided more differentiated assessments of this component. Experts confirmed the strengths of the offline-first approach and identified priorities for further improvement, including more intuitive navigation and expanded teacher reporting tools (notably, exporting results).  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Multimodal Behavioral Patterns Analysis with Eye-Tracking and LLM-Based Reasoning
Source title: ICMI 2025 - Proceedings of the 27th International Conference on Multimodal Interaction
Affiliations: Human-Centered Technologies for Learning, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Guo D., Human-Centered Technologies for Learning, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; Abdrabou Y., Human-Centered Technologies for Learning, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; Thaqi E., Human-Centered Technologies for Learning, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; Kasneci E., Human-Centered Technologies for Learning, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany
Abstract: Eye-tracking data reveals valuable insights into users' cognitive states but is difficult to analyze due to its structured, non-linguistic nature. While large language models (LLMs) excel at reasoning over text, they struggle with temporal and numerical data. This paper presents a multimodal human-AI collaborative framework designed to enhance cognitive pattern extraction from eye-tracking signals. The framework includes: (1) a multi-stage pipeline using horizontal and vertical segmentation alongside LLM reasoning to uncover latent gaze patterns; (2) an Expert-Model Co-Scoring Module that integrates expert judgment with LLM output to generate trust scores for behavioral interpretations; and (3) a hybrid anomaly detection module combining LSTM-based temporal modeling with LLM-driven semantic analysis. Our results across several LLMs and prompt strategies show improvements in consistency, interpretability, and performance, with up to 50% accuracy in difficulty prediction tasks. This approach offers a scalable, interpretable solution for cognitive modeling and has broad potential in adaptive learning, human-computer interaction, and educational analytics. © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Distilling DDSP: Exploring Real-Time Audio Generation on Embedded Systems
Source title: AES: Journal of the Audio Engineering Society
Affiliations: Department of Information Engineering and Computer Science, University of Trento, Trento, Italy; Centre for Digital Music, Queen Mary University of London, London, United Kingdom; Department of Information Engineering, Università Politecnica delle Marche, Ancona, Italy

Abstract: This paper investigates the feasibility of running neural audio generative models on embedded systems, by comparing the performance of various models and evaluating their trade-offs in audio quality, inference speed, and memory usage. This work focuses on differentiable digital signal processing (DDSP) models, due to their hybrid architecture, which combines the efficiency and interoperability of traditional DSP with the flexibility of neural networks. In addition, the application of knowledge distillation (KD) is explored to improve the performance of smaller models. Two types of distillation strategies were implemented and evaluated: audio distillation and control distillation. These methods were applied to three foundation DDSP generative models that integrate Harmonic-plus-Noise, FM, and Wavetable synthesis. The results demonstrate the overall effectiveness of KD: the authors were able to train student models that are up to 100× smaller than their teacher counterparts while maintaining comparable performance and significantly improving inference speed and memory efficiency. However, cases where KD failed to improve or even degrade student performance have also been observed. The authors provide a critical reflection on the advantages and limitations of KD, exploring its application in diverse use cases and emphasizing the need for carefully tailored strategies to maximize its potential. © 2025 Audio Engineering Society. Title: TGN-PL: Learning to Socialize Using Privileged Information and Temporal Graph Networks
Source title: ICMI 2025 - Companion Publication of the 27th International Conference on Multimodal Interaction
Affiliations: Honda Research Institute Japan, Saitama, Japan; School of Interactive Computing, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, United States

Abstract: Social interaction dynamics underpin empathetic interaction between robots, virtual agents, and humans, in particular during multiparty group interaction. However, learning robust policies from multimodal observations remains challenging—especially in real-time, in-the-wild environments where only audiovisual data are easily available. We present the Temporal Graph Networks with Privileged Learning (TGN-PL)—a framework that fuses continuous-time dynamic-graph modeling with the Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm. During training, a teacher network leverages high-bandwidth multimodal signals (speech prosody, full-body motion capture from camera images, dialogue transcription, physiological responses, etc), most that are unavailable during deployment after training, distilling them into a compact student model that relies solely on real-time audiovisual streams at deployment. Evaluated on a newly collected in-house multimodal human-robot multiparty interaction dataset, TGN-PL is benchmarked with multiple baselines, and the results suggest TGN-PL outperforms these baselines. Our main contribution is the TGN-PL framework for multiparty interactions between humans and intelligent systems like robots or agents in-the-wild environments using only the easily available audiovisual observations. © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s)

Abstract: The evolution of digital education tools has reshaped learning experiences, particularly for adult learners juggling diverse commitments. This study explores the transformative role of iSmartGuide, an AI-powered educational platform developed by the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS), in addressing the unique needs of this demographic. By integrating cutting-edge technologies such as Generative AI (GenAI) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), iSmartGuide offers personalized, adaptive, and equitable learning experiences. The platform’s AI Tutor provides context-aware, tailored responses, enhancing student engagement and self-directed learning while equipping educators with actionable insights through advanced analytics. Features like mobile accessibility, interactive formats, and flexible personalization further support learners in navigating their educational journeys. This study examines the development, applications, and impact of iSmartGuide, highlighting its potential to set new benchmarks in lifelong learning and digital pedagogy. Future directions for AI in education and its implications for promoting accessibility and equity are also discussed, emphasizing the platform’s role in shaping the future of education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: A Systematic Review of International Studies on AI-Supported Teacher Professional Development–Extended Abstract
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: School of Humanities Jiangnan University Wuxi, Wuxi, China
Authors with affiliations: Cai H., School of Humanities Jiangnan University Wuxi, Wuxi, China; Sun J., School of Humanities Jiangnan University Wuxi, Wuxi, China; Han B., School of Humanities Jiangnan University Wuxi, Wuxi, China
Abstract: Teacher Professional Development (TPD) is a critical pathway for enhancing educational quality and supporting educators’ professional growth. With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), AI-supported TPD has emerged as a transformative trend in educational innovation. This study employs a systematic literature review to analyze international cases from 2019 to 2024, identifying and examining key applications of AI in TPD. From a technological empowerment perspective, the study synthesizes four core application scenarios of AI-supported TPD. The findings indicate that AI primarily supports TPD through intelligent learning analytics, intelligent chatbots, intelligent online systems, and intelligent virtual spaces. By analyzing these representative scenarios, the study further proposes practical pathways and strategic implications for the future development of AI-supported TPD, offering insights to guide the digital transformation and high-quality advancement of TPD in China. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Title: Explainable learning style classification using LIME and ensemble models in the VARK framework
Source title: Proceedings of SPIE - The International Society for Optical Engineering

Authors with affiliations: Gao B., School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architectureline, Beijing, China; Li J., School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architectureline, Beijing, China
Abstract: This study investigates the use of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in classifying student learning styles through machine learning. A synthetic dataset simulating quiz-based interaction data was generated based on the VARK model (Visual, Auditory, Read/Write, Kinesthetic) to represent diverse learning preferences. Two state-of-the-art ensemble classifiers-Random Forest and XGBoost-were trained to predict learning styles from quiz responses and evaluated using standard classification metrics. To interpret the predictions, we employed LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations), producing both visual and HTML-based explanations at the individual level. Experimental results demonstrate high predictive performance and highlight LIME's ability to provide transparent, feature-level insights into model decisions. This work underscores the potential of XAI to support interpretable and personalized learning analytics in educational environments. © 2025 Published by SPIE.

Title: KnowTrace: Bootstrapping Iterative Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Structured Knowledge Tracing
Source title: Proceedings of the ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
Affiliations: Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China, Beijing, China; Huawei Noah's Ark Lab, Shenzhen, China
Authors with affiliations: Li R., Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China, Beijing, China; Dai Q., Huawei Noah's Ark Lab, Shenzhen, China; Zhang Z., Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China, Beijing, China; Chen X., Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China, Beijing, China; Dong Z., Huawei Noah's Ark Lab, Shenzhen, China; Wen J.-R., Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China, Beijing, China
Abstract: Recent advances in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) furnish large language models (LLMs) with iterative retrievals of relevant information to handle complex multi-hop questions. These methods typically alternate between LLM reasoning and retrieval to accumulate external information into the LLM's context. However, the ever-growing context inherently imposes an increasing burden on the LLM to perceive connections among critical information pieces, with futile reasoning steps further exacerbating this overload issue. In this paper, we present KnowTrace, an elegant RAG framework to (1) mitigate the context overload and (2) bootstrap higher-quality multi-step reasoning. Instead of simply piling the retrieved contents, KnowTrace autonomously traces out desired knowledge triplets to organize a specific knowledge graph relevant to the input question. Such a structured workflow not only empowers the LLM with an intelligible context for inference, but also naturally inspires a reflective mechanism of knowledge backtracing to identify contributive LLM generations as process supervision data for self-bootstrapping. Extensive experiments show that KnowTrace consistently surpasses existing methods across three multi-hop question answering benchmarks, and the bootstrapped version further amplifies the gains.  © 2025 ACM.

Title: AI-Based Early Learning Difficulty Detection from Student Text

Abstract: Early identification of students with learning difficulties is essential for providing timely instructional support. Although Natural Language Processing (NLP) enables automated analysis of student-written text, most existing models are opaque black boxes, which limits teacher confidence in AI-assisted learning analytics [29], [30]. This paper proposes an Explainable AI (XAI) framework for early learning difficulty detection based on a fine-tuned Hybrid Meta-Classifier that combines a crossencoder BERT architecture with explicit linguistic features. The model was evaluated on 2,208 student responses, achieving a binary classification accuracy of 83.71% and an ROC AUC of 0.90. Although the standalone fine-tuned BERT model achieves a marginally higher raw accuracy (84.84%), the Hybrid Meta-Classifier deliberately trades a small reduction in accuracy for substantially improved interpretability: fusing linguistic features with neural probabilities enables human-readable, token-level diagnostic feedback via SHAP [17], which is essential for educator trust and actionable intervention. Data efficiency was validated through few-shot transfer learning on a separate 4,380-sample reading comprehension dataset, requiring as few as 100 training samples to adapt. An algorithmic fairness analysis [7] and a microservice deployment architecture for Learning Management System (LMS) integration are also presented. These findings indicate that explainable, bias-aware NLP analytics can support actionable early detection of learning difficulties in real classroom settings.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Longitudinal Shifts in Student Peer Feedback Before and During the GenAI Era
Source title: 2026 22nd International Conference on Information Technology Based Higher Education and Training, ITHET 2026
Affiliations: Johannes Kepler University, Institute Of Digital Business, Linz, Austria; Johannes Kepler University, Department Of Digital Education, Linz, Austria
Authors with affiliations: Stabauer M., Johannes Kepler University, Institute Of Digital Business, Linz, Austria; Katzlinger E., Johannes Kepler University, Department Of Digital Education, Linz, Austria
Abstract: Peer review is widely used to scale formative assessment and develop feedback literacy, yet evidence about how student peer feedback evolves over multiple cohorts remains scarce. This paper analyzes a longitudinal corpus of anonymized peer reviews on seminar papers collected across eight annual cohorts (2019-2026). Each student reviewed three peers using a rubric with criterion-level ratings and open comments, plus an overall assessment. We quantify changes in the discourse of peer feedback using reproducible text-based measures (verbosity, lexical diversity, rhetorical markers) and relate these to rating severity and review timing. To examine shifts plausibly associated with widespread adoption of generative AI tools following the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, we compare a pre-period (2019-2022) with a post-period (2024-2026), treating 2023 as a transition year. Results show a marked increase in criterion-comment length after 2024 (+54% words), a concurrent decrease in lexical diversity, and a rise in summary/conclusion markers (e.g., "insgesamt", "Fazit"). At the same time, criterion grades become slightly more critical. We discuss these shifts as signatures of changing peer-feedback practices in a GenAI era and derive design implications for preserving authenticity and learning value in rubric-based peer assessment.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Model distillation has become essential for creating deployable language models, but their widespread deployment raises concerns about about their resilience to adversarial manipulation. This paper investigates how adversaries can inject subtle biases into teacher models through minimal data poisoning during training, which propagates to a smaller distilled student model and becomes significantly amplified. We identify two propagation modes: Untargeted (affecting multiple tasks) and Targeted (focusing on specific task while maintaining normal behavior elsewhere). With only 25 poisoned samples (0.25% poisoning rate), student models generate biased responses 76.9% of the time in targeted scenarios versus 69.4% in teachers, while untargeted propagation shows 5.7×-29.2× higher adversarial bias rate in students on unseen tasks. We validate across six bias types (targeted advertisement, phishing link, narrative manipulations, insecure coding practices), various distillation methods, and text/code generation modalities. Current defense mechanisms-including perplexity filtering, bias detectors, and LLM-based autoraters-prove inadequate against these attacks. We propose practical design principles for building effective adversarial bias mitigation strategies to address this threat vector. © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: Purpose: This study examines the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced instructional tools on science learning, engagement, and social interaction among primary school students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The research addresses a gap in the literature by exploring how adaptive, multisensory technologies can support conceptual understanding of “Light and Color” and foster inclusive learning experiences in special education settings. Methods: A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design was implemented with 34 students with ASD, divided into an experimental group and a control group receiving traditional teaching. Quantitative data were collected through science knowledge tests, teacher-rated engagement scales, and AI-generated learning analytics. Qualitative data were obtained through structured observations and teacher reflective journals. Statistical analyses included paired t-tests, ANOVA, MANOVA, and effect size calculations, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. Results: Students in the AI-enhanced group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in conceptual understanding compared to the control group, with large effect sizes across most test items. Engagement and motivation ratings were also higher for the experimental group. Qualitative observations revealed increased curiosity, sustained attention, collaborative behaviors, emotional regulation, and autonomy when interacting with the robot and VR environments. Conclusion: AI-enhanced, multisensory instruction substantially benefits neurodiverse learners by promoting deeper conceptual learning, supporting emotional and behavioral engagement, and enhancing inclusive participation. Findings highlight the pedagogical value of integrating adaptive AI tools into science education for students with ASD and suggest that AI can serve as an effective co-mediator alongside teachers in special education contexts. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Applications on University Teaching Quality and Students’ Self-Directed Learning Skills
Source title: Social Science Forum

Authors with affiliations: Al-Otaibi M., Department of Basic Sciences and Humanities, Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Amman Arab University, Amman, Jordan
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) applications are rapidly reshaping university teaching through adaptive tutoring, generative dialogue, automated feedback, learning analytics, predictive support, and AI-assisted assessment. Yet the educational value of these applications depends not merely on access to technology but on how they are embedded in pedagogy. This study examines the impact of AI applications on university teaching quality and students’ self-directed and self-regulated learning skills. It uses a systematic integrative review and a secondary quantitative synthesis of verified, peer-reviewed evidence. The principal quantitative corpus comprises 85 higher-education studies, 387 dependent effect-size estimates, and 9,564 participants published between 2015 and 2025. Descriptive analyses were reconstructed from publicly available supplementary data, while inferential conclusions were based on published three-level and random-effects meta-analytic estimates; no synthetic data were used. AI feedback had a medium positive average effect on self-regulated learning (Hedges’ g = 0.509), but its 95% prediction interval ranged from −0.661 to 1.678, indicating that effects are highly conditional. Generative-AI interventions also improved academic performance (g = 0.683, 95% CI [0.17, 1.19]), while ChatGPT-supported learning improved behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement. However, heterogeneity was substantial, AI feedback did not clearly outperform human feedback, and experimental evidence identified risks of dependence, shallow processing, and “metacognitive laziness.” Teacher support emerged as a decisive pedagogical condition in the academic-performance literature: teacher-supported student–AI interaction produced a large effect (g = 1.426), whereas unsupported use produced a near-zero effect (g = 0.077). The study concludes that AI can improve university teaching quality and learner autonomy when it functions as a scaffold within teacher-designed learning, not as a substitute for disciplinary teaching, human feedback, reflective judgment, or independent performance. © 2026 Slovenian Sociological Association. Abstract: While AI literacy frameworks are becoming more widely adopted, a key gap remains: we still lack practical infrastructure for educators to collect, share, and understand real classroom cases that connect framework ideas to situated teaching practice. Such infrastructure may help strengthen the connection between theory and practice. In this work, we present AILitHub, a multilingual and scalable web system that enables teachers to contribute AI-related educational cases and annotate them with stakeholders and competencies defined in the OECD AI Literacy Framework. We position AILitHub as an early infrastructure for future professional learning and research. It contributes a scalable case-collection mechanism and may provide practice-grounded evidence that can inform future framework refinement and AI education design. In a preliminary deployment within an AI literacy professional training program, we successfully collected 53 complete teacher-contributed cases. Early results suggest that, while teachers showed strength in contributing positive cases demonstrating AI literacy, they may lack the skill or awareness to identify and provide negative examples. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: This paper presents an explainable AI (XAI) education tool designed for K-12 classrooms, particularly for students aged 11-16. The tool was designed for interventions on the fundamental processes behind social media platforms, focusing on four AI- and data-driven core concepts: data collection, user profiling, engagement metrics, and recommendation algorithms. An Instagram-like interface and a monitoring tool for explaining the data-driven processes make these complex ideas accessible and engaging for young learners. The tool provides hands-on experiments and real-time visualizations, illustrating how user actions influence their personal experience on the platform as well as the experience of others. This approach seeks to enhance learners' data agency, AI literacy, and sensitivity to AI ethics. The paper includes a case example from 12 two-hour test sessions involving 209 children, using learning analytics to demonstrate how they navigated their social media feeds and the browsing patterns that emerged. Abstract: Machine learning (ML) is emerging as a revolutionary force in the evolution of self-service technologies (SSTs), transforming their design, implementation, and delivery across various industries. These self-organizing systems leverage ML to autonomously learn from interactions, process vast volumes of data, and make intelligent decisions without explicit programming. This chapter explores the pivotal role of artificial intelligence (AI) in advancing SSTs, focusing on key applications such as customer service chatbots, automated kiosks, and intelligent virtual assistants. In conclusion, this chapter emphasizes how ML is revolutionizing the SSTs' future development. The use of NLP, predictive analytics and adaptive learning is making the existing ML solutions accurate, efficient and highly personalized as never before. Further improving data credibility, privacy, and ethics issues will enhance the development of these systems to meet our needs and aspirations and continue to strengthen them as the foundations of global business and progress. © 2025, IGI Global Scientific Publishing.

Abstract: This paper explores challenges and opportunities of AI's transformative potential in educational leadership and management, examining its impact on administrative efficiency, personalised learning, and data-driven decision-making. Despite promising AI tools like chatbots, learning analytics, and adaptive learning systems, widespread adoption in education remains limited due to infrastructure gaps, cost, and lack of expertise. Findings suggest that AI can streamline tasks, support personalised education, and empower leaders with actionable insights, yet its full potential is unachieved in most institutions. Recommendations include fostering AI literacy, investing in infrastructure, and creating supportive policies for sustainable integration. This study underscores the need for strategic planning to advance AI's role in educational leadership, balancing innovation with institutional readiness and ethical considerations.. © 2025, IGI Global Scientific Publishing.

Title: Ensemble Learning for Early Academic Performance Prediction: A Case Study in Engineering Leveling Courses
Source title: Proceedings of the LACCEI international Multi-conference for Engineering, Education and Technology
Affiliations: Escuela Politécnica Nacional, Ecuador
Authors with affiliations: Carrera I., Escuela Politécnica Nacional, Ecuador; Armendáriz R., Escuela Politécnica Nacional, Ecuador; Ramos V., Escuela Politécnica Nacional, Ecuador
Abstract: Student attrition in engineering leveling courses is a persistent challenge in Latin American higher education, often exacerbated by the lack of timely identification mechanisms. Traditional Early Warning Systems (EWS) frequently rely on midterm grades, limiting their capacity for preventive intervention. This paper presents an Ensemble Learning model designed to predict final academic performance using exclusively pre-enrollment data, combining sociodemographic, previous academic records, and socioeconomic and psychometric variables. This study analyzed historical records of 1,533 students (7,210 instances) from a polytechnic university in Ecuador. Five machine learning algorithm families were evaluated through rigorous hyperparameter optimization involving 9,972 configurations. The proposed Stacking architecture, which integrates the top-performing XGBoost models via a Ridge Regression meta-learner, achieved a Coefficient of Determination (R2) of 0.749 and a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 3.783 on a 0-40 scale, demonstrating superior generalization compared to single models. Furthermore, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis revealed that non-cognitive factors, such as study habits and academic self-confidence, are critical predictors alongside high school GPA and mathematics admission scores. To validate its practical utility, the model was deployed for the 2025-B cohort (N=900), identifying 9.2% of incoming students as "High Risk" before the start of classes. These results demonstrate the technical feasibility and ethical viability of using advanced ensemble methods for proactive, evidence-based academic management. © 2026 Latin American and Caribbean Consortium of Engineering Institutions. Title: Learning analytics: support from an AI-based virtual assistant in teacher training; [Analítica del aprendizaje: apoyo de un asistente virtual basado en IA en la formación docente]
Source title: Proceedings of the LACCEI international Multi-conference for Engineering, Education and Technology
Affiliations: Universidad Bolivariana del Ecuador, Ecuador
Authors with affiliations: Jesús Mérida-Córdova E., Universidad Bolivariana del Ecuador, Ecuador; Francisco Vera Mosquera J., Universidad Bolivariana del Ecuador, Ecuador; Vergel-Parejo E., Universidad Bolivariana del Ecuador, Ecuador; Lopéz-Fernández R., Universidad Bolivariana del Ecuador, Ecuador; Yasmil Echeverría-Guzmán Á., Universidad Bolivariana del Ecuador, Ecuador; Martínez Isacc R., Universidad Bolivariana del Ecuador, Ecuador; Eva Cantos Farías R., Universidad Bolivariana del Ecuador, Ecuador
Abstract: Learning analytics has become a strategic field in higher education, enabling the pedagogical interpretation of academic and contextual data for informed decision-making. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of using a virtual assistant based on generative artificial intelligence on the development of learning analytics competencies in postgraduate teacher training programs within the Master's Program in Digital Environments. A quasi-experimental design with a quantitative approach was employed, applying a pre-test and a post-test to 170 teacher trainees at the Bolivarian University of Ecuador. The results show statistically significant improvements in analytical skills, with a very large effect size in the statistical analysis dimension. Positive correlations were also identified between the use of the virtual assistant and its perceived pedagogical value. The findings confirm that the assistant acted as an effective pedagogical mediator, integrating statistical analysis and educational interpretation. It is concluded that the virtual assistant not only optimizes the analysis of educational data but also contributes to redefining learning analytics as a formative practice geared toward responsible and contextualized decision-making. © 2026 Latin American and Caribbean Consortium of Engineering Institutions. Title: Reframing artificial intelligence and learning analytics in emerging higher education: towards a human-centred and contextually responsive future
Source title: Frontiers in Education
Affiliations: College of Business Studies, Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET), Kuwait City, Kuwait
Authors with affiliations: Alenezi A.F., College of Business Studies, Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET), Kuwait City, Kuwait
Abstract: Introduction – Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics (LA) are increasingly used to enhance student outcomes and support institutional decision-making in higher education. However, evidence from emerging economies remains fragmented and unevenly distributed across regions. This critical scoping review synthesises current evidence on AI and LA implementation across higher education institutions in Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East. Methods – The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework and was reported in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Systematic searches of eight academic databases and selected grey literature sources identified 31 eligible publications published between 2019 and 2026. The evidence base comprised 20 empirical studies, 6 conceptual papers, and 5 policy or grey literature sources. To enhance transparency, studies were classified using a structured evidence-grading framework ranging from Grade A (high evidence) to Grade D (conceptual and policy evidence). Results – Four dominant application areas emerged: predictive early-warning systems, adaptive learning platforms, generative AI tools, and institutional analytics dashboards. Considerable regional variation was identified. Latin America demonstrated comparatively greater implementation maturity, while Sub-Saharan Africa placed greater emphasis on governance, ethics, and data justice. South Asia showed strong technical sophistication but limited pedagogical integration, whereas evidence from the Middle East reflected predominantly early-stage implementation. Across all regions, evaluation focused primarily on technical performance, with comparatively limited attention given to educational impact, equity outcomes, and long-term sustainability. Through a three-stage analytical synthesis, the review develops the Human-Centred AI and Learning Analytics Implementation Framework (HCAI-LIF), comprising four interdependent dimensions: Governance, Pedagogy, Equity, and Sustainability. Discussion – The review reframes AI and LA as socio-technical systems that require context-sensitive adaptation and responsible implementation rather than technology-driven adoption alone. The proposed framework provides an evidence-informed foundation for policymakers, institutional leaders, and researchers seeking to promote equitable, sustainable, and human-centred digital transformation in higher education across emerging economies. © 2026 Alenezi.

Title: AI and discourse analysis: Implications for ESP genre pedagogy in EFL settings
Source title: International Journal of Language Studies
Affiliations: Università degli Studi di Milano, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Catenaccio P., Università degli Studi di Milano, Italy
Abstract: The advent of generative AI is bound to revolutionize professional writing practices. This will inevitably have an impact on writing pedagogies, particularly in the ESP writing courses where speakers of English as a second language are taught to master the principles of domain-specific communication alongside general language skills. While concerns have been raised as to the future of professional writing and writing pedagogy in the era of AI, this article argues that learning to use generative AI tools offers an unprecedented opportunity for students to develop discourse analytical skills that have traditionally been sidelined in ESP genre teaching as they pertained more to the writing process than to the product, the latter taking typically priority—in the minds of students and teachers alike—over the former. This is a welcome development which does justice to the principles of genre pedagogy. © 2025 IJLS.

Title: Fact-Check-Game for Cognitive Defense: Log-Based Evidence and Pedagogical Design Implications for AI-Age Information Literacy

Affiliations: Institute of Arts and Sciences, Yamagata University, Yamagata, Japan
Authors with affiliations: Kanoh H., Institute of Arts and Sciences, Yamagata University, Yamagata, Japan
Abstract: Misinformation risks have intensified with the spread of social media and generative AI, increasing the need for repeated practice of fact-checking as a behavioral skill. This study designed, implemented, and deployed Fact-Check-Game; a lightweight Share/Verify/Skip serious game built with Google Apps Script and Google Sheets to support classroom practice and log-based learning analytics. In a classroom deployment (n = 6 5 sessions; 553 completed trials), Verify was used in only 42/553 trials (7.6%), while false sharing persisted (20 553,3.6% of completed trials). Theme-wise analyses suggested that verification behavior varied by topic, and reaction time distributions indicated greater cognitive effort when learners engaged in verification. We discuss pedagogical implications for teaching fact-checking as cognitive defense and provide design recommendations to better align incentives and scaffolding with verification habits in the AIage.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Industry 5.0 emphasizes human-centricity, sustainability, and resilient cyber-physical collaboration. Engineering education must therefore evolve beyond traditional Outcome-Based Education (OBE) frameworks toward AI-Integrated OBE 4.0, where artificial intelligence supports adaptive curriculum alignment, predictive competency mapping, and intelligent assessment analytics. This paper proposes a comprehensive AI-driven OBE 4.0 architecture tailored for Industry 5.0 readiness. The framework integrates learning analytics, digital twins, generative AI tutors, competency knowledge graphs, and continuous industry feedback loops. A simulation-based evaluation demonstrates improvements in learning outcome attainment, assessment consistency, and early-risk identification compared to conventional OBE systems. Results indicate enhanced constructive alignment, reduced grading variance, and measurable growth in Industry 5.0 competencies such as human-AI collaboration and sustainable systems design. The proposed model supports accreditation compliance (e.g., Washington Accord) while embedding AI governance and ethical safeguards. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Enhancing Multimodal Entity Linking via Distillation and Multimodal Large Language Models
Source title: CIKM 2025 - Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management
Affiliations: College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China
Authors with affiliations: Huang J., College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China; Wang D., College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China; Li S., College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China; Peng Y., College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China; Jin R., College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China
Abstract: Multimodal entity linking (MEL) aims to link ambiguous multimodal mentions to their corresponding entities in a multimodal knowledge graph. Although many existing methods have been dedicated to exploring fine-grained intra- and cross-modal interactions between mentions and entities and have achieved good results, the discrepancies between the data distributions in training and real-world applications, as well as the noisy onehot labels, still impede the generalization of MEL models, which leads to poor performance when encountering unseen entities. Although general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are powerful, it is costly and time-consuming to apply them directly to the MEL task. To address the above issues, we propose a Distillation-Enhanced framework for Multimodal Entity Linking (DEMEL). During training, DEMEL takes the best-trained MEL model so far as the teacher model, and distills the knowledge of the teacher model into the student model, i.e. the MEL model of the current iteration, when training it with onehot labels. This imposes regularization on the model, balances bias and variance in the training process, and improves the generalization ability of the MEL model. Moreover, DEMEL employs an MLLM to selectively rerank predictions for uncertain samples in the inference phase, improving accuracy while minimizing invocation costs. Extensive experiments on three public MEL datasets demonstrate that DEMEL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving 3.27% improvement with MLLM reranking for just 8.59% of test samples, and up to 4.8% H@1 enhancement in low-resource settings even without using MLLM reranking.  © 2025 ACM.

Abstract: Despite substantial instructional attention to large-enrollment university courses in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), they tend to have high rates of D, F, and Withdraw (DFW) at the introductory level that disproportionally disadvantage historically minoritized and underrepresented students, such as students identified as women, low-income, first-generation, or of color. While postsecondary institutions have recently explored big data and learning analytics to drive their institutional student success efforts, well-known shortfalls in student success in large STEM courses remain. This chapter documents an evidence-based approach at a large, R1 midwestern university that enriches robust data infrastructure with qualitative ethnographic methods. Applied to a gateway computer science course, these methods center students’ day-to-day learning realities, including disparate educational opportunities, in ways that interrogate barriers to and shortfalls in student success. The resulting case study describes our ethnographic approach, the shortfalls it uncovers, our future directions with this work, and how other faculty members and institutions can apply lessons learned to promote efficacy, attainment, and equity in gateway STEM courses. Implementations drawn from course vignettes point to revisions in design and preparation of group learning activities, strategic integration of lecture and lab sessions, course navigation aids, and pedagogical training for teaching assistants. © 2025 by the authors.

Abstract: This study reviewed 50 years of research on technology-enhanced science and mathematics education published in Computers & Education (1976–2026). Following PRISMA 2020 framework, 519 empirical studies were identified. BERTopic-based topic modeling was applied to derive the thematic structure of the corpus, and each article was coded for education level, theoretical framework, primary technology, and technology function. Seventeen topics were identified, including ten science-related, four mathematics-related, and three domain-general ones. Topic membership was more strongly associated with primary technology and technology function than with education level and theoretical framework. Game-based learning split into separate science and mathematics topics, and a mathematics-centered AI/agent topic emerged, while AI-related science studies were found to be mainly assigned to existing topics such as argumentation, collaborative learning, and inquiry. VR was a distinct technological topic and served several instructional functions. Besides, research within this corpus shifted from computer-centered instructional agendas toward a more diverse space encompassing learning analytics, games, mobile and immersive environments, eye tracking, and AI, with integrated STEM and eye-tracking topics emerging in this corpus around the mid-2010s. Science-related work differentiated around disciplinary practices, whereas mathematics-related work clustered around forms of instructional support rather than mathematical subdomains. Future work can extend the BERTopic framework to a broader set of journals to fully understand the overall trends, or apply BERTopic method separately to publications within fixed intervals to examine how research topics evolve over time. © 2026 The Authors

Title: STUDENT EXAM PERFORMANCE PREDICTION AND PERSONALIZED EDUCATIONAL DECISION-MAKING BASED ON TRANSFORMER AND SHAP
Source title: Journal of Nonlinear and Convex Analysis
Affiliations: University of International Business and Economics, China
Authors with affiliations: Ye W., University of International Business and Economics, China; Xie S., University of International Business and Economics, China; Wang X., University of International Business and Economics, China; Huang X., University of International Business and Economics, China
Abstract: Predicting student academic performance and understanding its influencing factors are crucial for educational optimization. This study employs a Transformer model for exam score prediction and compares its performance with random forest and LASSO regression. The Transformer model achieves R2 = 0.754 on the validation set, representing a 12.03% improvement over random forest (R2 = 0.673) and a 72.1% improvement over LASSO regression (R2 = 0.438). Five-fold cross-validation confirms robustness with average R2 of 0.685 ± 0.017 and coefficient of variation of 0.026. Using SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) from Explainable AI, we reveal that previous scores, study hours, and attendance are the most crucial factors, followed by resource access, parental involvement, and tutoring sessions. Local prediction explanations demonstrate personalized decision-making: Student 642 achieved excellence through high study hours (SHAP +3.0) and attendance (SHAP +1.7); Student 4428 showed insufficient learning efficiency despite high attendance; Student 4814 had good attendance but negative impacts from study time; Student 5452 relied on parental involvement but was constrained by lower historical scores. This study contributes new methodologies combining high-precision Transformer prediction with deep SHAP interpretability for educational data science. © Copyright 2026.

Affiliations: North Eastern Mindanao State University, Computer Science Department, Surigao del Sur, Tagbina, Philippines; College of Compuitng and Information Sciences, Agusan Del Sur State College of Agriculture and Technology, Bunawan, Philippines

Abstract: This The increasing adoption of AI-powered assistants such as ChatGPT in higher education has reshaped how students perform academic tasks, creating a growing need to understand the behavioral factors that drive satisfaction and continued use. This study proposes a predictive modeling approach to assess student satisfaction and reuse intention based exclusively on AI assistant interaction data. A dataset comprising 10,000 AI-assisted learning sessions was analyzed, incorporating behavioral and contextual features such as session duration, number of prompts, task type, perceived assistance level, and learning outcomes. Following data preprocessing and feature engineering, XGBoost classifier was implemented to model reuse intention and identify key predictors of satisfaction. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of 0.92, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing non-linear relationships within student-AI interaction data. Results reveal that longer interaction sessions, higher prompt frequencies, and greater perceived assistance levels are strongly associated with increased satisfaction and higher likelihood of reuse. Moreover, cognitively demanding tasks such as writing and coding exhibited higher satisfaction ratings compared to routine academic tasks. The findings highlight the potential of machine learning-based predictive modeling as a data-driven approach for understanding student engagement with AI assistants, offering actionable insights for educators and system designers to enhance AI-supported learning environments and foster sustained student engagement. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) assesses students’ mastery of specific knowledge concepts and predicts their problem-solving abilities by analyzing their interactions with intelligent tutoring systems. Although recent years have seen significant improvements in tracking accuracy with the introduction of deep learning and graph neural network techniques, existing research has not sufficiently focused on the impact of difficulty on knowledge state. The text understanding difficulty and knowledge concept difficulty of programming problems are crucial for students’ responses; thus, accurately assessing these two types of difficulty and applying them to knowledge state prediction is a key challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a Difficulty awareProgrammingKnowledgeTracing via Large Language Models(DPKT) to extract the text understanding difficulty and knowledge concept difficulty of programming problems. Specifically, we analyze the relationship between knowledge concept difficulty and text understanding difficulty using an attention mechanism, allowing for dynamic updates to students’ s. This model combines an update gate mechanism with a graph attention network, significantly improving the assessment accuracy of programming problem difficulty and the spatiotemporal reflection capability of knowledge state. Experimental results demonstrate that this model performs excellently across various language datasets, validating its application value in programming education. This model provides an innovative solution for programming knowledge tracing and offers educators a powerful tool to promote personalized learning. © The Author(s) 2025.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed digital education by enabling personalized and data-driven learning experiences. By incorporating machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and multimodal analytics, AI systems adapt instructional content to match individual learner profiles in real time. This systematic review examines AI-powered adaptive learning technologies with an emphasis on supervised and unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning (RL), and multimodal data integration. It assesses how these technologies enhance personalization, boost learner engagement, and promote educational equity. Adhering to PRISMA guidelines, this review analyzes 142 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025, sourced from databases including Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore. Studies were selected based on their application of AI techniques in personalized digital learning environmen. Supervised learning models such as support vector machines (SVMs) and decision trees support learner classification and performance prediction. Unsupervised clustering techniques uncover behavioral patterns, while reinforcement learning enables dynamic content sequencing to foster learner autonomy. Multimodal approaches that integrate affective and biometric data further refine personalization. Despite these advances, critical challenges persist in model interpretability, data privacy, and scalability, especially in low-resource settings. This review highlights the expanding influence of AI in personalized education and outlines future research directions, including the use of explainable AI (XAI), modular system designs, and culturally responsive frameworks. These advancements are vital for developing ethical, inclusive, and scalable learning systems. © The Author(s) 2025.

Title: Multimodal Commonsense Knowledge Distillation for Visual Question Answering
Source title: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
Affiliations: University of Melbourne, Australia; University of Western Australia, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Yang S., University of Melbourne, Australia; Luo S., University of Western Australia, Australia; Han S.C., University of Melbourne, Australia, University of Western Australia, Australia
Abstract: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and Visual Language Pretrained Models (VLPMs) have shown remarkable performances in general Visual Question Answering (VQA). However, these models struggle with VQA questions that require external commonsense knowledge due to the challenges in generating high-quality prompts and the high computational costs of fine-tuning. In this work, we propose a novel graph-based multimodal commonsense knowledge distillation framework that constructs a unified relational graph over commonsense knowledge, visual objects and questions through a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) following a teacher-student environment. This proposed framework is flexible with any type of teacher and student models without further fine-tuning, and has achieved competitive performances on the ScienceQA dataset. The code is in https://github.com/adlnlp/MCKDVQA. Copyright © 2025, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.

Abstract: Generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and extended reality (XR) enable STEM learning experiences that adapt to individual progress while preserving alignment with the course outcomes. This paper proposes an Educational Intelligence Delivery System (EIDS), a student-centered architecture with governance controls and human oversight for high-stakes academic decisions that integrates a RAG-grounded pedagogical engine, XR, and metaverse modules for guided experiential practice, and competency-aligned assessment analytics for outcome-based education. EIDS is framed as an implementable blueprint: it specifies how learner interactions and artifacts can be captured, filtered through governance gates (privacy, safety, and fairness), and translated into personalized activities, feedback, and measurable competency evidence under instructor oversight. To support deployability, this paper outlines illustrative scenarios, such as virtual laboratories and digital-twin capstone projects, and presents a staged roadmap for evaluating feasibility, learning effectiveness, equity, and instructional workload in future pilots. Overall, the EIDS consolidates AI tutoring, immersive practice, and assessment evidence into a closed-loop workflow that aims to make adaptive STEM ecosystems more accountable and scalable. This work is presented as a vision and a position paper. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Adaptive Chain-of-Thought Distillation Based on LLM Performance on Original Problems
Source title: Mathematics
Affiliations: School of Information Engineering, Chinese People’s Armed Police Force Engineering University, Xi’an, 710086, China
Authors with affiliations: Shen J., School of Information Engineering, Chinese People’s Armed Police Force Engineering University, Xi’an, 710086, China; Cui X., School of Information Engineering, Chinese People’s Armed Police Force Engineering University, Xi’an, 710086, China; Gao Z., School of Information Engineering, Chinese People’s Armed Police Force Engineering University, Xi’an, 710086, China; Sheng X., School of Information Engineering, Chinese People’s Armed Police Force Engineering University, Xi’an, 710086, China
Abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) approach in large language models (LLMs) has markedly enhanced their performance on complex tasks; however, effectively distilling this capability into LLMs with smaller parameter scales remains a challenge. Studies have found that small LLMs do not always benefit from CoT distillation. Inspired by the concept of teaching students in accordance with their aptitude, we propose an adaptive chain-of-thought distillation (ACoTD) framework. The core idea is to dynamically and adaptively customize distillation data and supervision signals for student models based on their performance on the original problems. Specifically, ACoTD initially evaluates and categorizes the original problems according to the capabilities of the student model. Subsequently, for Easy- and Medium-level problems, a short CoT distillation is employed for a brief lecture to reinforce knowledge and enhance training efficiency, for high-difficulty problems where the student model underperforms, and a detailed long CoT distillation is utilized for in-depth explanation to infuse richer reasoning logic. This differentiated distillation strategy ensures that student models achieve a better grasp of learning. We conducted experiments on multiple benchmark datasets. The results indicate that, compared to the baseline, our method can significantly improve the inference performance of small LLMs. Our method provides a new student-centered paradigm for knowledge distillation, demonstrating that adaptive adjustment of teaching strategies based on student feedback is an effective way to enhance small LLMs’ reasoning ability. © 2025 by the authors.

Abstract: We have witnessed the emergence of superhuman intelligence thanks to the fast development of large language models (LLMs) and multimodal language models. As the application of such superhuman models becomes increasingly popular, a critical question arises: how can we ensure they still remain safe, reliable, and aligned well with human values encompassing moral values, Schwartz’s Values, ethics, and many more? In this position paper, we discuss the concept of superalignment from a learning perspective to answer this question by outlining the learning paradigm shift from large-scale pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, to alignment training. We define superalignment as designing effective and efficient alignment algorithms to learn from noisy-labeled data (point-wise samples or pair-wise preference data) in a scalable way when the task is very complex for human experts to annotate and when the model is stronger than human experts. We highlight some key research problems in superalignment, namely, weak-to-strong generalization, scalable oversight, and evaluation. We then present a conceptual framework for superalignment, which comprises three modules: an attacker which generates the adversary queries trying to expose the weaknesses of a learner model, a learner which refines itself by learning from scalable feedbacks generated by a critic model with minimal human experts, and a critic which generates critics or explanations for a given query-response pair, with a target of improving the learner by criticizing. We discuss some important research problems in each component of this framework and highlight some interesting research ideas that are closely related to our proposed framework, for instance, self-alignment, self-play, self-refinement, and more. Last, we highlight some future research directions for superalignment, including the identification of new emergent risks and multi-dimensional alignment. © Science China Press 2025.

Title: Enhancing Learning Design Workflows with Generative AI using Navigation Support

Abstract: Learning Analytics (LA) stands as a core pillar in leveraging generative AI for smart learning environments, yet its full potential is notably hindered by critical shortcomings in current AI-assisted Learning Design (LD) tools. While general-purpose AI tools offer interactive flexibility, they neither align with discipline-specific pedagogical frameworks nor embed LA capabilities. To address these gaps, we constructed the research framework around design-aware learning analytics, developing a generative AI-assisted chatbot centered on a specialized navigation bar. For educators who often feel overwhelmed or disoriented when using digital LD tools, the navigation bar provides explicit, structured guidance to enhance their understanding of the platform’s workflow. Grounded in the Learning Design Triangle (LDT), the chatbot’s navigation bar spans the full LD process, proactively delivering stage-tailored Learning Analytics Questions (LAQs), discipline-adapted cases, and LA solutions via intuitive, step-by-step navigation support. This study provides both theoretical and practical framework support for education, validating the value of human-centered, design-aware generative AI with embedded navigation support. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in education, yet little is known about how teachers’ professional knowledge and self-regulatory processes unfold when working with these tools. This pilot study introduces an analytical approach for tracing how teacher competence intersects with the generative capabilities of artificial intelligence during lesson design. The approach combines situation-specific perception–interpretation–decision skills, self-regulated learning processes and technological pedagogical content knowledge to observe teachers’ real-time reasoning. Analysing interactions through this approach made teachers’ underlying reasoning processes visible, revealing how pedagogical reasoning, contextual awareness and ethical judgement shaped the way AI-generated ideas were adapted or constrained. Findings suggest that the integration of teacher expertise and AI capabilities was more apparent when teachers engaged in critical and ethical regulation of the design process. These insights may inform future work on Learning Analytics approaches that recognise teachers’ reasoning patterns and support more balanced forms of human–AI collaboration in lesson design. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: Effective student performance prediction enables timely support in Educational Data Mining (EDM). However, most predictive models lack interpretability and do not provide actionable feedback for learners. To address prediction accuracy and explanation, this study integrates an optimized XGBoost classifier with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD), our model employs SMOTE-based class balancing and randomized hyperparameter tuning, achieving better performance than existing research. Moreover, the model supports early predictions using demographic, assessment, and behavioral data, making it suitable for timely interventions. To address the challenge that predictive models typically function as black boxes without providing concrete guidance for instructors and students, SHAP explanations generate individualized reports that highlight the most influential features for each student’s predicted outcome. These explanations are mapped to targeted, prioritized feedback aligned with students’ learning needs. Case studies demonstrate how the system offers concrete and interpretable guidance for both at-risk and high-performing students. This study addresses a key EDM gap by moving beyond prediction to support personalized intervention. Abstract: The rapid expansion of online education has exposed significant gaps in traditional "one-size-fits-all"delivery models, which often lack the personalized, real-time intervention of human tutors. This research addresses these limitations by designing and implementing a Voice-Enabled Intelligent Educational Chatbot that integrates Natural Language Processing (NLP) with Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) to create an adaptive learning environment. The system utilizes a microservices architecture combining Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) with transformer-based intent classification to facilitate natural spoken interaction. Methods involving fine-tuning DistilBERT for educational intent recognition and the deployment of a real-time mastery estimation engine were evaluated. Results from a controlled study with 150 undergraduate students demonstrate that the voice-enabled adaptive interface leads to a 34% improvement in learning outcomes and a 53% increase in student engagement compared to static text platforms. These findings suggest that multimodal conversational interfaces effectively reduce cognitive load and enhance accessibility in digital education, providing a scalable solution for personalized instruction. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Can theory-driven learning analytics dashboard enhance human-AI collaboration in writing learning? Insights from an empirical experiment
Source title: Internet and Higher Education
Affiliations: Department of Educational Technology, of Education, Peking University, Beijing, 100871, China; School of Humanities, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 102206, China
Authors with affiliations: Chen A., Department of Educational Technology, of Education, Peking University, Beijing, 100871, China; Lian J., School of Humanities, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 102206, China; Kuang X., Department of Educational Technology, of Education, Peking University, Beijing, 100871, China; Jia J., Department of Educational Technology, of Education, Peking University, Beijing, 100871, China
Abstract: The integration of Generative AI (GenAI) into education has raised concerns about over-reliance and superficial learning, particularly in writing tasks in higher education. This study explores whether a theory-driven learning analytics dashboard (LAD) can enhance human-AI collaboration in the academic writing task by improving writing knowledge gains, fostering self-regulated learning (SRL) skills and shaping different human-AI dialogue characteristics. Grounded in Zimmerman's SRL framework, the LAD provided real-time feedback on learners' goal-setting, writing processes and reflection, while monitoring the quality of learner-AI interactions. A quasi-experiment was conducted involving 52 postgraduate students in a human-AI collaborative writing task. The students were divided into an experimental group (EG) that used the LAD and a control group (CG) that did not. Pre- and post- knowledge tests, questionnaires measuring SRL and cognitive load, and students' dialogue data with GenAI were collected and analyzed. Results showed that the EG achieved significantly higher writing knowledge gains and improved SRL skills, particularly in self-efficacy and cognitive strategies. However, the EG also reported increased test anxiety and cognitive load, possibly due to heightened metacognitive awareness. Epistemic Network Analysis revealed that the EG engaged in more reflective, evaluative interactions with GenAI, while the CG focused on more transactional and information-seeking exchanges. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on the educational use of GenAI and highlight the importance of designing interventions that complement GenAI tools, ensuring that technology enhances rather than undermines the learning process. © 2025 Elsevier Inc.

Title: How does artificial intelligence compare to human feedback? A meta-analysis of performance, feedback perception, and learning dispositions
Source title: Educational Psychology
Affiliations: Department of Education, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway; Centre for the Science of Learning & Technology (SLATE), University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway; School of Computing, University of Eastern Finland, Joensuu, Finland
Authors with affiliations: Kaliisa R., Department of Education, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway; Misiejuk K., Centre for the Science of Learning & Technology (SLATE), University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway; López-Pernas S., School of Computing, University of Eastern Finland, Joensuu, Finland; Saqr M., School of Computing, University of Eastern Finland, Joensuu, Finland
Abstract: This exploratory meta-analysis synthesises current research on the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated feedback compared to traditional human-provided feedback. Drawing on 41 studies involving a total of 4813 students, the findings reveal no statistically significant differences in learning performance between students who received AI-generated feedback and those who received human-provided feedback. The pooled effect size was small and statistically insignificant (Hedge’s g = 0.25, CI [−0.11; 0.60]), indicating that AI feedback is potentially as effective as human feedback. A separate meta-analysis focusing exclusively on studies in the domain of language and writing confirmed similar findings, with high heterogeneity persisting (I2 = 95%). The study further explored differences in feedback perception and found a small, negative, and statistically insignificant effect size (Hedge’s g = −0.20, CI [−0.67; 0.27]). The study advocates for a hybrid approach, leveraging the scalability of AI while retaining the deep, empathetic, and contextual features of human feedback. © 2025 The Author(s). Title: Creating Artificial Students that Never Existed: Leveraging Large Language Models and CTGANs for Synthetic Data Generation

Abstract: In this study, we explore the growing potential of AI and deep learning technologies, particularly Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Large Language Models (LLMs), for generating synthetic tabular data. Access to quality students' data is critical for advancing learning analytics, but privacy concerns and stricter data protection regulations worldwide limit their availability and usage. Synthetic data offers a promising alternative. We investigate whether synthetic data can be leveraged to create artificial students for serving learning analytics models. Using the popular GAN model- CTGAN and three LLMs- GPT2, DistilGPT2, and DialoGPT, we generate synthetic tabular student data. Our results demonstrate the strong potential of these methods to produce high-quality synthetic datasets that resemble real students' data. To validate our findings, we apply a comprehensive set of utility evaluation metrics to assess the statistical and predictive performance of the synthetic data and compare the different generator models used, specially the performance of LLMs. Our study aims to provide the learning analytics community with valuable insights into the use of synthetic data, laying the groundwork for expanding the field's methodological toolbox with new innovative approaches for learning analytics data generation. © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: The digitization of higher education has generated vast datasets, creating a dual opportunity to enhance academic outcomes and optimize administrative integrity. This paper conducts a structured survey of two critical, yet frequently siloed, research domains: (1) machine learning for student performance prediction and (2) secure, automated attendance systems. Our review traces the evolution of predictive models from traditional classifiers to high-accuracy ensemble methods like Random Forest and XGBoost, noting the parallel rise of eXplainable AI (XAI) to ensure stakeholder trust. Concurrently, we analyze the technological progression of attendance systems from manual logs to modern, fraud-resistant solutions, such as QR codes combined with geofencing, designed to combat proxy attendance. We identify a significant research gap: the lack of integration between these two fields. While performance models rely on attendance data, they seldom account for its integrity. We conclude by proposing a conceptual framework for a unified system that feeds high-integrity, verified attendance data directly into an XAI-driven predictive engine. This holistic approach would provide educational institutions with a single, reliable tool to support at-risk students and improve overall success.  © 2026 IEEE.
