Abstract: This full research paper presents a delayed posttest study on the effects of classroom activities and educational technologies in the context of engineering education, specifically AI education, using social media algorithms as a context. School projects were carried out with 12 regular classes of Finnish 5th and 8th grade students, using two newly developed educational apps designed for classroom use. Data were collected through a pre-test, post-test, and a delayed post-test administered six months after the intervention. This study investigated whether, and to what extent, did the conceptual improvements found immediately after the intervention persist. A logistic mixed model analysis of students' (N=142) responses in delayed post-test indicated an improved understanding of social media mechanisms compared to the pre-test, but a slight overall decrease compared to the post-test. The results suggest that children can gradually develop more sophisticated and scientifically grounded understandings of the opaque, data-driven systems they encounter in everyday life, but this requires systematic scaffolding and cumulative learning trajectories. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: LLM on a Budget: Active Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Classification of Large Text Corpora

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are highly accurate in classification tasks, however, substantial computational and financial costs hinder their large-scale deployment in dynamic environments. Knowledge Distillation (KD) where a LLM 'teacher' trains a smaller and more efficient 'student' model, offers a promising solution to this problem. However, the distillation process itself often remains costly for large datasets, since it requires the teacher to label a vast number of samples while incurring significant token consumption. To alleviate this challenge, in this work we explore the active learning (AL) as a way to create efficient student models at a fraction of the cost while preserving the LLM's performance. In particular, we introduce M-RARU (Multi-class Randomized Accept/Reject Uncertainty Sampling), a novel AL algorithm that significantly reduces training costs. M-RARU employs an innovative strategy combining uncertainty with a randomized accept-reject mechanism to select only the most informative data points for the LLM teacher. This focused approach significantly minimizes required API calls and data processing time. We evaluate M-RARU against random sampling across five diverse student models (SVM, LDA, RF, GBDT, and DistilBERT) on multiple benchmark datasets. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed method achieves up to 80% reduction in sample requirements as compared to random sampling, substantially improving classification accuracy while reducing financial costs and overall training time. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Characterizing Teacher Agency in Processes of Evaluation, Co-Design, and Orchestration of Intelligent Technologies: A Multicase Study
Source title: CEUR Workshop Proceedings
Affiliations: Faculty of Education and Social Work, Universidad de Valladolid, Valladolid, Spain; School of Telecommunications Engineering, Universidad de Valladolid, Valladolid, Spain; School of Computer Engineering, Universidad de Valladolid, Valladolid, Spain

Abstract: Teacher agency refers to the capacity of educators to enact educational transformations that align with their personal stances, beliefs, values, and goals. To exercise agency effectively, teachers must navigate the complexities of their working environments. In Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) contexts, the increasing use of intelligent technologies—such as Learning Analytics systems that provide adaptive recommendations or AI-driven feedback—has led to the automation of tasks traditionally performed by teachers. This automation, which occurs during the enactment of learning activities, can either empower or challenge the teacher’s role. Nevertheless, the potential to influence teaching practices can be better understood by considering a broad range of factors, including the evaluation of technological systems, the co-design of learning activities and intelligent components, as well as aspects related to orchestration. Particularly through the lens of agency, whose implications for this context remain to be fully explored and understood. In this thesis, we are conducting a multicase study that spans three cases, each involving different technologies that support unique learning scenarios. Learning Analytics are central to the three cases because they support or hinder teachers’ agentic behavior as a result of the capacity to automate orchestration activities. Thus, we aim to provide an understanding of how teachers’ agency is shaped by intelligent technologies and by practitioners’ involvement in evaluation, co-design, and orchestration activities. So far, one case study involving a Smart Learning Environment has been conducted and fully analyzed. While two others, involving the co-design of a multi-agent generative AI architecture for a Computer Supported Collaborative Learning social platform and the evaluation of a Multimodal Learning Analytics system with AI-driven feedback, are in the final data collection phases. © 2025 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: To explore the construction methods of intelligent curricula, leveraging the powerful data processing, intelligent analysis, and autonomous decision-making capabilities of artificial intelligence technology, and utilizing advanced teaching theories such as constructivism, multiple intelligences, learning analytics, and connectivism to empower the development of intelligent curricula, a resource data platform, curriculum knowledge graph, and intelligent agent base for teaching large models have been established. This includes the development of curriculum-based teaching materials, curriculum framed by teaching materials, and an intelligent curriculum system, effectively addressing practical teaching issues such as outdated traditional curriculum content, rigid models, difficulties in sharing, one-sided evaluations, and weak foundations, resulting in improved teaching effectiveness.  © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Non-Autoregressive Translation Algorithm Based on LLM Knowledge Distillation in English Corpus
Source title: Engineering Reports
Affiliations: Department of Foreign Languages, Jinzhong University, Jinzhong, China; School of Computer Science, Sichuan University Jinjiang College, Meishan, China
Authors with affiliations: Ju F., Department of Foreign Languages, Jinzhong University, Jinzhong, China; Wang W., School of Computer Science, Sichuan University Jinjiang College, Meishan, China
Abstract: Although significant advancements have been made in the quality of machine translation by large-scale language models, their high computational costs and resource consumption have hindered their widespread adoption in practical applications. So this research introduces an English corpus-based machine translation algorithm that leverages knowledge distillation from large language model, with the goal of enhancing translation quality and reducing the computational demands of the model. Initially, we conducted a thorough analysis of the English corpus to identify prevalent language patterns and structures. Following this, we developed a knowledge distillation approach that transfers the translation expertise of a large teacher model to a smaller student model, thereby achieving increased translation accuracy and efficiency. We designed a dynamic temperature hyperparameter distillation strategy that effectively enhances the precision of translations. In the experimental phase, we utilized several standard English corpora to train and assess our algorithm. The findings indicate that, compared to current machine translation systems, our method significantly reduces the need for computational resources while preserving translation quality. © 2024 The Author(s). Title: Enhancing Knowledge Distillation of Large Language Models through Efficient Multi-Modal Distribution Alignment
Source title: Proceedings - International Conference on Computational Linguistics, COLING
Affiliations: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China; Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China; Wuhan AI Research, China; Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China
Authors with affiliations: Peng T., School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, Wuhan AI Research, China; Zhang J., School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, China, Wuhan AI Research, China, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Shanghai, China
Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective model compression method that can transfer the internal capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to smaller ones. However, the multi-modal probability distribution predicted by teacher LLMs causes difficulties for student models to learn. In this paper, we first demonstrate the importance of multi-modal distribution alignment with experiments and then highlight the inefficiency of existing KD approaches in learning multi-modal distributions. To address this problem, we propose Ranking Loss based Knowledge Distillation (RLKD), which encourages the consistency of the ranking of peak predictions between the teacher and student models. By incorporating word-level ranking loss, we ensure excellent compatibility with existing distillation objectives while fully leveraging the fine-grained information between different categories in peaks of two predicted distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that our method enables the student model to better learn the multi-modal distributions of the teacher model, leading to a significant performance improvement in various downstream tasks. © 2025 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Title: CustomKD: Customizing Large Vision Foundation for Edge Model Improvement via Knowledge Distillation
Source title: Proceedings of the IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition
Affiliations: Qualcomm Ai Research, China
Authors with affiliations: Lee J., Qualcomm Ai Research, China; Das D., Qualcomm Ai Research, China; Hayat M., Qualcomm Ai Research, China; Choi S., Qualcomm Ai Research, China; Hwang K., Qualcomm Ai Research, China; Porikli F., Qualcomm Ai Research, China
Abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach, CustomKD, that effectively leverages large vision foundation models (LVFMs) to enhance the performance of edge models (e.g., MobileNetV3). Despite recent advancements in LVFMs, such as DINOv2 and CLIP, their potential in knowledge distillation for enhancing edge models remains underexplored. While knowledge distillation is a promising approach for improving the performance of edge models, the discrepancy in model capacities and heterogeneous architectures between LVFMs and edge models poses a significant challenge. Our observation indicates that although utilizing larger backbones (e.g., ViT-S to ViT-L) in teacher models improves their downstream task performances, the knowledge distillation from the large teacher models fails to bring as much performance gain for student models as for teacher models due to the large model discrepancy. Our simple yet effective CustomKD customizes the well-generalized features inherent in LVFMs to a given student model in order to reduce model discrepancies. Specifically, beyond providing well-generalized original knowledge from teachers, CustomKD aligns the features of teachers to those of students, making it easy for students to understand and overcome the large model discrepancy overall. CustomKD significantly improves the performances of edge models in scenarios with unlabeled data such as unsupervised domain adaptation (e.g., OfficeHome and DomainNet) and semi-supervised learning (e.g., CIFAR-100 and ImageNet), achieving the new state-of-the-art performances.  © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Aligning Teaching Objectives with Formative Assessment to Uncover Student Learning Challenges
Source title: Lecture Notes in Informatics (LNI), Proceedings - Series of the Gesellschaft fur Informatik (GI)
Affiliations: LMU Munich, Institute for Informatics, Oettingenstraße 67, Munich, 80538, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Azaiz I., LMU Munich, Institute for Informatics, Oettingenstraße 67, Munich, 80538, Germany; Strickroth S., LMU Munich, Institute for Informatics, Oettingenstraße 67, Munich, 80538, Germany
Abstract: In higher education, especially in introductory computer science courses, student diversity challenges instructors to design student-centered curricula that address students’ actual learning needs. Although e-assessment and feedback systems play a critical role in supporting students’ acquisition of programming skills by delivering formative feedback, they often fail to integrate explicit teaching objectives into their evaluation and analysis strategies. To address this gap, we propose a rubric-based approach that allows educators to systematically evaluate student performance in relation to the defined teaching objectives through tutor-provided formative feedback. Systematic alignment of learning objectives, teaching methods and assessment data helps educators identify students’ difficulties, and reveals discrepancies between intended teaching objectives and actual assessment outcomes. This fosters a more student-centered environment, and offers instructors and students transparent insights into the achievement of teaching objectives. © 2025 Gesellschaft fur Informatik (GI). Title: DA-KD: Difficulty-Aware Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Large Language Models
Source title: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research

Abstract: Although knowledge distillation (KD) is an effec-tive approach to improve the performance of a smaller LLM (i.e., the student model) by trans-ferring knowledge from a large LLM (i.e., the teacher model), it still suffers from high training cost. Existing LLM distillation methods ignore the difficulty difference among different samples, making the distillation of easy samples unnec-essary. This leads to high distillation cost. In this paper, we propose difficulty-aware knowl-edge distillation (DA-KD) framework for efficient knowledge distillation, in which we dynamically adjust the distillation dataset based on the diffi-culty of samples. We further observe existing KD loss cannot perform well when most of samples are difficult in the distillation dataset because of unstable optimization and the neglect of hard sam-ples. Therefore, we also propose a new KD loss called bidirectional discrepancy loss (BDL) for effective KD. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our DA-KD framework is effective and ef-ficient. Without bells and whistles, DA-KD can outperform existing state-of-the-art KD methods by 2% with half training cost and even surpass the teacher model with 4.7× compression. © 2020 by the authors.

Authors with affiliations: Renuka K., Psg College of Technology, Department of Information Technology, Coimbatore, India; Anusuya R., Psg College of Technology, Department of Information Technology, Coimbatore, India; Naveen V., Psg College of Technology, Department of Information Technology, Coimbatore, India; Prince Albert R., Psg College of Technology, Department of Information Technology, Coimbatore, India; Ranjith R., Psg College of Technology, Department of Information Technology, Coimbatore, India; Shyam Surya S.G., Psg College of Technology, Department of Information Technology, Coimbatore, India
Abstract: The work, titled 'Optimizing Large Language Models for Edge Devices Using Knowledge Distillation', aims to develop an efficient and lightweight text classification system tailored for edge devices such as smartphones and embedded systems. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer high accuracy in natural language processing tasks, their computational and memory demands render them unsuitable for direct deployment on resource-constrained edge hardware. To address this limitation, the project employs knowledge distillation, where a compact student model is trained to emulate the behavior of a larger teacher model, preserving performance while significantly reducing complexity. Furthermore, the system incorporates quantization techniques to compress model parameters into lower-bit representations, enhancing memory efficiency and inference speed. Together, these approaches facilitate real-time, on-device disaster tweet classification without reliance on cloud infrastructure. The methodology demonstrates strong potential for broader applications, including healthcare alerts, cybersecurity threat detection, and filtering of misinformation.  © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Carry-forward effect: providing proactive scaffolding to learning processes
Source title: Behaviour and Information Technology
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway
Authors with affiliations: Sharma K., Department of Computer Science, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway; Giannakos M., Department of Computer Science, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway
Abstract: Multimodal data enables us to capture the cognitive and affective states of students to provide a holistic understanding of learning processes in a wide variety of contexts. With the use of sensing technology, we can capture learners' states in near real-time and support learning. Moreover, multimodal data allows us to obtain early predictions of learning performance, and support learning in a timely manner. In this contribution, we utilise the notion of ‘carry forward effect’, an inferential and predictive modelling approach that utilises multimodal data measurements detrimental to learning performance to provide timely feedback suggestions. Carry forward effect can provide a way to prioritise conflicting feedback suggestions in a multimodal data-based scaffolding tool. We showcase the empirical proof of the carry forward effect with the use of three different learning scenarios: game-based learning, individual debugging, and collaborative debugging. © 2024 The Author(s). Title: Beyond Output Matching: Bidirectional Alignment for Enhanced In-Context Learning
Source title: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
Affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Guangzhou, China; Princeton University, United States; Nanyang Technological University, Singapore; Salesforce Research, Singapore; Institute of High Performance Computing (IHPC), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore
Authors with affiliations: Qin C., The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Guangzhou, China, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore; Xia W., Princeton University, United States; Jiao F., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore; Chen C., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore; Hu Y., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore; Ding B., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore; Chen R., Institute of High Performance Computing (IHPC), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore; Joty S., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Salesforce Research, Singapore
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive few-shot generalization on many tasks via in-context learning (ICL). Despite their success in showing such emergent abilities, the scale and complexity of larger models also lead to unprecedentedly high computational demands and deployment challenges. In reaction, researchers explore transferring the powerful capabilities of larger models to more efficient and compact models by typically aligning the output of smaller (student) models with that of larger (teacher) models. Existing methods either train student models on the generated outputs of teacher models or imitate their token-level probability distributions. However, these distillation methods pay little to no attention to the input, which also plays a crucial role in ICL. Based on the finding that the performance of ICL is highly sensitive to the selection of demonstration examples, we propose Bidirectional Alignment (BiAlign) to fully leverage the models' preferences for ICL examples to improve the ICL abilities of student models. Specifically, we introduce the alignment of input preferences between student and teacher models by incorporating a novel ranking loss, in addition to aligning the token-level output distribution. With extensive experiments and analysis, we demonstrate that BiAlign can consistently outperform existing baselines on various tasks involving language understanding, reasoning, and coding. © 2025 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Title: Unified Reinforcement and Imitation Learning for Vision-Language Models
Source title: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
Affiliations: KAIST, South Korea; NVIDIA, United States; National Taiwan University, Taiwan
Authors with affiliations: Lee B.-K., KAIST, South Korea, NVIDIA, United States; Hachiuma R., NVIDIA, United States; Ro Y.M., KAIST, South Korea; Wang Y.-C.F., NVIDIA, United States, National Taiwan University, Taiwan; Wu Y.-H., NVIDIA, United States
Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, yet their large scale often renders them impractical for resource-constrained environments. This paper introduces Unified Reinforcement and Imitation Learning (RIL), a novel and efficient training algorithm designed to create powerful, lightweight VLMs. RIL distinctively combines the strengths of reinforcement learning with adversarial imitation learning. This enables smaller student VLMs not only to mimic the sophisticated text generation of large teacher models but also to systematically improve their generative capabilities through reinforcement signals. Key to our imitation framework is an LLM-based discriminator that adeptly distinguishes between student and teacher outputs, complemented by guidance from multiple large teacher VLMs to ensure diverse learning. This unified learning strategy, leveraging both reinforcement and imitation, empowers student models to achieve significant performance gains, making them competitive with leading closed-source VLMs. Extensive experiments on diverse vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RIL significantly narrows the performance gap with state-of-the-art open- and closed-source VLMs and, in several instances, surpasses them. © 2025 Neural information processing systems foundation. Title: TinyThinker: Distilling Reasoning through Coarse-to-Fine Knowledge Internalization with Self-Reflection
Source title: Proceedings of the 2025 Annual Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies: Long Papers, NAACL-HLT 2025
Affiliations: Yonsei University, Seoul, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Piao S., Yonsei University, Seoul, South Korea; Park S., Yonsei University, Seoul, South Korea
Abstract: Large Language Models exhibit impressive reasoning capabilities across diverse tasks, motivating efforts to distill these capabilities into smaller models through generated reasoning data. However, direct training on such synthesized reasoning data may lead to superficial imitation of reasoning process, rather than fostering a genuine integration of reasoning capabilities with underlying knowledge. To address this, we propose TinyThinker, a framework introducing two novel approaches. First, we introduce a three-stage process that incrementally guides the student model through the reasoning process, progressively refining knowledge from coarse to fine granularity. Second, we develop a two-phase training framework comprising an initial reasoning acquisition phase followed by a self-reflection phase utilizing self-generated data. Experiments on commonsense reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that TinyThinker achieves superior performance compared to baselines. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component in our framework. We expect that TinyThinker can be extended to other knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks, offering an alternative strategy for developing effective reasoning capabilities in smaller language models. Codes are available at https://github.com/shengminp/TinyThinker. © 2025 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Abstract: An interpretable and computationally efficient deep learning framework for the early screening of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) that exploits a Lightweight Vision Transformer (L ViT) has been proposed in this research. The model combines distillation and explanation consistency loss to balance accuracy, interpretability and efficiency. In addition, a teacher-student network framework is employed to distil semantic and spatial knowledge from a huge transformer to the small student model, which is beneficial for real time and edge applications. In addition, an explanation head incorporates attention rollout with gradient based saliency maps to enhance clinically significant retinal lesions (microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and exudates). Experiments on EyePACS, Messidor 2 and IDRiD datasets show that the proposed L ViT outperforms CNN and the existing ViT baselines with 95.6% accuracy and 0.982 AUC at a reduced computational cost. An interpretable and reliable diagnostic model, which is a stepping stone toward affordable AI based retinal screening in resource constrained environments has been developed. © 2025 IEEE.

Abstract: This empirical research investigates the role of NLP-based chatbots in personalised learning using secondary data. The research analyzes the performance of chatbots, learning results, and student engagement using machine learning tools and educational datasets. The outcomes indicate an increase of 23.4% in the engagement of students and a 18. 7% increase in learning retention with respect to the conventional approaches. The most important indicators are 89.2 percent of accurate response, 82.6% of satisfaction, and 76.8% of task accomplishment. Although its advantages are evident, such problems as prejudice, restricted access, and excessive dependence are also present. The research reveals the importance of ethical use and teacher-involvement to make sure that chatbots are really beneficial to the process of student learning in a meaningful and responsible manner.  © 2025 IEEE.

Abstract: The integration of Network Functions Virtualization (NFV) systems into mobile edge and core networks has heightened the need for effective anomaly detection and localization methods. The complexity of NFV demands robust mechanisms for network resilience, security, and performance. Machine Learning approaches have demonstrated promising solutions in crafting adaptive and efficient mechanisms for detecting and localizing potential anomalies within NFV systems. Particularly, Unsupervised Learning (UL) methods have garnered significant attention for their potential to detect anomalies without the need for labeled data. However, UL methods are susceptible to even minor levels of anomalous samples in the training data, termed contamination, which can severely compromise their performance. This paper proposes a novel approach using the Noisy-Student technique for anomaly detection. It addresses data contamination by combining a density-estimation teacher model for pseudo-labeling with a weakly-supervised student model based on a Masked Autoencoder trained on the pseudo-labeled data. For anomaly localization, we introduce a heuristic tailored for our anomaly detection model and two Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)-based approaches applicable to any detection model. Extensive experiments on three NFV datasets demonstrate superior performance, with up to a 20% improvement in anomaly detection and up to a 22% improvement in localization, in terms of F1-score. © 2002-2012 IEEE.

Title: MOSAIC-F: A Framework for Enhancing Students’ Oral Presentation Skills through Personalized Feedback
Source title: CEUR Workshop Proceedings

Abstract: In this article, we present a novel multimodal feedback framework called MOSAIC-F, an acronym for a data-driven Framework that integrates Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA), Observations, Sensors, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Collaborative assessments for generating personalized feedback on student learning activities. This framework consists of four key steps. First, peers and professors’ assessments are conducted through standardized rubrics (that include both quantitative and qualitative evaluations). Second, multimodal data are collected during learning activities, including video recordings, audio capture, gaze tracking, physiological signals (heart rate, motion data), and behavioral interactions. Third, personalized feedback is generated using AI, synthesizing human-based evaluations and data-based multimodal insights such as posture, speech patterns, stress levels, and cognitive load, among others. Finally, students review their own performance through video recordings and engage in self-assessment and feedback visualization, comparing their own evaluations with peers and professors’ assessments, class averages, and AI-generated recommendations. By combining human-based and data-based evaluation techniques, this framework enables more accurate, personalized and actionable feedback. We tested MOSAIC-F in the context of improving oral presentation skills. © 2025 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: This study presents a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework for interpretable learning analytics and feedback generation, designed to transform assessment data into structured, meaningful insights for educators and learners. The framework consists of three layers: Data Preprocessing, which organizes quiz data into a structured format; LLM Reasoning, which applies prompt engineering and context building to analyze performance; and Visualization, which generates feedback reports in a structured markup format for PDF export. Two language models, OpenAI GPT-4o and DeepSeek Reasoner (R1), were explored through their respective APIs and evaluated through expert review. Results showed that both models produced coherent, rubric-aligned feedback, with GPT-4o achieving slightly higher interpretability and linguistic fluency. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates the feasibility of using LLMs for automated and interpretable educational feedback, supporting scalable and data-driven formative assessment in digital learning environments. © 2025 IEEE.

Abstract: Recent efforts leverage knowledge distillation techniques to develop lightweight and practical sentiment analysis models. These methods are grounded in human-written instructions and large-scale user texts. Despite the promising results, two key challenges remain: (1) manually written instructions are limited in diversity and quantity, making them insufficient to ensure comprehensive coverage of distilled knowledge; (2) large-scale user texts incur high computational cost, hindering the practicality of these methods. To this end, we introduce COMPEFFDIST, a comprehensive and efficient distillation framework for sentiment analysis. Our framework consists of two key modules: attribute-based automatic instruction construction and difficulty-based data filtering, which correspondingly tackle the aforementioned challenges. Applying our method across multiple model series (Llama-3, Qwen-3, and Gemma-3), we enable 3B student models to match the performance of 20x larger teacher models on most tasks. In addition, our approach greatly outperforms baseline methods in data efficiency, attaining the same performance level with only 10% of the data. Title: Few-Shot Knowledge Distillation of LLMs With Counterfactual Explanations
Source title: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
Affiliations: University of Maryland, College Park, United States
Authors with affiliations: Hamman F., University of Maryland, College Park, United States; Dissanayake P., University of Maryland, College Park, United States; Fu Y., University of Maryland, College Park, United States; Dutta S., University of Maryland, College Park, United States
Abstract: Knowledge distillation is a promising approach to transfer capabilities from complex teacher models to smaller, resource-efficient student models that can be deployed easily, particularly in task-aware scenarios. However, existing methods of task-aware distillation typically require substantial quantities of data which may be unavailable or expensive to obtain in many practical scenarios. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing a novel strategy called Counterfactual-explanation-infused Distillation (COD) for few-shot task-aware knowledge distillation by systematically infusing counterfactual explanations. Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) refer to inputs that can flip the output prediction of the teacher model with minimum perturbation. Our strategy COD leverages these CFEs to precisely map the teacher's decision boundary with significantly fewer samples. We provide theoretical guarantees for motivating the role of CFEs in distillation, from both statistical and geometric perspectives. We mathematically show that CFEs can improve parameter estimation by providing more informative examples near the teacher's decision boundary. We also derive geometric insights on how CFEs effectively act as knowledge probes, helping the students mimic the teacher's decision boundaries more effectively than standard data. We perform experiments across various datasets and LLMs to show that COD outperforms standard distillation approaches in few-shot regimes (as low as 8-512 samples). Notably, COD only uses half of the original samples used by the baselines, paired with their corresponding CFEs and still improves performance. Abstract: To Provide individualized, adaptable learning environments, EduTrack, an AI-powered learning platform, seeks to revolutionize higher education. EduTrack incorporates state-of-the-art technology to enhance academic performance and student engagement. It is built on the MERN stack and employs Python-based microservices for machine learning. The platform features a hybrid video recommendation engine, adaptive learning pathways, real-time AI chatbot, and extensive performance statistics. This report highlights the research gaps that EduTrack fills, especially in the areas of scalability, personalization, and real-time learner support - areas where existing AI platforms often fail. Teachers and students have their own dashboards with EduTrack. While students may access study materials, performance tracking, and AI-driven assistance, teachers can post resources, give tests, and monitor their progress. A learning style detection engine that can provide content in a personalized manner, an AI chatbot that can answer questions in real time using Gemini or OpenAI, a hybrid video recommendation system that blends collaborative and content-based filtering, and a test performance analyzer that can adapt learning paths to each user's needs are some of its primary features. EduTrack uses algorithms like Random Forest, SVD, Decision Trees, and NLP to deliver a personalized learning experience. Learning analytics and digital identity systems can be combined to give teachers data-driven insights that raise student performance and engagement. By combining intelligent digital learning with traditional models, EduTrack aims to create a flexible, effective, and inclusive learning environment for a variety of educational needs. © 2025 IEEE.

Abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation has exploited semantics to reduce depth ambiguities in texture-less regions and object boundaries. However, existing methods struggle to obtain universal semantics across scenes for effective depth estimation. This paper proposes VFM-Depth, a novel self-supervised teacher-student framework, that effectively leverages the vision foundation model as semantic regularization to significantly improve the accuracy of monocular depth estimation. Firstly, we propose a novel Geometric-Semantic Aggregation Encoding, integrating universal semantic constraints from the foundation model to reduce ambiguities in the teacher model. Specifically, semantic features from the foundation model and geometric features from the depth model are first encoded and then fused through cross-modal aggregation. Secondly, we introduce a novel Multi-Alignment for Depth Distillation to distill semantic constraints from the teacher, further leveraging knowledge from the foundation model. We obtain a lightweight yet effective student model through an innovative approach that combines distance category alignment with complementary feature and depth imitation. Extensive experiments on KITTI, Cityscapes, and Make3D datasets demonstrate that VFM-Depth (both teacher and student) outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised methods by a large margin. © 1991-2012 IEEE.

Title: Investigating the Zone of Proximal Development of Language Models for In-Context Learning
Source title: 2025 Annual Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Proceedings of the Conference Findings, NAACL 2025
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, ETH Zürich, Switzerland
Authors with affiliations: Cui P., Department of Computer Science, ETH Zürich, Switzerland; Sachan M., Department of Computer Science, ETH Zürich, Switzerland
Abstract: In this paper, we introduce a learning analytics framework to analyze the in-context learning (ICL) behavior of large language models (LLMs) through the lens of the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), an established theory in educational psychology. ZPD delineates the the space between what a learner is capable of doing unsupported and what the learner cannot do even with support. We adapt this concept to ICL, measuring the ZPD of LLMs based on model performance on individual examples before and after ICL. Furthermore, we propose an item response theory (IRT) model to predict the distribution of zones for LLMs. Our findings reveal a series of intricate and multifaceted behaviors of ICL, providing new insights into understanding and leveraging this technique. Finally, we demonstrate how our framework can enhance LLM in both inference and fine-tuning scenarios: (1) By predicting a model’s zone of proximal development, we selectively apply ICL to queries that are most likely to benefit from demonstrations, achieving a better balance between inference cost and performance; (2) We propose a human-like curriculum for fine-tuning, which prioritizes examples within the model’s ZPD. The curriculum results in improved performance, and we explain its effectiveness through an analysis of the training dynamics of LLMs. ©2025 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Title: SUPERCORRECT: ADVANCING SMALL LLM REASONING WITH THOUGHT TEMPLATE DISTILLATION AND SELF-CORRECTION
Source title: 13th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2025
Affiliations: Peking University, China; Skywork AI, United States; National University of Singapore, Singapore; UC Berkeley, United States; Stanford University, United States
Authors with affiliations: Yang L., Peking University, China; Yu Z., Peking University, China; Zhang T., UC Berkeley, United States; Xu M., Stanford University, United States; Gonzalez J.E., UC Berkeley, United States; Cui B., Peking University, China; Yan S., Skywork AI, United States, National University of Singapore, Singapore
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4, DeepSeek-R1, and ReasonFlux have shown significant improvements in various reasoning tasks. However, smaller LLMs still struggle with complex mathematical reasoning because they fail to effectively identify and correct reasoning errors. Recent reflection-based methods aim to address these issues by enabling self-reflection and self-correction, but they still face challenges in independently detecting errors in their reasoning steps. To overcome these limitations, we propose SUPERCORRECT, a novel two-stage framework that uses a large teacher model to supervise and correct both the reasoning and reflection processes of a smaller student model. In the first stage, we extract hierarchical high-level and detailed thought templates from the teacher model to guide the student model in eliciting more fine-grained reasoning thoughts. In the second stage, we introduce cross-model collaborative direct preference optimization (DPO) to enhance the self-correction abilities of the student model by following the teacher's correction traces during training. This cross-model DPO approach teaches the student model to effectively locate and resolve erroneous thoughts with error-driven insights from the teacher model, breaking the bottleneck of its thoughts and acquiring new skills and knowledge to tackle challenging problems. Extensive experiments consistently demonstrate our superiority over previous methods. Notably, our SUPERCORRECT-7B model significantly surpasses powerful DeepSeekMath-7B by 7.8%/5.3% and Qwen2.5-Math-7B by 15.1%/6.3% on MATH/GSM8K benchmarks, achieving new SOTA performance among all 7B models. © 2025 13th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2025. Abstract: Learning performance data, such as correct or incorrect answers and problem-solving attempts in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), facilitate the assessment of knowledge mastery and the delivery of effective instructions. However, these data tend to be highly sparse (80%\sim90% missing observations) in most real-world applications. This data sparsity presents challenges to using learner models to effectively predict learners' future performance and explore new hypotheses about learning. This article proposes a systematic framework for augmenting learning performance data to address data sparsity. First, learning performance data can be represented as a 3-D tensor with dimensions corresponding to learners, questions, and attempts, effectively capturing longitudinal knowledge states during learning. Second, a tensor factorization method is used to impute missing values in sparse tensors of collected learner data, thereby grounding the imputation on knowledge tracing (KT) tasks that predict missing performance values based on real observations. Third, data augmentation using generative artificial intelligence models, including generative adversarial network (GAN), specifically vanilla GANs and generative pretrained transformers (GPTs, specifically GPT-4o), generate data tailored to individual clusters of learning performance. We tested this systemic framework on adult literacy datasets from AutoTutor lessons developed for adult reading comprehension. We found that tensor factorization outperformed baseline KT techniques in tracing and predicting learning performance, demonstrating higher fidelity in data imputation, and the vanilla GAN-based augmentation demonstrated greater overall stability across varying sample sizes, whereas GPT-4o-based augmentation exhibited higher variability, with occasional cases showing closer fidelity to the original data distribution. This framework facilitates the effective augmentation of learning performance data, enabling controlled, cost-effective approach for the evaluation and optimization of ITS instructional designs in both online and offline environments prior to deployment, and supporting advanced educational data mining and learning analytics. © 2025 IEEE. Title: Knowledge Distillation in RAG: Enabling Small Models to Efficiently Leverage Large-Scale Knowledge Bases
Source title: 2025 6th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Computer Engineering, ICAICE 2025
Affiliations: San Francisco, 94108, CA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Zhang Z., San Francisco, 94108, CA, United States
Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines neural retrieval and text generation to improve factuality and reduce hallucination in large language models. However, large RAG systems such as Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) and DeepMind's RETRO are computationally expensive and challenging to deploy in low-resource or latency-sensitive environments, as also observed in recent studies on compressed contexts and efficient inference. This paper presents RAG-KD, a unified dual-stage knowledge distillation (KD) framework that transfers both retrieval and generation capabilities from large teacher RAG models to smaller students. Our approach introduces a retrieval- generation consistency loss aligning document- and token-level attribution, inspired by attribution-based interpretability methods. Extensive experiments on Natural Questions (NQ), HotpotQA, and FiQA demonstrate that our student models retain over 90% of teacher performance while achieving lower latency and smaller memory footprint. We further analyze robustness under noisy retrieval and interpretability of the distilled models. © 2025 IEEE.

Abstract: The concept of Education 5.0 has emerged as a response to the rise of Information and Communication Technology (ICT), especially Artificial Intelligence (AI), which has established a significant niche in education. This paper elaborates on two areas of AI that have been used to revolutionize higher education in teaching and learning: Machine Learning (ML) and Generative AI (GAI). In particular, we discuss the applications of ML in predicting student performance, personalized learning, learning analytics, and plagiarism detection. Additionally, we provide an overview of the applications of GAI in higher education, including AI-powered tutoring, automated content creation, academic writing and research, as well as grading and feedback. Finally, we present challenges and open research problems to guide future research in this area. © 2025 IEEE.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional reasoning capabilities in complex fault diagnosis tasks, but their massive parameter requirements hinder deployment in resource-constrained industrial environments. To address this challenge, this study proposes a Chain-of-Thought (CoT)-driven reasoning distillation framework for transferring logical inference capabilities from large teacher models to lightweight student models. By leveraging LLMs as teachers, structured reasoning chains containing multi-step diagnostic logic are elicited through meticulously designed prompts. Alarm signals are then used as inputs, with the reasoning chains encapsulated within ¡reasoning¿ tags serving as critical supervisory signals. The final diagnostic work orders and reasoning chains constitute a comprehensive instruction-tuning dataset. To enhance model generalization, semantic-preserving paraphrasing is employed to augment input signals. Experimental results demonstrate that the distilled student models achieve significant accuracy improvements while maintaining reasoning trace fidelity comparable to teacher models. This research establishes a feasible pathway for deploying interpretable AI diagnostic systems on industrial edge devices with limited computational resources. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Mapping the Knowledge Construction Process Through Interactions with an Embodied GenAI Agent in Mixed Reality
Source title: Proceedings - 25th IEEE International Conference on Advanced Learning Technologies, ICALT 2025
Affiliations: University of Oulu, Learning, Education, and Technology (LET) Research Lab, Oulu, Finland
Authors with affiliations: Nguyen A., University of Oulu, Learning, Education, and Technology (LET) Research Lab, Oulu, Finland; Dang B., University of Oulu, Learning, Education, and Technology (LET) Research Lab, Oulu, Finland; Gul F., University of Oulu, Learning, Education, and Technology (LET) Research Lab, Oulu, Finland; Huynh L., University of Oulu, Learning, Education, and Technology (LET) Research Lab, Oulu, Finland
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is emerging as a transformative tool in education, offering the potential to reshape traditional learning experiences. In parallel, recent advancements in mixed reality (MR) have the potential to create a unique learning environment that seamlessly blends physical and artificial entities, fostering immersive and interactive educational experiences. Despite the promise of deploying embodied GenAI in MR settings for enhancing learning experiences, empirical research examining its roles in learning processes remains limited. This study examines the process of knowledge construction through learners' interactions with an embodied GenAI agent in MR learning environments. The study examines 1162 interactions collected from twenty-six graduate students participating in an interactive learning session on AI ethics in the MR learning environment with an embodied GenAI agent. Using a learning analytics approach combined with process mining techniques, we mapped the sequential patterns of knowledge construction processes observed in this smart learning environment. Findings indicate that real-time feedback and adaptive interactions from embodied GenAI agents enhance engagement and facilitate an iterative cycle of inquiry for knowledge construction. Our study has practical implications for the design and implementation of educational technologies, guiding the effective incorporation of GenAI-driven interactive agents into MR for next-generation smart learning environments.  © 2025 IEEE.

Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) continues to transform various sectors, its integration within education, particularly in STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics) education, is gaining momentum. This paper explores how AI can enhance STEAM education for K-12 students, preparing them for a rapidly evolving digital world. A review of current literature demonstrates that AI technologies, including virtual reality, augmented reality, machine learning, and IoT, can revolutionize both teaching and learning by promoting critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills. AI-driven tools like ChatGPT, learning analytics, and chatbots provide personalized learning experiences, making education more interactive and engaging. The paper also highlights AI's role in fostering inclusivity and bridging gender gaps within STEAM, particularly in arts education. Furthermore, the paper examines the challenges of AI integration, such as teacher readiness, trust in technology, and the need for professional development. The findings underscore AI's potential to empower educators and students alike, suggesting a roadmap for AI-enhanced STEAM education aligned with sustainable development goals. This research advocates for incorporating AI literacy in curricula to equip students with essential skills for the future. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Automating SSRL Detection in Asynchronous OCL via LLMs
Source title: 2025 7th International Conference on Computer Science and Technologies in Education, CSTE 2025
Affiliations: Faculty of Education, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China
Authors with affiliations: Li M., Faculty of Education, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China; Qin W., Faculty of Education, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China; Tang Z., Faculty of Education, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China; Fang X., Faculty of Education, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China; He T., Faculty of Education, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China; Cao X., Faculty of Education, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China
Abstract: Socially Shared Regulation of Learning (SSRL) in online collaborative learning (OCL) presents significant challenges due to the complexity of asynchronous interactions and the limitations of conventional content analysis methods. However, existing tools struggle to scale effectively with the heterogeneous nature of peer discussions, which are context-dependent and linguistically nuanced. This study introduces a novel, modular, intelligent coding system that integrates SSRL theory with large language models (LLMs), enabling automated content analysis. Using 1,380 peer-discussion entries from a 16-week undergraduate course, we evaluated three LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o1, and DeepSeek-R1) with a three-stage experimental pipeline: Zero-shot, Few-shot, and Few-shot Chain-of-Thought prompting. Results showed that Few-shot Chain-of-Thought prompting improved contextual reasoning, with DeepSeek-R1 achieving 83.3% accuracy in phase identification, leveraging attention-based modeling of implicit linguistic cohesion in collaborative discussions. The system innovatively encodes SSRL's pedagogical constructs into hierarchical prompt templates, allowing for automatic detection of regulatory patterns while mitigating semantic ambiguity. A case study further demonstrates its effectiveness in distinguishing between surface-level consensus and genuine co-construction behaviors. This work pioneers the integration of SSRL frameworks with generative AI, offering a scalable tool for SSRL regulation analysis in educational settings. Future research should focus on lightweight domain adaptation techniques, such as LoRA fine-tuning, and hybrid models combining cognitive diagnostics to enhance interpretability and bridge the gap between AI outputs and expert judgment in content analysis. © 2025 IEEE.

Authors: Yang X.; Wang S.; Luking L.; Chen Y.
Title: Enabling Visual Foundation Models to Teach Compact Students via Mixture of Distillation
Source title: IJCAI International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
Affiliations: Newcastle University, United Kingdom; University of Science and Technology Beijing, China
Authors with affiliations: Yang X., Newcastle University, United Kingdom; Wang S.; Luking L.; Chen Y., University of Science and Technology Beijing, China
Abstract: In this paper, we present a novel Mixture of Distillation (MoD) framework for distilling lightweight student models using Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) as teachers. Knowledge distillation (KD) is a crucial training strategy for improving model performance. However, conventional KD methods face two main challenges: (1) selecting & training appropriate teacher models and (2) designing effective knowledge distillation techniques. To address the first challenge, we leverage recent VFMs like CLIP, Grounding DINO, and SAM as teachers, capitalizing on their remarkable zero-shot generalization abilities and low fine-tuning requirements for new tasks, thereby avoiding expensive retraining of teachers. For the second challenge, our MoD framework focuses on extracting and decomposing the feature and logit knowledge from VFMs into multiple knowledge experts, which capture modality-specific information across batches, channels, and instances. Each knowledge expert undergoes separate projections, reshaping, normalization, and learnable magnitude operations. Then, we employ sparse knowledge gates with a softmax function followed by a KeepTopK operation for different knowledge experts. In this way, our MoD not only bridges the distillation gap between VFMs and students but also allows the adaptive transfer of useful knowledge across different domains. Extensive experiments on various classification, detection, and medical segmentation tasks validate the effectiveness of our approach with other models. Moreover, our MoD framework demonstrates the potential for transferring zero-shot abilities from VFMs without relying on ground-truth labels. Notably, our MoD achieves impressive performance, attaining 72.48% for RepViT with 76.20% CLIP teacher on ImageNet-1K without annotations. © 2025 International Joint Conferences on Artificial Intelligence. Title: A Comprehensive Review of Current Practices in AI-Assisted Learning

Affiliations: University of Mumbai, Thakur College of Engineering and Technology, Dept. of Information Technology, Mumbai, India; University of Mumbai, Thakur College of Engineering and Technology, Department of Information Technology, Mumbai, India

Abstract: Through the creation of data-driven, customized, and adaptive learning experiences, artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the face of education. In order to evaluate the current practices, trends, and difficulties in AI-assisted learning, this study provides a thorough analysis of 26 recent works. According to the research, there is a lot of emphasis on machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) approaches, which are used in tools like chatbots, automated feedback systems, and adaptive learning platforms. The application field is dominated by higher education, with particular emphasis on computer programming and language acquisition. Significant gaps still exist, nevertheless, such as the lack of a consensus definition for AI-assisted learning, the little investigation of multimodal integration, and the lack of focus on moral issues like algorithmic prejudice and data privacy. Furthermore, rather of using actual learning settings, the majority of research depend on simulations or small-scale setups. In order to overcome these constraints, this paper suggests an integrative architecture that combines multimodal inputs such as text, audio, and video, explainable AI (XAI) for transparency, and ethical governance. Additionally, it promotes more involvement of underrepresented fields including K-12 and vocational education as well as research into hybrid AI- human teaching methods. This paper provides a path for the moral, practical, and inclusive development of AI-assisted learning systems in addition to synthesizing existing information. © 2025 IEEE.

Author full names: Choudhury, Sanjiban (55842232500); Sodhi, Paloma (55421037300)
Title: BETTER THAN YOUR TEACHER: LLM AGENTS THAT LEARN FROM PRIVILEGED AI FEEDBACK
Source title: 13th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2025
Affiliations: Cornell University, NY, United States
Authors with affiliations: Choudhury S., Cornell University, NY, United States; Sodhi P.
Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) show impressive decision-making abilities, current methods lack a mechanism for automatic self-improvement from errors during task execution. We propose LEAP, an iterative fine-tuning framework that continually improves LLM agents using feedback from AI expert teachers. Our key insight is to equip the expert teachers with a privileged state -information available during training but hidden at test time. This allows even weak experts to provide precise guidance, significantly improving the student agent's performance without access to privileged information at test time. We evaluate LEAP on multiple decision-making benchmarks, including text-based games (ALFWorld), web navigation (WebShop), and interactive coding (Intercode Bash). Our experiments show that LEAP (1) outperforms behavior cloning and ReAct baselines (2) enables weak student models (e.g., Llama3-8B) to exceed performance of strong teacher models (GPT-4o), and (3) allows weak models to self-improve using privileged versions of themselves. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that LEAP's success hinges on balancing privileged information with student's realizability, which we empirically validate. Our code is available at https://leap-llm.github.io. © 2025 13th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2025. All rights reserved.

Abstract: Learning Analytics Dashboards (LADs) are tools designed to visualize data on student behavior, performance, and engagement to support learning and teaching. Whilst their adoption has increased significantly in recent years, users often struggle to interpret the visual information they provide. To address this, recent research has begun incorporating Data Storytelling elements to enhance understanding. However, generating such narratives at scale remains a complex challenge. In this paper we present the work we have carried out to explore the use of Generative AI to facilitate the scalable creation of data-driven narratives. We present findings from three distinct studies and discuss the conclusions drawn from them. © 2025 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Title: Mitigating Cognitive Biases in Predicting Student Dropout: Global and Local Explainability with Explainable Boosting Machine
Source title: Journal of Universal Computer Science
Affiliations: Universidade Presbiteriana Mackenzie, São Paulo, Brazil
Authors with affiliations: Camargos R.C., Universidade Presbiteriana Mackenzie, São Paulo, Brazil; Silveira I.F., Universidade Presbiteriana Mackenzie, São Paulo, Brazil
Abstract: This study explores the application of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to mitigate cognitive biases in predicting student dropout. Focusing on the Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM), we compare its performance and explainability with Logistic Regression and XGBoost models. While EBM and Logistic Regression have inherent explainability, we employ SHAP and Morris Sensitivity Analysis for XGBoost to provide both local and global explanations. Our findings indicate that the inherently interpretable nature of EBM supports clear and actionable decision-making in educational settings. When integrated with additional XAI methods for comparative analysis with models like Logistic Regression and XGBoost, the approach can further enhance the understanding of key factors contributing to student dropout. © 2025, IICM. Title: An Active Learning Framework for Inclusive Generation by Large Language Models
Source title: Proceedings - International Conference on Computational Linguistics, COLING
Affiliations: School of Computing and Information, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, United States; Khoury College of Computer Science, Northeastern University, Boston, MA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Hassan S., School of Computing and Information, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, United States; Sicilia A., Khoury College of Computer Science, Northeastern University, Boston, MA, United States; Alikhani M., Khoury College of Computer Science, Northeastern University, Boston, MA, United States
Abstract: Ensuring that Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text representative of diverse sub-populations is essential, particularly when key concepts related to under-represented groups are scarce in the training data. We address this challenge with a novel clustering-based active learning framework, enhanced with knowledge distillation. The proposed framework transforms the intermediate outputs of the learner model, enabling effective active learning for generative tasks for the first time. Integration of clustering and knowledge distillation yields more representative models without prior knowledge of underlying data distribution and overbearing human efforts. We validate our approach in practice through case studies in counter-narration and style transfer. We construct two new datasets in tandem with model training, showing a performance improvement of 2%-10% over baseline models. Our results also show more consistent performance across various data subgroups and increased lexical diversity, underscoring our model's resilience to skewness in available data. Further, our results show that the data acquired via our approach improves the performance of secondary models not involved in the learning loop, showcasing practical utility of the framework. © 2025 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Authors: Ye F.; Bors A.G.
Title: Training a Dynamic Growing Mixture Model for Lifelong Learning
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
Affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, School of Information and Software Engineering, Chengdu, 611731, China; University of York, Department of Computer Science, York, YO10 5GH, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Ye F., University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, School of Information and Software Engineering, Chengdu, 611731, China; Bors A.G., University of York, Department of Computer Science, York, YO10 5GH, United Kingdom
Abstract: Lifelong learning (LLL) defines a training paradigm that aims to continuously acquire and capture new concepts from a sequence of tasks without forgetting. Recently, dynamic expansion models (DEMs) have been proposed to address catastrophic forgetting under the LLL paradigm. However, the efficiency of DEMs lacks a thorough explanation based on theoretical analysis. In this article, we develop a new theoretical framework that interprets the forgetting process of the DEM as increasing the statistical discrepancy distance between the distribution of the probabilistic representation of the new data and the previously learned knowledge. The theoretical analysis shows that adding new components to a mixture model represents a trade-off between model complexity and its performance. Inspired by the theoretical analysis, we introduce a new DEM, called the growing mixture model (GMM), where generative data components are added according to the novelty of the incoming task information compared to what is already known. A new component selection mechanism considering the model's already acquired knowledge is employed for updating new DEM's components, promoting efficient future task learning. We also train a compact student model with samples drawn through the generative mechanisms of the GMM, aiming to accumulate cross-domain representations over time. By employing the student model, we can significantly reduce the number of parameters and make quick inferences during the testing phase.  © 2012 IEEE.

Abstract: Previous studies have shown that early dropout rates in universities range from 17% to 25%, depending on the institution and the program, generating a current problem for universities, and society. Assessing the degree of self-regulated learning among first-year students is essential for enhancing their motivation, integration, and outcomes, which correlates with reducing the risk of dropout. This study presents the results of two instruments that evaluate the degree of student self-regulation and discusses the relationships between variables from both instruments to determine possible relations. The aim is to streamline the monitoring process of self-regulation by potentially using only one instrument in future iterations. The results indicate an apparent disconnection between the instruments despite measuring similar aspects and highlight the need for further research to uncover hidden relationships between variables, including the use of generative artificial intelligence systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

Title: A White-Box Knowledge Distillation Approach for Task-Optimized Large Language Model Compression
Source title: Proceedings of the International Joint Conference on Neural Networks
Affiliations: Sri Sivasubramaniya Nadar College of Engineering, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Chennai, India
Authors with affiliations: Subhankar S., Sri Sivasubramaniya Nadar College of Engineering, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Chennai, India; Palaniappan M., Sri Sivasubramaniya Nadar College of Engineering, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Chennai, India; Jayasimhan A., Sri Sivasubramaniya Nadar College of Engineering, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Chennai, India
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various NLP tasks but remain computationally expensive, limiting their deployment in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a widely used compression technique where a smaller student model learns from a larger teacher model. However, existing research primarily focuses on black-box KD, where only final layer outputs guide the student. This approach overlooks the rich intermediate representations within the teacher model, potentially limiting knowledge transfer. To address this gap, we explore white-box KD, integrating intermediate layer matching with traditional KD techniques. Our research evaluates multiple KD strategies across question answering, text classification, and summarization tasks. We distill models such as T5-Small (60M), BERT-Base (109M), and Pegasus-XSum (569M) into custom student models - T5-Compact (54.9M), BERT-Compact (35M), and Pegasus-Compact (318M) - while assessing the impact of forward KL divergence, reverse KL divergence, and intermediate layer matching.Our findings demonstrate that forward KL divergence with intermediate layer matching is best suited for text classification and question answering, while reverse KL divergence with intermediate layer matching is optimal for text generation and summarization. The student models achieve significant reductions in parameters while maintaining performance close to their respective teacher models. This highlights the potential of white-box KD as an effective strategy for LLM distillation, offering a scalable approach for deploying efficient models in edge devices and resource-constrained environments.  © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Evaluating distillation methods for data-efficient syntax learning
Source title: EMNLP 2025 - 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, Findings of EMNLP 2025
Affiliations: Stanford University, United States; Princeton University, United States; Yale University, United States
Authors with affiliations: Yamakoshi T., Stanford University, United States; Griffiths T.L., Princeton University, United States; McCoy R.T., Yale University, United States; Hawkins R.D., Stanford University, United States
Abstract: Data-efficient training requires strong inductive biases. To the extent that transformer attention matrices encode syntactic relationships, we would predict that knowledge distillation (KD) targeting attention should selectively accelerate syntax acquisition relative to conventional logit-based KD. To test this hypothesis, we train GPT-2 student models on datasets ranging from 10K to 5M sentences using both distillation methods, evaluating them on both syntactic benchmarks and perplexity. Surprisingly, while logit-based KD dramatically improves data-efficiency, attention-based KD provides minimal benefit even for syntactic tasks. This suggests that output distributions provide sufficient supervisory signal for syntax acquisition, indicating that syntactic knowledge may be distributed throughout the network rather than localized in attention patterns.1 ©2025 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Title: Task-Specific Bidirectional Knowledge Distillation: Transforming General Large Language Models into Lightweight Models
Source title: Proceedings of 2025 IEEE 26th China Conference on System Simulation Technology and its Applications, CCSSTA 2025
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Automation, Hefei, China
Authors with affiliations: Jin Z., University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Automation, Hefei, China; Wang Y., University of Science and Technology of China, Department of Automation, Hefei, China
Abstract: Large language models have shown impressive capabilities in natural language processing tasks, but their deployment is hindered by high computational costs and lack of domain specificity. Existing knowledge distillation methods, which transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, often fail to capture the nuances of specialized tasks owing to domain differences. To address this issue, we propose a task-specific bidirectional knowledge distillation (TBKD) method. This method fine-tunes the teacher model on domain-specific data to capture key features, and then distills it into a student model using bidirectional KL divergence, balancing coverage, and diversity. Experiments on a petrochemical fire prevention dataset show that our method achieves lower perplexity and higher BLEU scores than existing methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in compressing large language models while preserving task-specific performance. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Self-Evolution Knowledge Distillation for LLM-based Machine Translation
Source title: Proceedings - International Conference on Computational Linguistics, COLING
Affiliations: Nanjing University, China; The University of Sydney, Australia; China University of Petroleum (East China), China
Authors with affiliations: Song Y., Nanjing University, China; Ding L., The University of Sydney, Australia; Zan C., China University of Petroleum (East China), China; Huang S., Nanjing University, China
Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has shown great promise in transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models. However, existing KD strategies for large language models often minimize output distributions between student and teacher models indiscriminately for each token. This overlooks the imbalanced nature of tokens and their varying transfer difficulties. In response, we propose a distillation strategy called Self-Evolution KD. The core of this approach involves dynamically integrating teacher distribution and one-hot distribution of ground truth into the student distribution as prior knowledge, which promotes the distillation process. It adjusts the ratio of prior knowledge based on token learning difficulty, fully leveraging the teacher model's potential. Experimental results show our method brings an average improvement of approximately 1.4 SacreBLEU points across four translation directions in the WMT22 test sets. Further analysis indicates that the improvement comes from better knowledge transfer from teachers, confirming our hypothesis. © 2025 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Title: Large Language Model-based Multimodal Knowledge Distillation: A Review of Methodologies and Applications
Source title: 9th SLAAI - International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, SLAAI-ICAI 2025
Affiliations: Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka, Faculty of Graduate Studies, Belihuloya, Sri Lanka; Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka, Department of Software Engineering, Belihuloya, Sri Lanka; University of Ruhuna Galle, Department of Interdisciplinary Studies, Sri Lanka; Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka, Department of Physical Sciences and Technology, Belihuloya, Sri Lanka

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become essential to the development of multimodal AI, enabling the creation of systems capable of understanding and combining information from text, images, audio, and video. Despite their impressive capabilities, these models are often difficult to implement in practice due to their high processing and memory requirements. Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a promising solution: a large teacher model transfers its knowledge to a smaller student model, creating leaner, faster, and more practical systems without loss of accuracy. This article provides a systematic review of recent work on multimodal KD for LLMs, focusing on both the technical methods and their applications. Based on the PRISMA guidelines, 46 studies published between 2024 and 2025 were analyzed, covering approaches such as the teacher-student framework, parametrically efficient methods like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), pre-trained pipelines, and compression strategies including pruning and quantization. This review highlights that KD offers clear efficiency advantages, but challenges remain in areas such as handling noise or data diversity, reliance on synthetic labels, and evaluation practices often limited to accuracy alone. Applications in healthcare, social media analytics, and audiovisual segmentation demonstrate the potential of KD, but also reveal its shortcomings in terms of robustness and reproducibility. By mapping these methods into a structured taxonomy and identifying their limitations, this review opens prospects for the reproducibility, customization, and scalable implementation of multimodal KD with LLM.  © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Toward hybrid teaching intelligence: investigating the potential of teacher–AI collaboration using large language models
Source title: Behaviour and Information Technology
Affiliations: Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway
Authors with affiliations: Rokkones R.K., Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway; Giannakos M., Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway
Abstract: This study examines Norwegian teachers’ dispositions regarding the use of large language models (LLMs) to support their teaching. To achieve this, we conducted a qualitative exploratory study that employed semi-structured interviews. Specifically, we interviewed 13 Norwegian school teachers with previous experience in artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled learning systems, and asked them about their understanding and concerns regarding the use of LLMs in education. The coding of the interview corpus suggests that teachers have diverse opinions on the use of LLMs for teaching, and, in some areas, lack knowledge and require further training and support. At the same time, they perceive LLMs as an opportunity for specific teaching tasks, such as marking and personalised learning. Maintaining agency is perceived as an extremely important quality for successful and symmetric teacher–LLM collaboration. Moreover, we identify challenges relating to a lack of reliable evidence on the effectiveness of LLMs, as well as a need for clarity concerning the legal frameworks that control how LLMs collect and use teacher and student data. We discuss the findings of the work and elaborate on its implications and areas for future research in the context of hybrid teaching intelligence. © 2025 The Author(s).
